questions.name: #1 Happy New Year
questions.en:
Happy New Year!
And if you’ve been away from work for a few days, you deserve some time off.
After all, you’ve traveled far.
Even if you just stayed at home.
According to NASA, just by being on the planet Earth in the last year, you’ve zipped about 584 million miles around the sun.
At an average speed of about 67,000 miles per hour.
Hey, I wasn’t speeding—in my inertial reference frame.
Of course, the trip was not a perfect circle.
As Kepler showed, the Earth’s orbit is an ellipse ,with the sun at one of the two focal points.
He also figured out the planet goes faster when it’s at perihelion, nearer the sun, than when it’s at aphelion, its furthest distance.
Which would explain why summer seems to zip by, except that the seasons are a function of the tilt of the Earth’s axis ,not its different distances from the sun.
And the Earth rotated 365 and a quarter times during its sweep around the sun.
The trip took 8,766 hours.
Or 525,960 minutes.
Or 31,557,600 seconds.

sense_groups.english: The trip took 8,766 hours.

sense_groups.english: Or 525,960 minutes.

questions.name: #2 Woodpecker
questions.en:
Humans can recognize each other by voice alone.
I sound different from other 60-Second Science reporters, for example.
In fact, lots of nonhuman animals, of all types, use voices to distinguish familiar individuals, including frogs, fish, lemurs, and penguins.
And that ______ audio fingerprint extends to a sound you may have heard in the forest on occasion: the drumming of a woodpecker.
Researchers recorded ______ drum rolls, from 41 great spotted woodpeckers—colorful red, white and black birds—living in Polish forests.
They then used audio software to analyze them.
And they found that the length of the drumrolls, and the spacing between beats varied enough from bird to bird to tell the woodpeckers apart by drumming alone.
The study is in the journal PLOS ONE.
The scientists say this fact might be useful to woodpeckers, in ______ each other.
And to ______ biologists, trying to tease one bird from another in a recording, for example, to count individuals in a given area.
The birds' head-banging could thus do away with that research headache.
questions.full:
Humans can recognize each other by voice alone.
I sound different from other 60-Second Science reporters, for example.
In fact, lots of nonhuman animals, of all types, use voices to distinguish familiar individuals, including frogs, fish, lemurs, and penguins.
And that ______ audio fingerprint extends to a sound you may have heard in the forest on occasion: the drumming of a woodpecker.
Researchers recorded ______ drum rolls, from 41 great spotted woodpeckers—colorful red, white and black birds—living in Polish forests.
They then used audio software to analyze them.
And they found that the length of the drumrolls, and the spacing between beats varied enough from bird to bird to tell the woodpeckers apart by drumming alone.
The study is in the journal PLOS ONE.
The scientists say this fact might be useful to woodpeckers, in ______ each other.
And to ______ biologists, trying to tease one bird from another in a recording, for example, to count individuals in a given area.
The birds' head-banging could thus do away with that research headache.

答案:
1. unique
2. multiple
3. identifying
4. conservation

sense_groups.english: Humans can recognize each other by voice alone.
sense_groups.chinese: 人类仅凭声音就能认出彼此。

sense_groups.english: I sound different from other 60-Second Science reporters, for example.
sense_groups.chinese: 比如，我的声音就和其他《60秒科学》记者不同。

sense_groups.english: In fact, lots of nonhuman animals, of all types, use voices to distinguish familiar individuals, including frogs, fish, lemurs, and penguins.
sense_groups.chinese: 事实上，许多非人类动物，各种类型的，都用声音来区分熟悉的个体，包括青蛙、鱼、狐猴和企鹅。

sense_groups.english: And that unique audio fingerprint extends to a sound you may have heard in the forest on occasion: the drumming of a woodpecker.
sense_groups.chinese: 而这种独特的音频指纹也延伸到了你偶尔在森林里听到的一种声音：啄木鸟的敲击声。

sense_groups.english: Researchers recorded multiple drum rolls, from 41 great spotted woodpeckers—colorful red, white and black birds—living in Polish forests.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员记录了生活在波兰森林中的41只大斑啄木鸟（红白黑相间的彩色鸟类）的多次敲击声。

sense_groups.english: They then used audio software to analyze them.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后他们用音频软件进行分析。

sense_groups.english: And they found that the length of the drumrolls, and the spacing between beats varied enough from bird to bird to tell the woodpeckers apart by drumming alone.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，敲击声的长度和节拍之间的间隔在不同鸟类之间差异足够大，仅凭敲击声就能区分啄木鸟。

sense_groups.english: The study is in the journal PLOS ONE.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《公共科学图书馆·综合》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: The scientists say this fact might be useful to woodpeckers, in identifying each other.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家表示，这一事实可能对啄木鸟识别彼此有用。

sense_groups.english: And to conservation biologists, trying to tease one bird from another in a recording, for example, to count individuals in a given area.
sense_groups.chinese: 对保护生物学家也有用，比如在录音中区分不同的鸟，以统计特定区域内的个体数量。

sense_groups.english: The birds' head-banging could thus do away with that research headache.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，鸟类的这种敲击行为可以消除研究中的这一难题。

questions.name: #3 El Niño
questions.en:
Parts of the planet warm and cool during El Niño and La Niña.
And infectious ______ also wax and wane in step with the climate cycle.
Take malaria—shown to spike in northern Venezuela during cool, La Niña conditions.
Or flu pandemics, which often follow months after La Niña sets in.
Now researchers have linked another public health risk to El Niño climate cycling: poisonous viper bites.
Their study area was Costa Rica—where health centers keep rigorous records on snakebites.
They compared nine years of those snakebite records—including some 6,500 bites—to climate data over the same period.
And they found that ______ were two to three times as prevalent in the hottest and coldest years of the El Niño climate cycle.
Sounds counterintuitive, right —you might expect the climate extremes to have opposite effects.
But the researchers say in hot, dry years, plant productivity peaks, driving an ______ in the number of rodents—aka snake food, potentially increasing the number of snakes.
And snakes tend to move around more in hot, dry weather—increasing chances they'll encounter—and attack—an unlucky farmer.
In cold, wet years, on the other hand, prey numbers plummet—forcing snakes to travel beyond their usual slithering grounds to eat—again increasing chances of an unlucky meeting.
The study is in the journal Science Advances.
The researchers also found two more variables that ______ strongly with Costa Ricans' odds of being bit: poverty and destitute housing.
A reminder that, when it comes to dangers from environmental disruption, it's often the least ______ who are at the greatest risk.
questions.full:
Parts of the planet warm and cool during El Niño and La Niña.
And infectious ______ also wax and wane in step with the climate cycle.
Take malaria—shown to spike in northern Venezuela during cool, La Niña conditions.
Or flu pandemics, which often follow months after La Niña sets in.
Now researchers have linked another public health risk to El Niño climate cycling: poisonous viper bites.
Their study area was Costa Rica—where health centers keep rigorous records on snakebites.
They compared nine years of those snakebite records—including some 6,500 bites—to climate data over the same period.
And they found that ______ were two to three times as prevalent in the hottest and coldest years of the El Niño climate cycle.
Sounds counterintuitive, right —you might expect the climate extremes to have opposite effects.
But the researchers say in hot, dry years, plant productivity peaks, driving an ______ in the number of rodents—aka snake food, potentially increasing the number of snakes.
And snakes tend to move around more in hot, dry weather—increasing chances they'll encounter—and attack—an unlucky farmer.
In cold, wet years, on the other hand, prey numbers plummet—forcing snakes to travel beyond their usual slithering grounds to eat—again increasing chances of an unlucky meeting.
The study is in the journal Science Advances.
The researchers also found two more variables that ______ strongly with Costa Ricans' odds of being bit: poverty and destitute housing.
A reminder that, when it comes to dangers from environmental disruption, it's often the least ______ who are at the greatest risk.

答案:
1. diseases
2. snakebites
3. increase
4. correlate
5. fortunate

sense_groups.english: Parts of the planet warm and cool during El Niño and La Niña.
sense_groups.chinese: 在厄尔尼诺和拉尼娜现象期间，地球的部分地区会变暖和变冷。

sense_groups.english: And infectious diseases also wax and wane in step with the climate cycle.
sense_groups.chinese: 传染病也会随着气候周期而增减。

sense_groups.english: Take malaria—shown to spike in northern Venezuela during cool, La Niña conditions.
sense_groups.chinese: 以疟疾为例——研究表明，在凉爽的拉尼娜条件下，委内瑞拉北部的疟疾发病率会激增。

sense_groups.english: Or flu pandemics, which often follow months after La Niña sets in.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者流感大流行，通常会在拉尼娜现象出现几个月后发生。

sense_groups.english: Now researchers have linked another public health risk to El Niño climate cycling: poisonous viper bites.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，研究人员将另一种公共卫生风险与厄尔尼诺气候周期联系起来：毒蛇咬伤。

sense_groups.english: Their study area was Costa Rica—where health centers keep rigorous records on snakebites.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们的研究区域是哥斯达黎加——那里的健康中心对蛇咬伤有严格的记录。

sense_groups.english: They compared nine years of those snakebite records—including some 6,500 bites—to climate data over the same period.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们将九年的蛇咬伤记录（包括约6500次咬伤）与同一时期的气候数据进行了比较。

sense_groups.english: And they found that snakebites were two to three times as prevalent in the hottest and coldest years of the El Niño climate cycle.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，在厄尔尼诺气候周期中最热和最冷的年份，蛇咬伤的发病率是其他年份的两到三倍。

sense_groups.english: Sounds counterintuitive, right —you might expect the climate extremes to have opposite effects.
sense_groups.chinese: 听起来违反直觉，对吧——你可能会认为极端气候会产生相反的效果。

sense_groups.english: But the researchers say in hot, dry years, plant productivity peaks, driving an increase in the number of rodents—aka snake food, potentially increasing the number of snakes.
sense_groups.chinese: 但研究人员表示，在炎热干燥的年份，植物生产力达到顶峰，导致啮齿动物（也就是蛇的食物）数量增加，从而可能增加蛇的数量。

sense_groups.english: And snakes tend to move around more in hot, dry weather—increasing chances they'll encounter—and attack—an unlucky farmer.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且蛇在炎热干燥的天气里更活跃，增加了它们遇到并攻击不幸农民的机会。

sense_groups.english: In cold, wet years, on the other hand, prey numbers plummet—forcing snakes to travel beyond their usual slithering grounds to eat—again increasing chances of an unlucky meeting.
sense_groups.chinese: 另一方面，在寒冷潮湿的年份，猎物数量骤减，迫使蛇离开它们通常的活动范围去寻找食物，这同样增加了不幸相遇的机会。

sense_groups.english: The study is in the journal Science Advances.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《科学进展》杂志上。

sense_groups.english: The researchers also found two more variables that correlate strongly with Costa Ricans' odds of being bit: poverty and destitute housing.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员还发现了另外两个与哥斯达黎加人被咬几率密切相关的变量：贫困和破败的住房。

sense_groups.english: A reminder that, when it comes to dangers from environmental disruption, it's often the least fortunate who are at the greatest risk.
sense_groups.chinese: 这提醒我们，在环境破坏带来的危险面前，往往是最不幸的人面临最大的风险。

questions.name: #4 Vaccine
questions.en:
In the ______ vaccine wars, I'm siding with actress Amanda Peet.
And comedian Bill Maher, well, I like your show, but when it comes to vaccines you don't know a punchline from a clothesline.
Maher recently tweeted to his Twitter followers "if u get a swine flu shot ur an idiot." On his HBO program Real Time last week, Maher went head-to-head with former Senator Dr. Bill Frist, who patiently ______ why vaccines were in fact good.
But Maher wasn't buying it.
He advocates a healthy lifestyle over vaccines.
But polio and smallpox outmatched many robust immune systems.
Actress Amanda Peet, meanwhile, has used her celebrity to encourage vaccinations, specifically in response to the alleged vaccine-autism connection, for which there's no scientific evidence, but which has some parents afraid of ______ vaccinations.
In a letter to a parenting magazine, Peet wrote: (quote)"It's ______ to suggest that virtually the entire medical community, and the CDC, and the American Academy of Pediatrics are behind a massive cover-up about vaccine safety."(end quote) See you in the line for the flu shot.
questions.full:
In the ______ vaccine wars, I'm siding with actress Amanda Peet.
And comedian Bill Maher, well, I like your show, but when it comes to vaccines you don't know a punchline from a clothesline.
Maher recently tweeted to his Twitter followers "if u get a swine flu shot ur an idiot." On his HBO program Real Time last week, Maher went head-to-head with former Senator Dr. Bill Frist, who patiently ______ why vaccines were in fact good.
But Maher wasn't buying it.
He advocates a healthy lifestyle over vaccines.
But polio and smallpox outmatched many robust immune systems.
Actress Amanda Peet, meanwhile, has used her celebrity to encourage vaccinations, specifically in response to the alleged vaccine-autism connection, for which there's no scientific evidence, but which has some parents afraid of ______ vaccinations.
In a letter to a parenting magazine, Peet wrote: (quote)"It's ______ to suggest that virtually the entire medical community, and the CDC, and the American Academy of Pediatrics are behind a massive cover-up about vaccine safety."(end quote) See you in the line for the flu shot.

答案:
1. celebrity
2. explained
3. childhood
4. irresponsible

sense_groups.english: In the ______ vaccine wars, I'm siding with actress Amanda Peet.
sense_groups.chinese: 在______疫苗战争中，我站在女演员阿曼达·皮特一边。

sense_groups.english: And comedian Bill Maher, well, I like your show, but when it comes to vaccines you don't know a punchline from a clothesline.
sense_groups.chinese: 至于喜剧演员比尔·马赫，嗯，我喜欢你的节目，但说到疫苗，你分不清笑点和晾衣绳。

sense_groups.english: Maher recently tweeted to his Twitter followers "if u get a swine flu shot ur an idiot."
sense_groups.chinese: 马赫最近在推特上对他的粉丝说：“如果你打猪流感疫苗，你就是个白痴。”

sense_groups.english: On his HBO program Real Time last week, Maher went head-to-head with former Senator Dr. Bill Frist, who patiently ______ why vaccines were in fact good.
sense_groups.chinese: 上周在他的HBO节目《实时》中，马赫与前参议员比尔·弗里斯特博士正面交锋，弗里斯特耐心地______为什么疫苗实际上是有益的。

sense_groups.english: But Maher wasn't buying it.
sense_groups.chinese: 但马赫并不买账。

sense_groups.english: He advocates a healthy lifestyle over vaccines.
sense_groups.chinese: 他主张健康的生活方式胜过疫苗。

sense_groups.english: But polio and smallpox outmatched many robust immune systems.
sense_groups.chinese: 但脊髓灰质炎和天花曾击败了许多强大的免疫系统。

sense_groups.english: Actress Amanda Peet, meanwhile, has used her celebrity to encourage vaccinations, specifically in response to the alleged vaccine-autism connection, for which there's no scientific evidence, but which has some parents afraid of ______ vaccinations.
sense_groups.chinese: 与此同时，女演员阿曼达·皮特利用她的名人身份鼓励接种疫苗，特别是针对所谓的疫苗与自闭症之间的联系，这种联系没有科学证据，但却让一些家长害怕______疫苗接种。

sense_groups.english: In a letter to a parenting magazine, Peet wrote: (quote)"It's ______ to suggest that virtually the entire medical community, and the CDC, and the American Academy of Pediatrics are behind a massive cover-up about vaccine safety."(end quote)
sense_groups.chinese: 在一封给育儿杂志的信中，皮特写道：（引文）“认为几乎整个医学界、疾病控制中心和美国儿科学会都在大规模掩盖疫苗安全问题是______的。”（引文结束）

sense_groups.english: See you in the line for the flu shot.
sense_groups.chinese: 流感疫苗注射队伍里见。

questions.name: #5 Less Energy
questions.en:
Using less energy saves money and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
And various studies have looked at ways to get households to use less energy.
Now there's evidence that people in such a study use less energy…because they're in a study.
The general phenomenon is called the Hawthorne effect: study subjects change their ______ because they're being observed.
So ______ collaborated with a utility to test for the Hawthorne effect in electricity use.
They ______ almost 5,600 randomly ______ households.
Half received a postcard saying that their energy use would be monitored for a month for research purposes.
They also got four follow-up reminder postcards over the month.
They received no other information, instructions or incentives.
The control group monitored for the study got no notifications.
That group continued using the same amount of electricity.
But the families being tracked reduced energy use 2.7 percent.
And when the study period ended, their energy use shot back up.
The report is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Clearly, mindful consumers can find ways to easily lower their energy consumption.
Perhaps policy makers can find a way to use the Hawthorne effect to everyone's advantage.
questions.full:
Using less energy saves money and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
And various studies have looked at ways to get households to use less energy.
Now there's evidence that people in such a study use less energy…because they're in a study.
The general phenomenon is called the Hawthorne effect: study subjects change their ______ because they're being observed.
So ______ collaborated with a utility to test for the Hawthorne effect in electricity use.
They ______ almost 5,600 randomly ______ households.
Half received a postcard saying that their energy use would be monitored for a month for research purposes.
They also got four follow-up reminder postcards over the month.
They received no other information, instructions or incentives.
The control group monitored for the study got no notifications.
That group continued using the same amount of electricity.
But the families being tracked reduced energy use 2.7 percent.
And when the study period ended, their energy use shot back up.
The report is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Clearly, mindful consumers can find ways to easily lower their energy consumption.
Perhaps policy makers can find a way to use the Hawthorne effect to everyone's advantage.

答案:
1. behavior
2. researchers
3. monitored
4. selected

sense_groups.english: Using less energy saves money and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
sense_groups.chinese: 使用更少的能源可以省钱并减少温室气体排放。

sense_groups.english: And various studies have looked at ways to get households to use less energy.
sense_groups.chinese: 各种研究已经探索了让家庭减少能源使用的方法。

sense_groups.english: Now there's evidence that people in such a study use less energy…because they're in a study.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在有证据表明，参与这类研究的人会减少能源使用……因为他们正在被研究。

sense_groups.english: The general phenomenon is called the Hawthorne effect: study subjects change their behavior because they're being observed.
sense_groups.chinese: 这一普遍现象被称为霍桑效应：研究对象因为被观察而改变自己的行为。

sense_groups.english: So researchers collaborated with a utility to test for the Hawthorne effect in electricity use.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，研究人员与一家公用事业公司合作，测试电力使用中的霍桑效应。

sense_groups.english: They selected almost 5,600 randomly selected households.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们随机选择了近5600户家庭。

sense_groups.english: Half received a postcard saying that their energy use would be monitored for a month for research purposes.
sense_groups.chinese: 一半家庭收到明信片，告知他们的能源使用情况将因研究目的而被监测一个月。

sense_groups.english: They also got four follow-up reminder postcards over the month.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们还在一个月内收到了四张后续提醒明信片。

sense_groups.english: They received no other information, instructions or incentives.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们没有收到其他信息、指示或激励。

sense_groups.english: The control group monitored for the study got no notifications.
sense_groups.chinese: 作为研究对照组的家庭没有收到任何通知。

sense_groups.english: That group continued using the same amount of electricity.

sense_groups.english: But the families being tracked reduced energy use 2.7 percent.

sense_groups.english: The report is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

sense_groups.english: Clearly, mindful consumers can find ways to easily lower their energy consumption.

sense_groups.chinese: 也许政策制定者可以找到一种方法，利用霍桑效应造福所有人。

questions.name: #7 Light
questions.en:
It follows from the special theory of relativity that mass and energy are different manifestations of the same thing.
Now ______ have stopped light cold - and then brought it back to life - or light - in an ______ different place.
The Harvard researchers sent a light pulse into a sodium cloud cooled to about 460 degrees below zero.
That's the ______ point where matter stops all movement.
The light pulse was compressed by a factor of about 50 million at the extreme temperature, and it actually changed state - sort of like frozen water.
But it also split into two forms of matter.
One stayed frozen in the sodium, while the other crawled along at just 200 meters per hour.
That second form - called a matter wave - contains the exact information of the original light wave.
And when researchers sent it into a second sodium cloud a fraction of a ______ away, the wave was converted back into light.
And since fiber-optic ______ use light, that means that someday we may be able to stop them, store them and turn them back on, just like a light switch.
questions.full:
It follows from the special theory of relativity that mass and energy are different manifestations of the same thing.
Now ______ have stopped light cold - and then brought it back to life - or light - in an ______ different place.
The Harvard researchers sent a light pulse into a sodium cloud cooled to about 460 degrees below zero.
That's the ______ point where matter stops all movement.
The light pulse was compressed by a factor of about 50 million at the extreme temperature, and it actually changed state - sort of like frozen water.
But it also split into two forms of matter.
One stayed frozen in the sodium, while the other crawled along at just 200 meters per hour.
That second form - called a matter wave - contains the exact information of the original light wave.
And when researchers sent it into a second sodium cloud a fraction of a ______ away, the wave was converted back into light.
And since fiber-optic ______ use light, that means that someday we may be able to stop them, store them and turn them back on, just like a light switch.

答案:
1. researchers
2. entirely
3. theoretical
4. millimeter
5. communications

sense_groups.english: It follows from the special theory of relativity that mass and energy are different manifestations of the same thing.
sense_groups.chinese: 根据狭义相对论，质量和能量是同一事物的不同表现形式。

sense_groups.english: Now researchers have stopped light cold - and then brought it back to life - or light - in an entirely different place.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，研究人员将光完全停止——然后又在完全不同的地方让它复活——或者说让光复活。

sense_groups.english: The Harvard researchers sent a light pulse into a sodium cloud cooled to about 460 degrees below zero.
sense_groups.chinese: 哈佛大学的研究人员将一束光脉冲射入冷却到约零下460度的钠云中。

sense_groups.english: That's the theoretical point where matter stops all movement.
sense_groups.chinese: 那是理论上物质停止所有运动的点。

sense_groups.english: The light pulse was compressed by a factor of about 50 million at the extreme temperature, and it actually changed state - sort of like frozen water.
sense_groups.chinese: 在极端温度下，光脉冲被压缩了约5000万倍，并且实际上改变了状态——有点像结冰的水。

sense_groups.english: But it also split into two forms of matter.
sense_groups.chinese: 但它也分裂成两种物质形式。

sense_groups.english: One stayed frozen in the sodium, while the other crawled along at just 200 meters per hour.
sense_groups.chinese: 一种停留在钠中冻结，而另一种则以每小时仅200米的速度缓慢移动。

sense_groups.english: That second form - called a matter wave - contains the exact information of the original light wave.
sense_groups.chinese: 第二种形式——称为物质波——包含原始光波的精确信息。

sense_groups.english: And when researchers sent it into a second sodium cloud a fraction of a millimeter away, the wave was converted back into light.
sense_groups.chinese: 当研究人员将其送入仅相隔几分之一毫米的第二个钠云时，该波被转换回光。

sense_groups.english: And since fiber-optic communications use light, that means that someday we may be able to stop them, store them and turn them back on, just like a light switch.
sense_groups.chinese: 由于光纤通信使用光，这意味着有一天我们可能能够像电灯开关一样停止、存储和重新开启它们。

questions.name: #8 Music Evolution
questions.en:
That's Generation Zero of DarwinTunes.
It's a Web site ______ are using to study how ______ preferences affect the evolution of music.
A new study claims that the taste of the public exerts a force on music similar to natural selection.
The findings support the theory that culture and art are shaped not only by their producers, but by consumers too.
The report is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Researchers created short tunes and allowed them to procreate—that is, they'd combine aspects of the parent tunes to produce a new ______ of music.
User ratings on the ______ site provided the evolutionary selection, with only the most appealing tunes allowed to create progeny.
The researchers found that quality ______ quickly at the beginning: the random sounds rapidly gave rise to ______ an awful lot like music.
Here's generation 600.
But after a while things stagnated.
The researchers plan to update the program to drive evolution further.
Meanwhile, here's DarwinTunes generation 3000.
questions.answer:
1. researchers
2. listener
3. generation
4. DarwinTunes
5. increased
6. something

sense_groups.english: That's Generation Zero of DarwinTunes.
sense_groups.chinese: 那是达尔文调频的零代。

sense_groups.english: It's a Web site ______ are using to study how ______ preferences affect the evolution of music.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是一个网站，研究人员用它来研究听众的偏好如何影响音乐的进化。

sense_groups.english: A new study claims that the taste of the public exerts a force on music similar to natural selection.
sense_groups.chinese: 一项新研究声称，公众的品味对音乐施加了一种类似于自然选择的力量。

sense_groups.english: The findings support the theory that culture and art are shaped not only by their producers, but by consumers too.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些发现支持了这样一种理论：文化和艺术不仅由其生产者塑造，也由消费者塑造。

sense_groups.english: The report is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
sense_groups.chinese: 该报告发表在《美国国家科学院院刊》上。

sense_groups.english: Researchers created short tunes and allowed them to procreate—that is, they'd combine aspects of the parent tunes to produce a new ______ of music.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员创作了短曲调，并允许它们繁殖——也就是说，它们会结合父辈曲调的特点，产生新一代的音乐。

sense_groups.english: User ratings on the ______ site provided the evolutionary selection, with only the most appealing tunes allowed to create progeny.
sense_groups.chinese: 用户在该网站上的评分提供了进化选择，只有最吸引人的曲调才能产生后代。

sense_groups.english: The researchers found that quality ______ quickly at the beginning: the random sounds rapidly gave rise to ______ an awful lot like music.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员发现，质量一开始迅速提高：随机的声音很快产生了听起来很像音乐的东西。

sense_groups.english: Here's generation 600.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是第600代。

sense_groups.english: But after a while things stagnated.
sense_groups.chinese: 但过了一段时间，事情停滞不前了。

sense_groups.english: The researchers plan to update the program to drive evolution further.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员计划更新程序以推动进一步进化。

sense_groups.english: Meanwhile, here's DarwinTunes generation 3000.
sense_groups.chinese: 与此同时，这是达尔文调频的第3000代。

questions.name: #9 HIW
questions.en:
I once took part in a vodka tasting contest, in which participants tried to tell an expensive brand from a cheap one.
I don't recall the exact outcome, for obvious reasons.
But I do know that several people swore they could taste the difference.
Well, maybe they could.
Because according to a study in the Journal of ______ and Food Chemistry, ______ vodkas can have different molecular "structures," which could drive drinkers to favor one brand over another.
Vodka's an ______ beverage that's supposed to be relatively flavorless.
So researchers got to wondering: how come people who enjoy the stuff often express brand preference?
Being good little scientists, they trotted out their ______ equipment and examined the ______ signatures of five different vodkas.
What they found is that each brand differs in how its ethanol molecules cluster.
In the ethanol-water mix we call vodka, some of the ethanol molecules get surrounded by a sort of "cage" made of water.
And different brands differ in how much ethanol is caged.
Vodkas with fewer cages might seem more "watery" than those with more structure.
Of course, drink enough of the stuff and it really won't matter how tightly caged it is.
You'll be loose as a grey goose.

questions.name: #10 Snack Sample
questions.en:
If you’ve spent any time hitting up the giant wholesalers or other markets this holiday season, you’ve probably figured out that you can make a full meal out of those ______ little samples they often dish out.
Which seems like a good thing, for you…and for your wallet.
But a new study shows that these tempting little treats really do entice you to buy what you try…and maybe some other stuff like it.
Researchers tracked the sales in half a dozen stores that provided samples of ______ in four categories: healthy, salty, frozen, or branded by a large coffee-shop chain.
They found that nothing while shopping convinces consumers to buy the ______ product more often than does simply seeing the product displayed at the end of the aisle.
They also found that repeating the sample offering multiple times translates into sustained interest in the product…and that stores that have a smaller assortment of products for sale benefit more than the warehouse-sized emporia.
The finding is served up in the Journal of Retailing.
The researchers also discovered that the effect extends beyond the product itself…such that, for example, nibbling on one brand of cookies makes you hungry for cookies in general—including those from competing brands.
Which suggests that a rising tide really does lift all boats.
Or at least that a tray of free taquitos will certainly lift a lot of shoppers’ spirits…and will keep those registers ringing well into the new year.

questions.name: #16 Article

I was asking myself this very question in the post office yesterday, standing in line waiting to sign for, as it so happens, an article.
A postal article.
Not the postal article.
Now before we get ahead of ourselves, an article in English is a ______ that precedes a noun, and simply indicates specificity.
This sounds quite complicated, and to be honest, it's quite complicated to say without spraying everyone within 15 feet, but the concept's quite simple.
The definite article in English is the word "the", and indicates a specific thing or type; for example, the train is an hour late.
By ______ , the indefinite article in English is any of the words "a", "an" or "some", and the indefinite article indicates a non-specific thing; for example, would you please pass me an apple.
We always ______ a word with "a" if it doesn't start with a vowel sound.
For example, take a hike; I'm spending a Weekend at Burnie's; or there's a Knight in Shining Armour.
Similarly, we precede words with the indefinite article "an" if they do start with a vowel sound, for example, an ostrich, an ______ mess or an Occupational Health and Safety Policy.

questions.name: #17 HIW
questions.en:
The term pygmy usually refers to a few groups of ______ people in ______ rain forest regions in Africa.
The existence of distinct populations of such people presented scientists with the opportunity to study the mechanisms by which typical human growth patterns have become altered there.
And they discovered that two groups became small in two ______ ways.
The study is in the journal Nature Communications.
The ______ collected data on some 500 members of a west African ethnic group called the Baka.
They discovered that Baka infants have a similar size range to most other infants, but have a low growth rate during their first two years, which produces a lasting effect.
This mechanism seems to be different from that of the east African groups called the Efé and Sua.
These peoples have slow ______ growth, so that the infants are born smaller.
The researchers say that the Baka population appears to have split from the Efé and Sua some 20,000 years ago.
The two different systems for achieving small stature—which appears to be advantageous in the equatorial rainforest environment—are thus an example of convergent evolution.
The researchers believe the findings say something important about human evolution and development in general: "Homo sapiens could therefore be characterized by its high ______ for growth plasticity during infancy.
This capacity, which may be unique to our species, may have played a fundamental role in the ______ adaptation that enabled its worldwide expansion and occupation of dissimilar environments within a short period after moving out of Africa."
questions.answer:

2. equatorial
3. different
4. researchers
5. prenatal
6. capacity
7. biological

sense_groups.english: The term pygmy usually refers to a few groups of short-statured people in equatorial rain forest regions in Africa.
sense_groups.chinese: ‘俾格米’一词通常指非洲赤道雨林地区的一些身材矮小的人群。

sense_groups.english: The existence of distinct populations of such people presented scientists with the opportunity to study the mechanisms by which typical human growth patterns have become altered there.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些独特人群的存在为科学家提供了研究典型人类生长模式如何改变的机会。

sense_groups.english: And they discovered that two groups became small in two different ways.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现两个群体以两种不同的方式变得矮小。

sense_groups.english: The study is in the journal Nature Communications.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《自然·通讯》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: The researchers collected data on some 500 members of a west African ethnic group called the Baka.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员收集了约500名西非巴卡族成员的数据。

sense_groups.english: They discovered that Baka infants have a similar size range to most other infants, but have a low growth rate during their first two years, which produces a lasting effect.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现巴卡婴儿的体型范围与大多数其他婴儿相似，但在头两年生长速度较慢，这产生了持久的影响。

sense_groups.english: This mechanism seems to be different from that of the east African groups called the Efé and Sua.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种机制似乎与东非的埃费族和苏阿族不同。

sense_groups.english: These peoples have slow prenatal growth, so that the infants are born smaller.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些人群的产前生长缓慢，因此婴儿出生时体型较小。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say that the Baka population appears to have split from the Efé and Sua some 20,000 years ago.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员表示，巴卡人似乎是在大约2万年前从埃费人和苏阿人中分离出来的。

sense_groups.english: The two different systems for achieving small stature—which appears to be advantageous in the equatorial rainforest environment—are thus an example of convergent evolution.
sense_groups.chinese: 这两种不同的矮小体型形成机制——在赤道雨林环境中似乎具有优势——因此是趋同进化的一个例子。

sense_groups.english: The researchers believe the findings say something important about human evolution and development in general: "Homo sapiens could therefore be characterized by its high capacity for growth plasticity during infancy.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员认为，这些发现总体上说明了人类进化和发展的重要方面：‘智人因此可以以其在婴儿期生长可塑性的高能力为特征。’

sense_groups.english: This capacity, which may be unique to our species, may have played a fundamental role in the biological adaptation that enabled its worldwide expansion and occupation of dissimilar environments within a short period after moving out of Africa."
sense_groups.chinese: 这种能力可能为我们人类所独有，在生物适应中发挥了基础性作用，使人类在走出非洲后的短时间内能够向全球扩张并占领不同环境。

sense_groups.english: It's an approach to pest control that's so crazy it just might work: convince the females that they're virgins.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是一种疯狂到可能有效的害虫控制方法：让雌性相信自己还是处女。

sense_groups.english: It would be useless as human birth control, of course, but the difference is that most female insects completely change their behavior after sex.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，这对人类避孕没用，但区别在于大多数雌性昆虫在交配后会完全改变行为。

sense_groups.english: For example, some mosquitoes suck blood.
sense_groups.chinese: 例如，有些蚊子会吸血。

sense_groups.english: Others lose interest in males and start laying eggs.
sense_groups.chinese: 其他的则对雄性失去兴趣，开始产卵。

sense_groups.english: What's behind this dramatic change in behavior?
sense_groups.chinese: 这种戏剧性的行为变化背后是什么？

sense_groups.english: Turns out it's a peptide in the males' seminal fluid.
sense_groups.chinese: 原来是一种雄性精液中的肽。

sense_groups.english: And now researchers in Vienna have found the females' receptor for this peptide.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在维也纳的研究人员找到了雌性对这种肽的受体。

sense_groups.english: They report online in Nature that fruitflies without the receptor lay many fewer eggs and continue to be interested in sex.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们在《自然》杂志在线报道，没有受体的果蝇产卵少得多，并且对性仍然感兴趣。

sense_groups.english: In other words, they act like virgins.
sense_groups.chinese: 换句话说，它们表现得像处女。

sense_groups.english: So, back to pest control.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以，回到害虫控制。

sense_groups.english: Most female insects should have this sort of receptor, including the kinds that spread disease and devastate crops.
sense_groups.chinese: 大多数雌性昆虫应该都有这种受体，包括那些传播疾病和破坏农作物的种类。

sense_groups.english: If we could deactivate it on a large scale, instead of fighting egg-laying blood-suckers, we could live in peace with born-again virgins.
sense_groups.chinese: 如果我们能大规模地使其失活，而不是与产卵的吸血者作斗争，我们就能与重生的处女和平共处。

In fact, for me, perhaps the most important subject there is.

And that's not the case in general.

Without evidence, anything goes.

Look at it!
Starts over here, ends over there.
It's uncommon sense that was needed to recognize that the Earth was turning on its axis.

We have to learn to be very careful and to question everything.

Put your hand up.
You've accepted it.
Almost nobody's put their hand up.
It's incredible.
Look at yourself, you've accepted this.

Find out what the evidence is for that, and find out what the evidence is for everything that you accept."

The frogs are tough New Yorkers—the center of their range appears to be Yankee Stadium.

questions.name: #25 HIW
questions.en:
Modern humans are masters of multitasking.
We eat while driving, watch TV while studying, and of course talk on our cell phones while doing, well, everything.
How do we do it?
A study in the July 16th issue of Neuron suggests that though we can train our brains to work faster as we juggle, we never actually manage to do more than one thing at a time.
Our brains aren't really built to handle the sort of parallel processing we think we're capable of.
The good news is: studies have shown that ______ training can make us better at doing two things at once.
But how?
One theory is that with lots of practice some routines become "automatic." And if we don't need to run every little thing past the part of the brain that's spends time ______ about stuff, we can multitask just fine.
But this new study finds that that's not the way it works.
Turns out that ______ still consult the prefrontal cortex, but training gets the "Thinking Brain" to think a little faster.
So we're actually switching tasks quickly enough to appear to be doing them simultaneously.
Which is still nothing to shake a stick and sneeze at.

questions.name: #26 Mobile Phone
questions.en:
This year, the number of mobile phones on cell networks is remembered to surpass the Earth's population. "More people now own cell phones than actually have access to working toilets." James Meadow, a microbial ecologist at the University of Oregon. Hidden in the data is the reality that some people work on their phones…on toilets.
If that grosses you out, consider this: "So it turns out we're just really leaky animals. We just, we leave our linear everywhere we go." Including, of course, our phones.
Meadow and his colleagues took a census of the bacteria on thumbs and index fingers of 17 volunteers—and on their smartphone touch screens. Overall, they ID'ed more than 7,000 types.
Looking at just the most common bacteria, those that appear more than 0.1 percent of the time, they found an 82 percent similarity between the overtones of fingers and phones. Meaning our phones are a pretty good mirror of ourselves, microbially, at least. The results appear in the journal PeerJ.
"We have always been covered in bacteria… and we will always be covered in bacteria." So the fact that our phones are also covered in bacteria is no reason for concern. In fact, the reasoners say that mobile phones may hold untapped potential as poison microbiome sensors.

questions.en:
Ah, daydreaming.
Is there anything more ______ than sitting back and letting your thoughts drift?
Well, yes: not letting your thoughts drift, for one.
Because according to a study published in the journal Science, people are least happy when their minds wander.
Humans, to a degree unmatched by other animals, are capable of ______ about things outside the here and now—something that happened yesterday, or ______ they hope will happen tomorrow.
It's that sort of itinerant ______ that allows us to plan and to learn.
But at what cost?
Psychologists at Harvard used an iPhone app to find out.
At random times throughout the day, the program asked some 2,200 participants what they were doing, what they were thinking about and how they felt.
Turns out that people spend nearly half their waking hours thinking about something other than what they're doing.
And that whether and where their thoughts tend to stray is a better predictor of their feelings than what they're ______ up to.
The ______ conclude that a wandering mind is an unhappy mind.
So try to focus on, and live in, the present.
You might ______ that happiness is just being where it's happening.

4. intellect
5. actually
6. scientists

questions.name: #28 HIW
questions.en:
Medicinal tablets are nothing new.
Doctors have been ______ pills for thousands of years.
And now archaeologists have turned up some of those ancient medicines, which were preserved in a shipwreck for close to two millennia.
The 2nd-century Pozzino wreck was discovered in 1974 off the coast of Italy.
It's cargo included medical ______ like a cupping vessel, iron probe, and tin boxes of supplies.
And in one of those boxes, researchers recovered five gray tablets.
Now, they've analyzed the antique medication.
The work is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The pills primarily contained zinc compounds, probably the active medicinal ingredients.
But researchers also detected starch, pollen, charcoal, fats and linen fibers.
Those fibers helped the tablets hold their round, loaf-like shape, which may be the key to the medication's use: the Greek word meaning "small round loaves" also inspired the word collyrium, or eye-wash.
The pills were probably either ______ in liquid or ground into a powder and used to treat eye conditions.
Who knows, maybe Hippocrates used them on his pupils.

questions.full:

One of the latest ______ to the tree of life is a new type of leopard frog.
Which might sound unremarkable, except for where it was found: New York City.

Those results appear in the journal Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.

sense_groups.english: Scientists discover new species all the time — on the order of 15,000 a year.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家们一直在发现新物种——每年大约有15000个。

sense_groups.english: One of the latest additions to the tree of life is a new type of leopard frog.
sense_groups.chinese: 生命之树的最新成员之一是一种新型豹蛙。

sense_groups.english: Which might sound unremarkable, except for where it was found: New York City.
sense_groups.chinese: 这听起来可能没什么特别，除了它被发现的地点：纽约市。

sense_groups.english: But how does a frog go unnoticed in the Big Apple?
sense_groups.chinese: 但一只青蛙怎么会在纽约市被忽视呢？

sense_groups.english: Well even experts have a hard time telling this new species from its northern and southern cousins on looks alone.
sense_groups.chinese: 即使是专家也很难仅凭外表区分这个新物种和它的北方及南方近亲。

sense_groups.english: But the new guy has a different croak, which raised ecologists' suspicions.
sense_groups.chinese: 但这个新家伙的叫声不同，这引起了生态学家的怀疑。

sense_groups.english: So they tracked down four leopard frog populations with the unique call — including one within view of the Statue of Liberty — and took DNA samples.
sense_groups.chinese: 于是他们追踪了四个有这种独特叫声的豹蛙种群——包括一个在自由女神像视野内的——并采集了DNA样本。

sense_groups.english: They had a genetic ancestry of their own — earning them new species status.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们有自己的遗传祖先——这使它们获得了新物种的地位。

sense_groups.english: Those results appear in the journal Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些结果发表在《分子系统发育与进化》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: The frogs are tough New Yorkers — the center of their range appears to be Yankee Stadium.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些青蛙是坚韧的纽约客——它们的分布中心似乎是洋基体育场。

sense_groups.english: But the researchers say that the urban amphibians face threats like pesticides and infectious diseases.
sense_groups.chinese: 但研究人员表示，这些城市两栖动物面临杀虫剂和传染病等威胁。

sense_groups.english: Not to mention real-life games of Frogger.
sense_groups.chinese: 更不用说现实版的《青蛙过河》游戏了。

questions.full:
It's good to keep on your toes.
Metaphorically, that is.
Not when you're ______ out for a stroll.

sense_groups.english: It's good to keep on your toes.
sense_groups.chinese: 保持警觉是好的。

sense_groups.english: Metaphorically, that is.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，这是比喻的说法。

sense_groups.english: Not when you're actually out for a stroll.
sense_groups.chinese: 但当你真的出去散步时，就不必了。

sense_groups.english: Because a new study suggests that it takes nearly twice as much energy to walk on your toes than it does to land on your heel.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为一项新研究表明，用脚尖走路比用脚跟着地要多消耗近一倍的能量。

sense_groups.english: Humans are among a small handful of animals that tend to strut heel-to-toe.
sense_groups.chinese: 人类是少数几种倾向于脚跟到脚尖走路的动物之一。

sense_groups.english: Chimps and other apes do it, as do bears.
sense_groups.chinese: 黑猩猩和其他猿类也是如此，熊也一样。

sense_groups.english: But most critters bounce on the balls of their feet—think cats and dogs—while others trot on their toes, like horses and deer.
sense_groups.chinese: 但大多数动物用脚掌弹跳——比如猫和狗——而其他动物用脚尖小跑，比如马和鹿。

sense_groups.english: To find out whether our gait gives us any advantages, scientists asked 27 volunteers to walk on a treadmill all three ways: heel-first, ball-of-the-foot first, or up on tippy toes.
sense_groups.chinese: 为了查明我们的步态是否有优势，科学家让27名志愿者在跑步机上以三种方式行走：脚跟着地、脚掌着地或踮着脚尖。

sense_groups.english: The participants also wore face masks that enabled the researchers to measure their oxygen consumption.
sense_groups.chinese: 参与者还戴着面罩，以便研究人员测量他们的耗氧量。

sense_groups.english: The results: the subjects walking on the balls of their feet, in addition to looking ridiculous, expended 50 percent more energy.

sense_groups.english: The ones prancing on their toes needed 83 percent more energy.
sense_groups.chinese: 那些踮着脚尖走路的人需要多消耗83%的能量。

questions.full:
In vitro ______ efforts can be helped by, oddly enough, oral contraceptives.
That's the finding from Tel Aviv University, site of the largest study on using birth control to help IVF.

sense_groups.english: In vitro fertilization efforts can be helped by, oddly enough, oral contraceptives.
sense_groups.chinese: 体外受精的努力，奇怪的是，可以通过口服避孕药得到帮助。

sense_groups.english: That's the finding from Tel Aviv University, site of the largest study on using birth control to help IVF.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是特拉维夫大学的发现，该大学进行了关于使用避孕药帮助试管婴儿的最大规模研究。

sense_groups.english: One of the challenges to IVF is timing.
sense_groups.chinese: 试管婴儿的挑战之一是时机。

sense_groups.english: Current hormone treatments to stimulate ovulation have to coincide with a particular moment in the woman's cycle.
sense_groups.chinese: 目前刺激排卵的激素治疗必须与女性周期的特定时刻相吻合。

sense_groups.english: Not knowing the exact timing for scheduling the egg retrieval and fertilization can be stressful, which can lower the odds of success.
sense_groups.chinese: 不知道安排取卵和受精的确切时间可能会带来压力，这会降低成功几率。

sense_groups.english: In the Tel Aviv study, researchers looked at women who underwent a 12-to-17-day treatment of oral contraception.
sense_groups.chinese: 在特拉维夫的研究中，研究人员观察了接受12至17天口服避孕药治疗的女性。

sense_groups.english: The women were checked to make sure there was absolutely no activity in their ovaries or uterus.

sense_groups.english: Then they began stimulation hormones to start the clock.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后她们开始使用刺激激素来启动计时。

sense_groups.english: Women who went through this protocol had similar numbers of pregnancies to a control group that didn't use birth control.
sense_groups.chinese: 经历这一方案的女性与未使用避孕药的对照组怀孕数量相似。

sense_groups.english: Which means that oral contraception didn't harm their ability to conceive.
sense_groups.chinese: 这意味着口服避孕药没有损害她们的受孕能力。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say that this treatment demands a slightly longer cycle and higher levels of ovulation-inducing hormones.

sense_groups.english: But they also say it could allow couples to more accurately plan for procedures, which might give couples more peace of mind.

sense_groups.english: Some findings: evidence for cocaine use was primarily in urban areas, almost nonexistent in rural regions; ecstasy use tended toward urban areas as well, and only turned up in about half of all communities; meth was everywhere.

sense_groups.english: More important than those one-day snapshot findings, however, is that this methodology was proven viable, and could be used to track patterns of drug use in multiple regions over time.
sense_groups.chinese: 然而，比这些单日快照发现更重要的是，这种方法被证明是可行的，并且可以用于长期追踪多个地区的药物使用模式。

questions.name: #35 Howler Monkey
questions.en:
Howler monkeys.
From their Central and South American rainforest home, they produce some of the loudest animal calls in the world.
They're about the size of an adult cocker spaniel, but they can sound as large as a tiger.
Biologists have long ______ that the monkeys' howls played a role in attracting mates.
The sounds are like the auditory version of peacock feathers or deer antlers that say, hey, check me out.
And now we know that the quality of the howl depends on a bone near their throats called the hyoid.
The bigger the hyoid, the deeper the howl.
Males with deeper calls sound more attractive to females.
Which means that males with smaller hyoids had to come up with another strategy.
"When you're in the field and you look up at the monkeys, you notice that in Alouatta palliata, the mantled howler monkey, that the testes are huge.
And they're white, they're really obvious."
University of Utah anthropologist Leslie Knapp.
She and her team found that howler monkeys face an anatomical trade-off: a species can either have a really big hyoid bone, or it can be very well endowed.
But not both.
That finding is in the journal Current Biology.
Those species with bigger hyoids live in single-male groups, so it makes sense to invest in what the ______ call "precopulatory traits," that is, their courtship strategy of attracting the female's attention.
But in a species where groups include ______ males, the best way to ensure passing on more genes is to make more sperm—by building bigger testes.
The researchers say the finding is the first evidence for an ______ ______ between mating calls and sperm production.
And they warn that while human women do tend to prefer males with deeper voices, we men advertise ourselves in many other ways as well.
So don't go clicking that pop-up ad that ______ to enlarge your hyoid.
questions.answer:
1. suspected
2. researchers
3. multiple
4. evolutionary
5. trade-off
6. promises

questions.name: #36 Height
questions.en:
Height is correlated with a lot of things.
Up to a certain height, taller people make more money than the vertically challenged.
And the taller ______ ______ almost always wins.
Now a study finds that your height as an adult has a profound effect on your perception of your health.
Short people judge their health to be worse than average or tall people judge theirs.
The research was published in the journal ______ Endocrinology.
Data for the study came from the 2003 Health Survey for England.
More than 14,000 participants filled out questionnaires and had their heights measured.
The study only looked at how good the subject thought his or her health was, not their actual health.
Questions focused on five areas: mobility, self-care, normal activities, pain or ______ and anxiety or depression.
Men shorter than about 5'4" and women shorter than 5' reported the worst impressions.
But small increases in height at the low end had much bigger effects on perception than the same increases among taller people.
Other studies have shown, ironically, that shorter people on average actually live longer.

sense_groups.chinese: 而且更高的候选人几乎总是获胜。

sense_groups.chinese: 现在一项研究发现，成年后的身高对你对自己健康的看法有深远影响。

sense_groups.english: Short people judge their health to be worse than average or tall people judge theirs.
sense_groups.chinese: 矮个子认为自己的健康状况比平均身高或高个子的人差。

sense_groups.english: The research was published in the journal Clinical Endocrinology.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《临床内分泌学》期刊上。

sense_groups.chinese: 问题集中在五个方面：行动能力、自理能力、日常活动、疼痛或不适以及焦虑或抑郁。

sense_groups.english: But small increases in height at the low end had much bigger effects on perception than the same increases among taller people.

sense_groups.chinese: 讽刺的是，其他研究表明，矮个子平均寿命实际上更长。

questions.name: #37 HIW
questions.en:

The study is in the journal Science.

Try adding some heart.

questions.name: #38 HIW
questions.en:
If you're a city-dweller feeling a bit blue, you may want to consider going somewhere that's more green—even if it's still in a city.
Because moving to greener urban areas provides both ______ and sustained mental health benefits.
So says a study in the journal Environmental Science and Technology.
The effort is one of the few to look at the effects of green spaces over an extended period of time.
  ______ analyzed data from the British Household Panel Survey over a five-year period, ______ participants into two groups: those who moved to greener urban areas and those who moved to less green urban areas.
In the year after people moved to greener spaces, they experienced a significant boost in mental health markers, such as mood and confidence.
And the benefits ______ for the next two years, indicating a shift in their baseline mental health.
People who wound up moving to less green areas experienced a temporary, but significant decrease in mental health.
The researchers say these ______ should inspire urban planners and policy makers.
Because it's uneasy being not green.

sense_groups.english: If you're a city-dweller feeling a bit blue,

sense_groups.chinese: 你可能会考虑去一个更绿的地方——即使它还在城市里。

sense_groups.english: Because moving to greener urban areas provides both immediate and sustained mental health benefits.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为搬到更绿的城市区域会带来即时和持续的心理健康益处。

sense_groups.chinese: 《环境科学与技术》期刊上的一项研究如是说。

sense_groups.english: The effort is one of the few to look at the effects of green spaces over an extended period of time.

sense_groups.english: Researchers analyzed data from the British Household Panel Survey over a five-year period,

sense_groups.chinese: 将参与者分为两组：

sense_groups.english: They call it culturomics: the obvious play on the word "genomics" looks at trends in human thought and culture.

sense_groups.english: But scientists say culturomics has been hampered by a lack of quantitative data.
sense_groups.chinese: 但科学家表示，文化组学因缺乏定量数据而受阻。

sense_groups.english: So researchers at Harvard, along with Google, Encyclopedia Britannica, and the American Heritage Dictionary, have come up with a new tool.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，哈佛大学的研究人员与谷歌、大英百科全书和美国传统词典合作，开发了一种新工具。

sense_groups.english: It's a database of 5.2 million books, published since the year 1500.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是一个包含520万本书籍的数据库，这些书自1500年以来出版。

sense_groups.english: That's four percent of all the books ever published, with a total of 500 billion words.
sense_groups.chinese: 这占所有出版书籍的4%，总共有5000亿个单词。

sense_groups.english: The focus is on English language culture, so three quarters of the books are in English.
sense_groups.chinese: 重点在于英语语言文化，因此四分之三的书籍是英文的。

sense_groups.english: Among the first findings of the research, published in the journal Science : about, 8500 new words enter the English language annually.
sense_groups.chinese: 该研究的首批发现发表在《科学》杂志上：每年大约有8500个新词进入英语。

sense_groups.english: But many of them don't end up in dictionaries.
sense_groups.chinese: 但其中许多词最终没有收录到词典中。

sense_groups.english: And about fame-actors become famous around age 30, writers around 40, and politicians around 50.
sense_groups.chinese: 关于名气——演员大约在30岁成名，作家在40岁左右，政治家在50岁左右。

sense_groups.english: But the fame of politicians can eventually exceed that of actors.
sense_groups.chinese: 但政治家的名气最终可能超过演员。

sense_groups.english: A Google tool called the Books Ngram Viewer is available based on this data.
sense_groups.chinese: 基于这些数据，谷歌推出了一款名为“书籍Ngram查看器”的工具。

sense_groups.english: Users can track the usage and frequency of a word or phrase over the past few centuries.
sense_groups.chinese: 用户可以追踪某个单词或短语在过去几个世纪中的使用情况和频率。

sense_groups.english: Thus, we can watch the fall and rise of Melville.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，我们可以观察梅尔维尔的兴衰。

sense_groups.english: And soon the rise and fall of Snooki.
sense_groups.chinese: 很快也能看到斯努基的起落。

questions.name: #40 US and Cuba
questions.en:
President Obama arrived in Cuba March 20th, the first visit by a U.S. leader since Calvin Coolidge in1928.
Last spring I spoke to Cornell Laboratory of Ornithology researcher Eduardo Inigo-Elias about what improved relations between the U.S. and Cuba could mean for science.
"For the last 12 years the lab of ______ has been involved in research and conservation and training, building local capacity with biologists and scientists from Cuba.
So you can imagine the amount of work that we have on the back from our lawyers from Cornell University to get the permits to work, to the treasury department and the state department here in the U.S. But also been a lot of paperwork to do the things that we want to do collaborating with Cuban scientists.
And our Cuban scientists have to deal also with their restrictions that they have…"
"I noticed there's a book on your desk called The Dawn of Conservation Diplomacy which gives you an idea of the kind of things we've been talking about.
Where you have to do this kind of thing where you're not just a research scientist.
You're also a diplomat."
"You need to be—there are many challenges.
Especially you learn this with ______ birds that there is a natural resource shared by ______ and there are many issues that affect.
When the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico happened, everybody was calling here and ringing: "Who are the people you know in Cuba that can help us to understand if the water changed in that direction and the oil starts going to the shore what are going to be the impacts especially now that the migratory birds are moving?"…
"So the thawing of the U.S.-Cuban relationship is a really big deal for you and your colleagues."
"I think so.
I think you will see that in the future there's gonna be more important ______ of what ______ we do.
And I know many other institutions, like the Smithsonian, have been very interested to ______ with Cuba because it's always one of the gaps that we have on information."
To hear the entire interview with Eduardo Inigo-Elias, most of which is about migratory bird research, just go to the podcast page at www.scientificamerican.com and find the June 18th, 2015, edition of the Science Talk podcast.
questions.answer:
1. ornithology
2. migratory
3. everybody
4. strengths
5. activities
6. collaborate

sense_groups.chinese: “所以美古关系的解冻对你和你的同事来说是一件大事。”

sense_groups.english: "I think so.
sense_groups.chinese: “我想是的。

sense_groups.english: I think you will see that in the future there's gonna be more important strengths of what activities we do.

sense_groups.english: And I know many other institutions, like the Smithsonian, have been very interested to collaborate with Cuba because it's always one of the gaps that we have on information."
sense_groups.chinese: 而且我知道许多其他机构，比如史密森尼学会，一直非常有兴趣与古巴合作，因为古巴一直是我们信息上的空白之一。”

sense_groups.english: To hear the entire interview with Eduardo Inigo-Elias, most of which is about migratory bird research, just go to the podcast page at www.scientificamerican.com and find the June 18th, 2015, edition of the Science Talk podcast.

questions.name: #41 HIW
questions.en:
Lost in the ______ of the so-called ______ email controversy is a key point about the IPCC's track record of climate change estimates.
James McCarthy is on the faculty of the Harvard Medical School Center for Health and the Global Environment.
He spoke February 21st at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in San Diego:
"If you were to go back and map the IPCC projection for sea level rise and temperature in 1990, look at it in 1995, look at it in 2000.
In retrospect you would find that they were conservative.
So we talk about errors.
If you were to do two ledgers—here are IPCC overestimates, here are IPCC underestimates—over the 20 or so years that these assessments have been running, the underestimate ledger would be much larger than the overestimate.
Even with glitches—clearly ______ editing or sloppy editing that led to these erroneous ______ that got us in trouble recently."
questions.full:

James McCarthy is on the faculty of the Harvard Medical School Center for Health and the Global Environment.

sense_groups.english: Lost in the ______ of the so-called ______ email controversy

questions.name: #42 HIW
questions.en:
We all know that elephants aren't really scared of mice.
But a new study shows that they're really not crazy about something even smaller: ants.
In fact, elephants dislike ants so much that they avoid acacia trees that harbor the tiny, six-legged nectar-suckers.
On the savanna, acacia trees growing in regions that get a lot of elephant traffic tend to get eaten.
But ______ noticed that one species of acacia was not much ______ by elephants.
And that the ______ acacia was a favorite ant habitat.
So the scientists stripped the ant-covered acacia of their ______ bugs, and sure enough, the elephants chowed down.
In addition, when the insects were placed on previously ant-free acacias, the elephants took a pass.
But how can teeny, tiny ants repel a big old elephant, which is, after all, about a billion times more massive?
The answer is in the trunk.
Or rather, not in the trunk.
Because, as you can probably relate, elephants really hate to have ants up their noses.
The ______ is published in the journal Current Biology.
And it suggests that adding ants could help preserve wooded areas on the savanna.
Because ants will ruin any picnic, even for pachyderms.
questions.full:
We all know that elephants aren't really scared of mice.
But a new study shows that they're really not crazy about something even smaller: ants.
In fact, elephants dislike ants so much that they avoid acacia trees that harbor the tiny, six-legged nectar-suckers.
On the savanna, acacia trees growing in regions that get a lot of elephant traffic tend to get eaten.
But ______ noticed that one species of acacia was not much ______ by elephants.
And that the ______ acacia was a favorite ant habitat.
So the scientists stripped the ant-covered acacia of their ______ bugs, and sure enough, the elephants chowed down.
In addition, when the insects were placed on previously ant-free acacias, the elephants took a pass.
But how can teeny, tiny ants repel a big old elephant, which is, after all, about a billion times more massive?
The answer is in the trunk.
Or rather, not in the trunk.
Because, as you can probably relate, elephants really hate to have ants up their noses.
The ______ is published in the journal Current Biology.
And it suggests that adding ants could help preserve wooded areas on the savanna.
Because ants will ruin any picnic, even for pachyderms.

答案:
1. researchers
2. bothered
3. untouched
4. bodyguard
5. research

sense_groups.english: We all know that elephants aren't really scared of mice.
sense_groups.chinese: 我们都知道大象其实并不怕老鼠。

sense_groups.english: But a new study shows that they're really not crazy about something even smaller: ants.
sense_groups.chinese: 但一项新研究表明，它们对更小的东西——蚂蚁——非常不感兴趣。

sense_groups.english: In fact, elephants dislike ants so much that they avoid acacia trees that harbor the tiny, six-legged nectar-suckers.
sense_groups.chinese: 事实上，大象非常讨厌蚂蚁，以至于它们会避开那些藏有这种六条腿的吸蜜小虫的金合欢树。

sense_groups.english: On the savanna, acacia trees growing in regions that get a lot of elephant traffic tend to get eaten.
sense_groups.chinese: 在热带草原上，生长在大象频繁出没地区的金合欢树往往会被吃掉。

sense_groups.english: But researchers noticed that one species of acacia was not much bothered by elephants.
sense_groups.chinese: 但研究人员注意到，有一种金合欢树不太受大象的侵扰。

sense_groups.english: And that the untouched acacia was a favorite ant habitat.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且这种未被触碰的金合欢树是蚂蚁最喜欢的栖息地。

sense_groups.english: So the scientists stripped the ant-covered acacia of their bodyguard bugs, and sure enough, the elephants chowed down.
sense_groups.chinese: 于是，科学家们把覆盖着蚂蚁的金合欢树上的这些“保镖”虫子清除掉，果然，大象就开始大吃特吃了。

sense_groups.english: In addition, when the insects were placed on previously ant-free acacias, the elephants took a pass.
sense_groups.chinese: 此外，当这些昆虫被放到原本没有蚂蚁的金合欢树上时，大象就绕道而行了。

sense_groups.english: But how can teeny, tiny ants repel a big old elephant, which is, after all, about a billion times more massive?
sense_groups.chinese: 但小小的蚂蚁怎么能赶走一头庞大的大象呢？毕竟大象的体型大约是蚂蚁的十亿倍。

sense_groups.english: The answer is in the trunk.
sense_groups.chinese: 答案就在象鼻子里。

sense_groups.english: Or rather, not in the trunk.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者更确切地说，是不在鼻子里。

sense_groups.english: Because, as you can probably relate, elephants really hate to have ants up their noses.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为，你可能也有同感，大象非常讨厌蚂蚁爬进它们的鼻子里。

sense_groups.english: The research is published in the journal Current Biology.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《当代生物学》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: And it suggests that adding ants could help preserve wooded areas on the savanna.
sense_groups.chinese: 这表明，引入蚂蚁可能有助于保护热带草原上的林地。

sense_groups.english: Because ants will ruin any picnic, even for pachyderms.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为蚂蚁会破坏任何野餐，即使是对厚皮动物来说也是如此。

questions.name: #43 Pricing
questions.en:
Music, film and video game makers face a new online, digital world.
And some are testing a revolutionary pricing system: "pay what you want." But a new study finds that when consumers can name their own price, many may opt out of buying at all.
The study is in the ______ of the National Academy of Sciences.
For the research, tour boat passengers posed for photos.
Each boat ride announced a price of $15 per picture.
But they then charged either $15, $5 or the option to pay what you want.
As expected, the fewest tourists purchased photos when they had to pay full price.
But more customers bought photos when they cost $5 than when prices were pay what you want—which could have saved passengers even more.
The researchers suggest that choosing to pay less than an announced ______ price made people feel cheap.
With choices then limited to spending more money or feeling like a tightwad, potential customers simply opted out of the purchase.
So on sea or land, a low, set price may catch the most fish.
questions.full:
Music, film and video game makers face a new online, digital world.
And some are testing a revolutionary pricing system: "pay what you want." But a new study finds that when consumers can name their own price, many may opt out of buying at all.
The study is in the ______ of the National Academy of Sciences.
For the research, tour boat passengers posed for photos.
Each boat ride announced a price of $15 per picture.
But they then charged either $15, $5 or the option to pay what you want.
As expected, the fewest tourists purchased photos when they had to pay full price.
But more customers bought photos when they cost $5 than when prices were pay what you want—which could have saved passengers even more.
The researchers suggest that choosing to pay less than an announced ______ price made people feel cheap.
With choices then limited to spending more money or feeling like a tightwad, potential customers simply opted out of the purchase.
So on sea or land, a low, set price may catch the most fish.

答案:
1. Proceedings
2. lower-than-expected

sense_groups.english: Music, film and video game makers face a new online, digital world.
sense_groups.chinese: 音乐、电影和电子游戏制作者面临着一个全新的在线数字世界。

sense_groups.english: And some are testing a revolutionary pricing system: "pay what you want."
sense_groups.chinese: 一些人正在测试一种革命性的定价系统：“随心付”。

sense_groups.english: But a new study finds that when consumers can name their own price, many may opt out of buying at all.
sense_groups.chinese: 但一项新研究发现，当消费者可以自己定价时，许多人可能根本不会购买。

sense_groups.english: The study is in the ______ of the National Academy of Sciences.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《美国国家科学院院刊》______上。

sense_groups.english: For the research, tour boat passengers posed for photos.
sense_groups.chinese: 在这项研究中，游船乘客摆好姿势拍照。

sense_groups.english: Each boat ride announced a price of $15 per picture.
sense_groups.chinese: 每次乘船游览都宣布每张照片15美元。

sense_groups.english: But they then charged either $15, $5 or the option to pay what you want.
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们随后收取15美元、5美元或提供随心付的选择。

sense_groups.english: As expected, the fewest tourists purchased photos when they had to pay full price.
sense_groups.chinese: 不出所料，当游客必须支付全价时，购买照片的人数最少。

sense_groups.english: But more customers bought photos when they cost $5 than when prices were pay what you want—which could have saved passengers even more.
sense_groups.chinese: 但照片售价5美元时，购买人数多于随心付时——后者本可以为乘客节省更多钱。

sense_groups.english: The researchers suggest that choosing to pay less than an announced ______ price made people feel cheap.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员认为，选择支付低于公布的______价格会让人觉得自己小气。

sense_groups.english: With choices then limited to spending more money or feeling like a tightwad, potential customers simply opted out of the purchase.
sense_groups.chinese: 当选择仅限于花更多钱或感觉自己像个吝啬鬼时，潜在顾客干脆放弃了购买。

sense_groups.english: So on sea or land, a low, set price may catch the most fish.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，无论是在海上还是陆地上，一个较低的固定价格可能最能吸引顾客。

questions.name: #44 Pollinators
questions.en:
The widespread death of honeybees has some farmers fretting, 'cause if honeybees disappear, who will pollinate their crops?
"Almost any kind of insect you can think of." Margie Mayfield, an ecologist at The ______ of Queensland in Australia.
"Globally speaking flies are probably the second largest group of crop pollinators.
In ______ a group called hoverflies, or syrphid flies.
And these are these sort of ______ flies that if you take a hike you sometimes see them ______ in front of your face."
Along with hoverflies, the army of under-appreciated pollinators ______ butterflies, moths, beetles, ants and wasps.
Mayfield and her colleagues analyzed more than three dozen studies on pollination, covering 17 crop plants grown on five continents.
And they found that some of these underdog insects accounted for some 40 percent of the flower visits.
Some of the crops in their review--especially tropical ones like mangoes and custard apples—did not rely on honeybees at all.
Even commodities like canola did fine without bees.
The meta-analysis is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Mayfield says part of the difficulty in gauging the importance of bees starts with the research methods: a third of the studies they initially considered, for example, ignored everything but bees.
"You know the European honeybee is obviously from Europe, so there's a lot of focus on the European honeybee there." Another issue, she says, is just raising awareness among farmers.
"I've encountered farmers in California and in South Africa and in Australia who spray their pesticides largely at night, because that's when the bees have gone back to their hives.
And they do that with the idea that we'll spare our pollinators and will be able to control our pests.
But that very much takes the ______ that only bees are important pollinators." Of course we should still do our best to save honeybees--the celebrity pollinators.
But agricultural practices should consider the rest of these tiny farm workers, too.
questions.answer:
1. University
2. particular
3. large-eyed
4. hovering
5. includes
6. assumption

sense_groups.english: The widespread death of honeybees has some farmers fretting, 'cause if honeybees disappear, who will pollinate their crops?
sense_groups.chinese: 蜜蜂大量死亡让一些农民忧心忡忡，因为如果蜜蜂消失了，谁来给他们的作物授粉呢？

sense_groups.english: "Almost any kind of insect you can think of." Margie Mayfield, an ecologist at the University of Queensland in Australia.
sense_groups.chinese: “几乎你能想到的任何昆虫。”玛吉·梅菲尔德，澳大利亚昆士兰大学的生态学家。

sense_groups.english: "Globally speaking flies are probably the second largest group of crop pollinators.
sense_groups.chinese: “从全球来看，苍蝇可能是第二大作物授粉群体。

sense_groups.english: In particular a group called hoverflies, or syrphid flies.
sense_groups.chinese: 特别是被称为食蚜蝇或蚜蝇的一类。

sense_groups.english: And these are these sort of large-eyed flies that if you take a hike you sometimes see them hovering in front of your face."
sense_groups.chinese: 这些是大眼睛的苍蝇，如果你去远足，有时会看到它们在你面前盘旋。”

sense_groups.english: Along with hoverflies, the army of under-appreciated pollinators includes butterflies, moths, beetles, ants and wasps.
sense_groups.chinese: 除了食蚜蝇，这支被低估的授粉大军还包括蝴蝶、蛾子、甲虫、蚂蚁和黄蜂。

sense_groups.english: Mayfield and her colleagues analyzed more than three dozen studies on pollination, covering 17 crop plants grown on five continents.
sense_groups.chinese: 梅菲尔德和她的同事分析了三十多项关于授粉的研究，涵盖了五大洲种植的17种作物。

sense_groups.english: And they found that some of these underdog insects accounted for some 40 percent of the flower visits.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，其中一些不起眼的昆虫占了大约40%的访花活动。

sense_groups.english: Some of the crops in their review--especially tropical ones like mangoes and custard apples—did not rely on honeybees at all.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们审查中的一些作物——尤其是芒果和番荔枝等热带作物——完全不依赖蜜蜂。

sense_groups.english: Even commodities like canola did fine without bees.
sense_groups.chinese: 甚至像油菜籽这样的商品在没有蜜蜂的情况下也表现良好。

sense_groups.english: The meta-analysis is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项荟萃分析发表在《美国国家科学院院刊》上。

sense_groups.english: Mayfield says part of the difficulty in gauging the importance of bees starts with the research methods: a third of the studies they initially considered, for example, ignored everything but bees.
sense_groups.chinese: 梅菲尔德说，评估蜜蜂重要性的部分困难源于研究方法：例如，他们最初考虑的研究中有三分之一只关注蜜蜂，忽略了其他一切。

sense_groups.english: "You know the European honeybee is obviously from Europe, so there's a lot of focus on the European honeybee there." Another issue, she says, is just raising awareness among farmers.
sense_groups.chinese: “你知道欧洲蜜蜂显然来自欧洲，所以那里对欧洲蜜蜂有很多关注。”她说，另一个问题就是提高农民的意识。

sense_groups.english: "I've encountered farmers in California and in South Africa and in Australia who spray their pesticides largely at night, because that's when the bees have gone back to their hives.
sense_groups.chinese: “我在加利福尼亚、南非和澳大利亚遇到过农民，他们主要在夜间喷洒农药，因为那时蜜蜂已经回巢了。

sense_groups.english: And they do that with the idea that we'll spare our pollinators and will be able to control our pests.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们这样做是认为这样可以保护授粉者，同时控制害虫。

sense_groups.english: But that very much takes the assumption that only bees are important pollinators." Of course we should still do our best to save honeybees--the celebrity pollinators.
sense_groups.chinese: 但这很大程度上是基于只有蜜蜂才是重要授粉者的假设。”当然，我们仍然应该尽力拯救蜜蜂——这些明星授粉者。

sense_groups.english: But agricultural practices should consider the rest of these tiny farm workers, too.
sense_groups.chinese: 但农业实践也应该考虑其他这些微小的农场工人。

questions.name: #45 HIW
questions.en:
Crop ______ is a recognized way to keep soil and the food ecosystem healthy.
Now, ______ are saying that rotation could be a useful tool—in the sea.
Researchers tracked a shallow-water, near-shore species used for food: sea cucumbers.
They're easy to harvest and are fairly valuable.
But those same attributes mean they're easy to overharvest.
The ______ has put some sea cucumber species at high risk of extinction, even in a relatively well-managed area, the Great Barrier Marine Park in Australia.
In 2004 authorities split the Great Barrier Reef into 154 zones, where each zone was fished only once every three years.
Fishers rotate through the region.
In computer models, the researchers ran through dozens of ______ of each zone, both before and after the divisions took place.
The trials revealed that even with an identical and ______ allowance in all cases, the sea cucumbers would recover more fully under the rotation strategy than by harvesting simultaneously ______ the region.
In fact, in trials that included rotations, the yield actually increased.
The research is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The scientists say their results suggest that such rotation might be beneficial in these kinds of shallow marine regions around the world, particularly for species that are in high demand.
Because you should not eat your seed corn.
Or your seed sea cucumbers.
questions.answer:
1. rotation
2. scientists
3. practice
4. simulations
5. low-catch
6. throughout
