sense_groups.english: and seeing how photosynthesis work.
sense_groups.chinese: 并观察光合作用是如何进行的。

questions.name: #130 Salty Food
questions.en:
Mmmm, chips.
One of the most sublime of salty snacks.
But have you ever ______ how they get that perfectly salty sheen on the outside?
"Salt is sprayed on the surface." Youngsoo Lee is a food engineer at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
And he says not all salty foods are created equal.
There's spray-on surface salt.
There's salty liquids, like canned soup.
And then there are salty solids, where the sodium is dissolved in a matrixlike structure.
Think: salamis and cheeses.
But when we eat those salty solids, only a fraction of the salt gets ______ before we swallow.
Meaning a lot of that salt has no effect on taste—but a big effect on our daily salt intake.
Lee's ______ that salty-solid conundrum for a company that wants to make cold cuts that taste the same but contain less salt.
He couldn't tell me which one.
"Um... I mean, it's a fairly big U.S.-based food company."
To find a salty solution he and his colleagues created blocks of whey protein with various proportions of fat, water and salt.
Then they squashed those tofulike blocks underwater, to measure how much sodium the blocks released.

questions.name: #131 Foliage Color
questions.en:
In Autumn, New England foliage turns vibrant shades of red, yellow, and orange.
Which brings in lots of green—as in the money spent by tourists who flock to the region to witness the explosion of color.
Because of fall's economic implications, exactly when the leaf-peeping season will begin is thus a source of constant speculation.
Scientists know that factors including frost, heat, rain and drought all affect the timing—but the whole colorful picture is still difficult to accurately predict.
Now scientists have picked apart satellite imagery from two New England forest ______ collected from 2001 to 2012 to try to get a better handle on exactly what factors ______ the autumn leaves.
The scientists looked at northeastern highlands and coastal zones.
They ______ ______ data on chills, frosts and heat, and rain, drought, and flooding.
In general, cold, wet and extreme heat made leaves change color sooner, while moderate heat and low rainfall delayed the coloration.
But the ______ ecosystems behaved differently.
Forests in the highlands reacted to frosts both in spring and in the fall, while the coast only responded to fall frosts.
The coastal region's forests were also particularly sensitive to rain and flooding.
Incorporating climate change predictions for the next century, the ______ propose that the highlands will change color later in the fall, while the coast may start to turn earlier.
The study is in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The researchers note that more data, such as for extreme weather events and flooding, need to be incorporated into future models.
Which could help New England states maximize fall's economic windfall.
questions.answer:
1. ecosystems
2. influence
3. incorporated
4. available
5. different
6. researchers

questions.name: #132 Botanical Boon
questions.en:
Global warming might seem like a botanical boon.
After all, milder ______ and more carbon dioxide and nitrogen should feed flora.
But a ______ study has found that any initial positive effect on plant growth from climate change may soon disappear.
The report is in the journal Nature Climate Change.
Researchers transplanted vegetation from four grassland ______ to lower, warmer elevations.
They also modified the precipitation at the transplant sites based on altered rainfall estimates.
For the first year, the plants did great, producing more biomass and churning out more oxygen for us.
But their productivity went down for the rest of the decade.
What happened?
Warming did speed up the nitrogen cycle, which should have increased nitrogen's ______ as plant fertilizer.
But a lot of the nitrogen left the soil through run-off or uptake into the atmosphere.
In addition, ______ native plants began to lose out to species that thrive at higher temperatures, but are less productive than the natives.
Warmer temperatures may spur immediate growth, but in the long term, we can't expect plants to like it hot.
questions.full:
Global warming might seem like a botanical boon.
After all, milder ______ and more carbon dioxide and nitrogen should feed flora.
But a ______ study has found that any initial positive effect on plant growth from climate change may soon disappear.
The report is in the journal Nature Climate Change.

But their productivity went down for the rest of the decade.
What happened?
Warming did speed up the nitrogen cycle, which should have increased nitrogen's ______ as plant fertilizer.
But a lot of the nitrogen left the soil through run-off or uptake into the atmosphere.
In addition, ______ native plants began to lose out to species that thrive at higher temperatures, but are less productive than the natives.
Warmer temperatures may spur immediate growth, but in the long term, we can't expect plants to like it hot.

答案:
1. temperatures
2. ten-year
3. ecosystems
4. availability
5. productive

sense_groups.english: Global warming might seem like a botanical boon.
sense_groups.chinese: 全球变暖可能看起来像是植物的福音。

sense_groups.english: After all, milder temperatures and more carbon dioxide and nitrogen should feed flora.
sense_groups.chinese: 毕竟，更温和的温度以及更多的二氧化碳和氮应该能滋养植物。

sense_groups.english: But a ten-year study has found that any initial positive effect on plant growth from climate change may soon disappear.
sense_groups.chinese: 但一项为期十年的研究发现，气候变化对植物生长的任何初步积极影响可能很快就会消失。

sense_groups.english: The report is in the journal Nature Climate Change.
sense_groups.chinese: 该报告发表在《自然气候变化》杂志上。

sense_groups.english: Researchers transplanted vegetation from four grassland ecosystems to lower, warmer elevations.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员将来自四个草原生态系统的植被移植到更低、更温暖的海拔地区。

sense_groups.english: They also modified the precipitation at the transplant sites based on altered rainfall estimates.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们还根据改变的降雨估计值调整了移植地点的降水量。

sense_groups.english: For the first year, the plants did great, producing more biomass and churning out more oxygen for us.
sense_groups.chinese: 第一年，植物表现良好，产生了更多的生物量，并为我们制造了更多的氧气。

sense_groups.english: But their productivity went down for the rest of the decade.
sense_groups.chinese: 但在接下来的十年里，它们的生产力下降了。

sense_groups.english: What happened?
sense_groups.chinese: 发生了什么？

sense_groups.english: Warming did speed up the nitrogen cycle, which should have increased nitrogen's availability as plant fertilizer.
sense_groups.chinese: 变暖确实加速了氮循环，这应该会增加氮作为植物肥料的可用性。

sense_groups.english: But a lot of the nitrogen left the soil through run-off or uptake into the atmosphere.
sense_groups.chinese: 但大量的氮通过径流或进入大气而离开了土壤。

sense_groups.english: In addition, productive native plants began to lose out to species that thrive at higher temperatures, but are less productive than the natives.
sense_groups.chinese: 此外，高产的本土植物开始输给那些在更高温度下茁壮成长但生产力低于本土植物的物种。

sense_groups.english: Warmer temperatures may spur immediate growth, but in the long term, we can't expect plants to like it hot.
sense_groups.chinese: 更高的温度可能会刺激即时生长，但从长远来看，我们不能指望植物喜欢炎热。

questions.name: #133 Plant Seeds
questions.en:
Plants can't choose where their seeds end up.
Some float on the wind, others on the water.
Many seeds hitch a ride on—or inside—animals.
And the farther a seed gets from its parent, and any predators or disease the parent might have, the better its chance of survival.
Or so the theory goes.
Researchers studied that phenomenon in the South American chili pepper Capsicum chacoense, which relies on birds like ______ to spread its seed.
To get realistic samples, researchers plucked chili seeds from the ______ of captive flycatchers.
Then they scattered them near and far from wild chili bushes in Bolivia.
Contrary to the prevailing theory, distant seeds fared no better than seeds directly beneath chili plants.
But it turns out the trip through the birds gave seeds a different ______ edge.
The passage stripped them of ______ chemicals and pathogenic fungi—which ______ the seeds' ______ rate, compared to their ______ counterparts.
The results appear in the journal Ecology Letters.
So even though these chili seeds don't need to go the distance to survive, you might say that a seed in the bird is worth about four on the bush.
questions.answer:
1. flycatchers
2. droppings
3. competitive
4. predator-attracting
5. quadrupled
6. survival
7. undigested
questions.full:

So even though these chili seeds don't need to go the distance to survive, you might say that a seed in the bird is worth about four on the bush.

2. droppings
3. competitive
4. predator-attracting
5. quadrupled
6. survival

sense_groups.english: Plants can't choose where their seeds end up.
sense_groups.chinese: 植物无法选择种子的最终去向。

sense_groups.english: Some float on the wind, others on the water.
sense_groups.chinese: 有些随风飘散，有些随水漂流。

sense_groups.english: Many seeds hitch a ride on—or inside—animals.
sense_groups.chinese: 许多种子搭上动物的便车——附着在它们身上或进入体内。

sense_groups.chinese: 种子离母株越远，远离母株可能携带的捕食者或疾病，其生存机会就越大。

sense_groups.english: Or so the theory goes.
sense_groups.chinese: 理论上是这样说的。

sense_groups.english: Researchers studied that phenomenon in the South American chili pepper Capsicum chacoense, which relies on birds like flycatchers to spread its seed.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员研究了南美辣椒（Capsicum chacoense）的这一现象，这种辣椒依赖像捕蝇鸟这样的鸟类传播种子。

sense_groups.english: To get realistic samples, researchers plucked chili seeds from the droppings of captive flycatchers.
sense_groups.chinese: 为了获得真实样本，研究人员从圈养捕蝇鸟的粪便中取出辣椒种子。

sense_groups.english: Then they scattered them near and far from wild chili bushes in Bolivia.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后，他们将种子撒在玻利维亚野生辣椒丛的远近各处。

sense_groups.english: But it turns out the trip through the birds gave seeds a different competitive edge.
sense_groups.chinese: 但事实证明，经过鸟类的旅程赋予了种子另一种竞争优势。

sense_groups.english: The results appear in the journal Ecology Letters.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究结果发表在《生态学快报》上。

sense_groups.english: So even though these chili seeds don't need to go the distance to survive, you might say that a seed in the bird is worth about four on the bush.

questions.name: #134 Rain Drop
questions.en:
When you get caught in a downpour, you ______ don't think about the size of the ______ that assault you as you run for cover.
But physicists do.
And they've come to the conclusion that the drops that hit the ground, or your head, are the shattered remains of bigger drops that fell from the clouds.
Raindrops come in a variety of sizes, even within the same storm.
And ______ used to think that, to get that kind of distribution, raindrops must crash into each other on the way down, breaking up into smaller droplets or coalescing into larger ones.
Now a team of French scientists has produced high-speed footage of falling water droplets.
And they find that drops of different dimensions don't require collision—they come from the fragmentation of individual, isolated droplets.
Their results appear online in the journal Nature Physics.
The video evidence reveals that water droplets first flatten out as they fall.
And as these plummeting pancakes get wider and thinner they eventually capture air, forming what look like little plastic grocery bags floating in a breeze.
And when the bags get big enough, they pop.
And you're left ______ why you can never ______ your umbrella.

sense_groups.chinese: 你______不会想到袭击你的______的大小，当你跑去找地方躲雨时。

sense_groups.english: But physicists do.
sense_groups.chinese: 但物理学家会。

sense_groups.english: And they've come to the conclusion that the drops that hit the ground, or your head, are the shattered remains of bigger drops that fell from the clouds.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们得出结论，打在地上或你头上的雨滴，是从云中落下的更大雨滴破碎后的残留物。

sense_groups.english: Raindrops come in a variety of sizes, even within the same storm.
sense_groups.chinese: 雨滴大小不一，即使在同一场暴风雨中也是如此。

sense_groups.english: And ______ used to think that, to get that kind of distribution, raindrops must crash into each other on the way down, breaking up into smaller droplets or coalescing into larger ones.
sense_groups.chinese: 而______过去认为，要得到那种分布，雨滴必须在下降过程中相互碰撞，分裂成更小的水滴或合并成更大的水滴。

sense_groups.english: Now a team of French scientists has produced high-speed footage of falling water droplets.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，一组法国科学家制作了水滴下落的高速影像。

sense_groups.english: And they find that drops of different dimensions don't require collision—they come from the fragmentation of individual, isolated droplets.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，不同大小的水滴不需要碰撞——它们来自单个孤立水滴的碎裂。

sense_groups.english: Their results appear online in the journal Nature Physics.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们的结果发表在《自然·物理》杂志的在线版上。

sense_groups.english: The video evidence reveals that water droplets first flatten out as they fall.
sense_groups.chinese: 视频证据显示，水滴在下落时首先变平。

sense_groups.english: And as these plummeting pancakes get wider and thinner they eventually capture air, forming what look like little plastic grocery bags floating in a breeze.
sense_groups.chinese: 随着这些下落的薄饼变得又宽又薄，它们最终捕获空气，形成像在微风中漂浮的小塑料袋一样的东西。

sense_groups.english: And when the bags get big enough, they pop.
sense_groups.chinese: 当这些袋子变得足够大时，它们就会破裂。

sense_groups.english: And you're left ______ why you can never ______ your umbrella.
sense_groups.chinese: 而你______为什么你永远______你的伞。

questions.name: #135 Depth Perception
questions.en:
You probably take your depth ______ for granted.
It allows you to easily judge distances.
Each eye sends a ______ signal to the brain, and the brain compares the two pictures.
But even using just one eye, the world doesn't suddenly appear flat.
So how can just one eye provide depth perception?
A team at the University of ______ recently published a possible answer to that question on-line in the journal Nature.
It has to do with a small part of our brain called the middle temporal area.
This region processes information both from visual cues and from the motion of our eyes.
Researchers ______ macaque monkeys ______ virtual reality.
Basically, the eye moves when ______ crosses the path of vision.
This middle temporal area picks up the speed of the objects relative to these eye movements.
Neurons in that brain region showed activity that signaled depth perception even in the absence of other cues.
This new information may be useful for creating better virtual reality.
And scientists also hope that it leads to better tools to assist children born with ______ eyes.
questions.answer:
1. perception
2. different
3. Rochester
4. examined
5. watching
6. something
7. misaligned
questions.full:
You probably take your depth ______ for granted.
It allows you to easily judge distances.
Each eye sends a ______ signal to the brain, and the brain compares the two pictures.
But even using just one eye, the world doesn't suddenly appear flat.
So how can just one eye provide depth perception?
A team at the University of ______ recently published a possible answer to that question on-line in the journal Nature.
It has to do with a small part of our brain called the middle temporal area.
This region processes information both from visual cues and from the motion of our eyes.
Researchers ______ macaque monkeys ______ virtual reality.
Basically, the eye moves when ______ crosses the path of vision.
This middle temporal area picks up the speed of the objects relative to these eye movements.
Neurons in that brain region showed activity that signaled depth perception even in the absence of other cues.
This new information may be useful for creating better virtual reality.
And scientists also hope that it leads to better tools to assist children born with ______ eyes.

答案:
1. perception
2. different
3. Rochester
4. examined
5. watching
6. something
7. misaligned

sense_groups.english: You probably take your depth perception for granted.
sense_groups.chinese: 你可能认为你的深度知觉是理所当然的。

sense_groups.english: It allows you to easily judge distances.
sense_groups.chinese: 它让你轻松判断距离。

sense_groups.english: Each eye sends a different signal to the brain, and the brain compares the two pictures.
sense_groups.chinese: 每只眼睛向大脑发送不同的信号，大脑比较这两幅图像。

sense_groups.english: But even using just one eye, the world doesn't suddenly appear flat.
sense_groups.chinese: 但即使只用一只眼睛，世界也不会突然变得平坦。

sense_groups.english: So how can just one eye provide depth perception?
sense_groups.chinese: 那么，仅凭一只眼睛如何提供深度知觉呢？

sense_groups.english: A team at the University of Rochester recently published a possible answer to that question on-line in the journal Nature.
sense_groups.chinese: 罗切斯特大学的一个团队最近在《自然》杂志在线发表了该问题的一个可能答案。

sense_groups.english: It has to do with a small part of our brain called the middle temporal area.
sense_groups.chinese: 这与我们大脑中一个叫做中颞区的小部分有关。

sense_groups.english: This region processes information both from visual cues and from the motion of our eyes.
sense_groups.chinese: 这个区域处理来自视觉线索和我们眼睛运动的信息。

sense_groups.english: Researchers examined macaque monkeys watching virtual reality.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员观察了观看虚拟现实的猕猴。

sense_groups.english: Basically, the eye moves when something crosses the path of vision.
sense_groups.chinese: 基本上，当有东西穿过视野时，眼睛会移动。

sense_groups.english: This middle temporal area picks up the speed of the objects relative to these eye movements.
sense_groups.chinese: 这个中颞区捕捉到物体相对于这些眼睛运动的速度。

sense_groups.english: Neurons in that brain region showed activity that signaled depth perception even in the absence of other cues.
sense_groups.chinese: 该脑区的神经元显示出活动，即使在缺乏其他线索时也能发出深度知觉的信号。

sense_groups.english: This new information may be useful for creating better virtual reality.
sense_groups.chinese: 这一新信息可能有助于创造更好的虚拟现实。

sense_groups.english: And scientists also hope that it leads to better tools to assist children born with misaligned eyes.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家们也希望这能带来更好的工具，帮助天生眼睛错位的儿童。

questions.name: #136 Fire
questions.en:
Some scientists say the use of fire helped make us modern humans—it ______ changed what and how we eat and may have even altered our anatomy.
But ______ of Utah anthropologist Polly Wiessner thinks that fire was also important in shaping human social interactions and ______ traditions.
Her conclusions are in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Wiessner evaluated day and night activities and conversations of Kalahari Bushmen from Botswana and Namibia.
These communities still live by hunting and gathering, as most humans did over evolutionary history.
During the day, nearly a third of the conversations dealt with economic issues such as hunting strategies and foraging plans.
Another third covered complaints, criticisms and gossip.
But at night around the fire, more than 80 percent of group conversations were storytelling, often about people living far away or in the spirit world.
Weissner says that humans are unique in that we create ties to others outside of our ______ group.
Gathering at the fire ______ listeners' imaginations and allowed for the ______ of cognitive processes that made it possible to form those links to distant communities.
Which makes fire the precursor to Facebook.
questions.answer:
1. dramatically
2. University
3. cultural
4. immediate
5. expanded
6. development
questions.full:
Some scientists say the use of fire helped make us modern humans—it ______ changed what and how we eat and may have even altered our anatomy.
But ______ of Utah anthropologist Polly Wiessner thinks that fire was also important in shaping human social interactions and ______ traditions.
Her conclusions are in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Wiessner evaluated day and night activities and conversations of Kalahari Bushmen from Botswana and Namibia.
These communities still live by hunting and gathering, as most humans did over evolutionary history.
During the day, nearly a third of the conversations dealt with economic issues such as hunting strategies and foraging plans.
Another third covered complaints, criticisms and gossip.
But at night around the fire, more than 80 percent of group conversations were storytelling, often about people living far away or in the spirit world.
Weissner says that humans are unique in that we create ties to others outside of our ______ group.
Gathering at the fire ______ listeners' imaginations and allowed for the ______ of cognitive processes that made it possible to form those links to distant communities.
Which makes fire the precursor to Facebook.

答案:
1. dramatically
2. University
3. cultural
4. immediate
5. expanded
6. development

sense_groups.english: Some scientists say the use of fire helped make us modern humans—it dramatically changed what and how we eat
sense_groups.chinese: 一些科学家说，火的使用帮助我们成为现代人类——它极大地改变了我们吃什么和怎么吃

sense_groups.english: and may have even altered our anatomy.
sense_groups.chinese: 甚至可能改变了我们的解剖结构。

sense_groups.english: But University of Utah anthropologist Polly Wiessner thinks that fire was also important in shaping human social interactions
sense_groups.chinese: 但犹他大学的人类学家波莉·维斯纳认为，火在塑造人类社交互动方面也很重要

sense_groups.english: and cultural traditions.
sense_groups.chinese: 和文化传统。

sense_groups.english: Her conclusions are in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
sense_groups.chinese: 她的结论发表在《美国国家科学院院刊》上。

sense_groups.english: Wiessner evaluated day and night activities and conversations of Kalahari Bushmen from Botswana and Namibia.
sense_groups.chinese: 维斯纳评估了来自博茨瓦纳和纳米比亚的卡拉哈里布须曼人的昼夜活动和对话。

sense_groups.english: These communities still live by hunting and gathering,
sense_groups.chinese: 这些社区仍然以狩猎和采集为生，

sense_groups.english: as most humans did over evolutionary history.
sense_groups.chinese: 就像大多数人类在进化历史上所做的那样。

sense_groups.english: During the day, nearly a third of the conversations dealt with economic issues such as hunting strategies and foraging plans.
sense_groups.chinese: 白天，近三分之一的对话涉及经济问题，如狩猎策略和觅食计划。

sense_groups.english: Another third covered complaints, criticisms and gossip.
sense_groups.chinese: 另外三分之一涉及抱怨、批评和八卦。

sense_groups.english: But at night around the fire, more than 80 percent of group conversations were storytelling,
sense_groups.chinese: 但在夜间的篝火旁，超过80%的群体对话是讲故事，

sense_groups.english: often about people living far away or in the spirit world.
sense_groups.chinese: 通常是关于生活在远方或灵界的人。

sense_groups.english: Weissner says that humans are unique in that we create ties to others outside of our immediate group.
sense_groups.chinese: 维斯纳说，人类独特之处在于我们与直接群体之外的人建立联系。

sense_groups.english: Gathering at the fire expanded listeners' imaginations
sense_groups.chinese: 在篝火旁聚集扩展了听众的想象力

sense_groups.english: and allowed for the development of cognitive processes
sense_groups.chinese: 并促进了认知过程的发展

sense_groups.english: that made it possible to form those links to distant communities.
sense_groups.chinese: 使得与远方社区建立联系成为可能。

sense_groups.english: Which makes fire the precursor to Facebook.
sense_groups.chinese: 这使得火成为Facebook的前身。

questions.name: #137 Tone Deaf
questions.en:
The ability to distinguish between sounds of varying pitch makes people capable of ______ and ______ speech and music.
And the way we are able to process pitch has been thought to be unique to our big-brained species.
But now, there's evidence that a tiny monkey—the common marmoset from Brazil—can distinguish pitch the same way we do.
That's according to a study in the ______ of the National Academy of Sciences.
Ten years ago, researchers identified a region of the marmoset brain that ______ to process pitch.
But they needed to confirm that the animals did indeed notice changes in pitch—which presented a challenge: they had to find a way to get the animal to indicate that it had heard something.
So they trained the marmosets to respond to a change in pitch with a behavior—specifically, they would lick a waterspout.
The researchers then had the animals listen to a series of notes with the same pitch.
And, at random, they'd change it up.
"Just like, for example, when I say, 'ma ma ma MA.' Right, at some point I make the pitch a little higher." Johns Hopkins ______ Xiaoqin Wang, lead researcher of the study.
The actual ______ in pitch, he says, was much smaller than that.
But you get the idea.
"And, when the animal hears that change, it will lick the waterspout to indicate they hear the difference." Which the miniscule monkeys indeed did.
Because both we and marmosets have this talent, the ability likely evolved in a common ancestor long-ago—this type of pitch perception may thus go back more than 40 million years ago, much earlier than ______ thought.
And the understanding of how the brain processes pitch may eventually explain why some people have perfect pitch, while others are tone deaf.
questions.answer:
1. producing
2. understanding
3. Proceedings
4. appeared
5. neuroscientist
6. difference
7. previously
questions.full:
The ability to distinguish between sounds of varying pitch makes people capable of ______ and ______ speech and music.
And the way we are able to process pitch has been thought to be unique to our big-brained species.
But now, there's evidence that a tiny monkey—the common marmoset from Brazil—can distinguish pitch the same way we do.
That's according to a study in the ______ of the National Academy of Sciences.
Ten years ago, researchers identified a region of the marmoset brain that ______ to process pitch.
But they needed to confirm that the animals did indeed notice changes in pitch—which presented a challenge: they had to find a way to get the animal to indicate that it had heard something.
So they trained the marmosets to respond to a change in pitch with a behavior—specifically, they would lick a waterspout.
The researchers then had the animals listen to a series of notes with the same pitch.
And, at random, they'd change it up.
"Just like, for example, when I say, 'ma ma ma MA.' Right, at some point I make the pitch a little higher." Johns Hopkins ______ Xiaoqin Wang, lead researcher of the study.
The actual ______ in pitch, he says, was much smaller than that.
But you get the idea.
"And, when the animal hears that change, it will lick the waterspout to indicate they hear the difference." Which the miniscule monkeys indeed did.
Because both we and marmosets have this talent, the ability likely evolved in a common ancestor long-ago—this type of pitch perception may thus go back more than 40 million years ago, much earlier than ______ thought.
And the understanding of how the brain processes pitch may eventually explain why some people have perfect pitch, while others are tone deaf.

答案:
1. producing
2. understanding
3. Proceedings
4. appeared
5. neuroscientist
6. difference
7. previously

sense_groups.english: The ability to distinguish between sounds of varying pitch makes people capable of producing and understanding speech and music.
sense_groups.chinese: 区分不同音高声音的能力使人们能够产生和理解语言和音乐。

sense_groups.english: And the way we are able to process pitch has been thought to be unique to our big-brained species.
sense_groups.chinese: 而我们处理音高的方式曾被认为是我们大脑发达的物种所独有的。

sense_groups.english: But now, there's evidence that a tiny monkey—the common marmoset from Brazil—can distinguish pitch the same way we do.
sense_groups.chinese: 但现在，有证据表明一种小型猴子——来自巴西的普通狨猴——能够以与我们相同的方式区分音高。

sense_groups.english: That's according to a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是根据《美国国家科学院院刊》上的一项研究得出的。

sense_groups.english: Ten years ago, researchers identified a region of the marmoset brain that appeared to process pitch.
sense_groups.chinese: 十年前，研究人员确定了狨猴大脑中一个似乎处理音高的区域。

sense_groups.english: But they needed to confirm that the animals did indeed notice changes in pitch—which presented a challenge: they had to find a way to get the animal to indicate that it had heard something.
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们需要确认这些动物确实注意到了音高的变化——这带来了一个挑战：他们必须找到一种方法让动物表明它听到了什么。

sense_groups.english: So they trained the marmosets to respond to a change in pitch with a behavior—specifically, they would lick a waterspout.
sense_groups.chinese: 于是他们训练狨猴用行为来回应音高的变化——具体来说，它们会舔舐水龙头。

sense_groups.english: The researchers then had the animals listen to a series of notes with the same pitch.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后研究人员让这些动物听一系列相同音高的音符。

sense_groups.english: And, at random, they'd change it up.
sense_groups.chinese: 并且，随机地，他们会改变音高。

sense_groups.english: "Just like, for example, when I say, 'ma ma ma MA.' Right, at some point I make the pitch a little higher." Johns Hopkins neuroscientist Xiaoqin Wang, lead researcher of the study.
sense_groups.chinese: "就像，例如，当我说'ma ma ma MA'。对，在某个时刻我把音高提高了一点。"约翰·霍普金斯大学的神经科学家王晓琴，该研究的首席研究员。

sense_groups.english: The actual difference in pitch, he says, was much smaller than that.
sense_groups.chinese: 他说，实际的音高差异比那要小得多。

sense_groups.english: But you get the idea.
sense_groups.chinese: 但你明白这个意思。

sense_groups.english: "And, when the animal hears that change, it will lick the waterspout to indicate they hear the difference." Which the miniscule monkeys indeed did.
sense_groups.chinese: "而且，当动物听到这种变化时，它会舔舐水龙头以表明它们听到了差异。"这些微小的猴子确实这样做了。

sense_groups.english: Because both we and marmosets have this talent, the ability likely evolved in a common ancestor long-ago—this type of pitch perception may thus go back more than 40 million years ago, much earlier than previously thought.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为人类和狨猴都有这种能力，这种能力很可能在很久以前的共同祖先中进化而来——因此这种音高感知可能可以追溯到4000多万年前，比之前认为的要早得多。

sense_groups.english: And the understanding of how the brain processes pitch may eventually explain why some people have perfect pitch, while others are tone deaf.
sense_groups.chinese: 而对大脑如何处理音高的理解最终可能解释为什么有些人拥有绝对音感，而另一些人则是音盲。

questions.name: #138 Beauty
questions.en:
Beauty is only skin deep.
And the beauty of shiny white teeth is even less deep.
Because a new study shows that fluoride forms a thinner ______ shield than experts thought it did.
The results appear in the surface science journal Langmuir.
American consumers spend more than $50 billion a year fighting cavities.
When we realized that fluoride could help, we put it in our drinking water, our toothpaste and our mouthwash.
But how does fluoride work its magic?
Many figured that fluoride chemically reacts with the main mineral in enamel to form a thick, ______ veneer.
But the latest ______ kicks that idea in the teeth.
Scientists in Germany used x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to get a detailed image of the surface of a treated tooth.
And they found that the protective covering is ______ only 6 ______ thick.
That's about a fifteen-thousandth as thick as a sheet of paper.
And a layer that skimpy would likely be worn away by ordinary chewing.
How fluoride keeps the tooth fairy away is a mystery that ______ are still working to unravel.
In the meantime, we may not know how it works, but we know that it works.
So keep brushing.
questions.answer:
1. protective
2. decay-resistant
3. research
4. actually
5. nanometers
6. researchers
questions.full:
Beauty is only skin deep.
And the beauty of shiny white teeth is even less deep.
Because a new study shows that fluoride forms a thinner ______ shield than experts thought it did.
The results appear in the surface science journal Langmuir.
American consumers spend more than $50 billion a year fighting cavities.
When we realized that fluoride could help, we put it in our drinking water, our toothpaste and our mouthwash.
But how does fluoride work its magic?
Many figured that fluoride chemically reacts with the main mineral in enamel to form a thick, ______ veneer.
But the latest ______ kicks that idea in the teeth.
Scientists in Germany used x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to get a detailed image of the surface of a treated tooth.
And they found that the protective covering is ______ only 6 ______ thick.
That's about a fifteen-thousandth as thick as a sheet of paper.
And a layer that skimpy would likely be worn away by ordinary chewing.
How fluoride keeps the tooth fairy away is a mystery that ______ are still working to unravel.
In the meantime, we may not know how it works, but we know that it works.
So keep brushing.

答案:
1. protective
2. decay-resistant
3. research
4. actually
5. nanometers
6. researchers

sense_groups.english: Beauty is only skin deep.
sense_groups.chinese: 美貌不过一层皮。

sense_groups.english: And the beauty of shiny white teeth is even less deep.
sense_groups.chinese: 而闪亮白牙的美貌更浅。

sense_groups.english: Because a new study shows that fluoride forms a thinner protective shield than experts thought it did.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为一项新研究表明，氟化物形成的保护层比专家们原先认为的更薄。

sense_groups.english: The results appear in the surface science journal Langmuir.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究结果发表在表面科学期刊《朗缪尔》上。

sense_groups.english: American consumers spend more than $50 billion a year fighting cavities.
sense_groups.chinese: 美国消费者每年花费超过500亿美元来对抗蛀牙。

sense_groups.english: When we realized that fluoride could help, we put it in our drinking water, our toothpaste and our mouthwash.
sense_groups.chinese: 当我们意识到氟化物有帮助时，就把它加进了饮用水、牙膏和漱口水中。

sense_groups.english: But how does fluoride work its magic?
sense_groups.chinese: 但氟化物是如何发挥魔力的呢？

sense_groups.english: Many figured that fluoride chemically reacts with the main mineral in enamel to form a thick, decay-resistant veneer.
sense_groups.chinese: 许多人认为氟化物与牙釉质中的主要矿物质发生化学反应，形成一层厚厚的抗腐蚀表层。

sense_groups.english: But the latest research kicks that idea in the teeth.
sense_groups.chinese: 但最新研究狠狠打击了这一观点。

sense_groups.english: Scientists in Germany used x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to get a detailed image of the surface of a treated tooth.
sense_groups.chinese: 德国科学家使用X射线光电子能谱技术，获得了处理过的牙齿表面的详细图像。

sense_groups.english: And they found that the protective covering is actually only 6 nanometers thick.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现保护层实际上只有6纳米厚。

sense_groups.english: That's about a fifteen-thousandth as thick as a sheet of paper.
sense_groups.chinese: 这大约是一张纸厚度的万分之一。

sense_groups.english: And a layer that skimpy would likely be worn away by ordinary chewing.
sense_groups.chinese: 这么薄的一层很可能被日常咀嚼磨损掉。

sense_groups.english: How fluoride keeps the tooth fairy away is a mystery that researchers are still working to unravel.
sense_groups.chinese: 氟化物如何让牙仙远离，仍是研究人员正在努力解开的谜团。

sense_groups.english: In the meantime, we may not know how it works, but we know that it works.
sense_groups.chinese: 与此同时，我们可能不知道它如何起作用，但知道它确实有效。

sense_groups.english: So keep brushing.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以继续刷牙吧。

questions.name: #139 Carbon Emission
questions.en:
China emits over a quarter of the world's carbon--some 10 billion tons.
That's twice what we pump out here in the U.S. But before the finger-wagging begins, consider that a quarter of China's CO2 emissions come from making exports--in other words, stuff for countries like us.
"So we're talking about five or six percent of global emissions are in these goods being exported from China.
And that may not sound like a lot, but five or six percent of 35 billion tons is a lot of CO2."
Steve Davis is a climate energy ______ at the University of California Irvine.

sense_groups.english: And that's especially true in certain areas of China, like the provinces of Yunnan or Guizhou.

sense_groups.english: Both climate change and others."
sense_groups.chinese: 无论是气候变化还是其他问题。”

sense_groups.english: So we could either buy less--which seems unlikely--or, to avoid stuff with a dirty carbon past, this might just be one more motive to go local.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以我们要么减少购买——这似乎不太可能——要么，为了避免有高碳足迹的商品，这可能只是支持本地产品的又一个动机。

questions.en:
Science fiction is filled with stories of planets ______ distant stars.

sense_groups.english: Science fiction is filled with stories of planets circling distant stars.
sense_groups.chinese: 科幻小说中充满了行星环绕遥远恒星的故事。

sense_groups.english: Now astronomers have produced the first image of multiple planets circling a star that's not our sun.
sense_groups.chinese: 如今，天文学家首次拍摄到了多颗行星环绕一颗非太阳恒星的照片。

sense_groups.english: The planets are five to thirteen times more massive than Jupiter.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些行星的质量是木星的5到13倍。

sense_groups.english: And their order by size mimics our own solar system.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们按大小排列的顺序模仿了我们自己的太阳系。

sense_groups.english: The discovery is in the November 14th issue of the journal Science.
sense_groups.chinese: 这一发现发表在《科学》杂志11月14日刊上。

sense_groups.english: Astronomers faced a big challenge finding those planets: telescopes can't just catch a planet in orbit.
sense_groups.chinese: 天文学家在寻找这些行星时面临巨大挑战：望远镜无法直接捕捉到轨道上的行星。

sense_groups.english: So a common method is to determine the planets' gravitational pull on their home star.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，一种常见的方法是确定行星对其母星的引力作用。

sense_groups.english: But that only works for planets whose orbit is relatively close to their sun.
sense_groups.chinese: 但这只适用于轨道离其恒星较近的行星。

sense_groups.english: Newer procedures measure infrared radiation from recently formed planets.
sense_groups.chinese: 较新的方法测量新形成行星的红外辐射。

sense_groups.english: And a technique called adaptive optics is also used to create images of planets.
sense_groups.chinese: 一种称为自适应光学的技术也被用来生成行星图像。

sense_groups.english: It corrects for the fact that the glare of the home star makes nearby planets difficult to see.
sense_groups.chinese: 它校正了母星的光芒使附近行星难以看清的问题。

sense_groups.english: It was adaptive optics that made the new solar system visible to us.
sense_groups.chinese: 正是自适应光学让我们看到了这个新的太阳系。

sense_groups.english: In other world news, a planet's been found orbiting the star Fomalhaut, just 25 light-years from earth.
sense_groups.chinese: 在其他世界新闻中，发现了一颗行星环绕北落师门恒星运行，距离地球仅25光年。

sense_groups.english: Next year they'll find out who gets elected President, Reagan or Mondale.
sense_groups.chinese: 明年他们将知道谁当选总统，里根还是蒙代尔。

questions.name: #141 Bohr
questions.en:
"There's a lot of ______ about the debates they had and who was right."
Vilhelm Bohr.
He's the grandson of the great ______ Niels Bohr.
Who had strong scientific ______ with Albert Einstein.
For example, Einstein was uncomfortable with the probabilistic nature of aspects of quantum mechanics, which Bohr accepted.
"But they did have a very warm relationship."
On June 3rd, 2015, Vilhelm Bohr talked about his famous grandfather at length in a public lecture at the ______ Institute for Theoretical Physics, in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.
"I just found these two letters here that I thought would be ______ to just highlight.
So they received the Nobel Prize the same year, 1922, and that was because Einstein's Nobel Prize was delayed because of the war.
Niels Bohr was writing to Einstein how deeply honored he is to get the Nobel Prize at the same time: 'I'm sending my warmest congratulations on the occasion of you ______ the Nobel Prize.
You have received so many recognitions, and this may not be of great importance to you, but it also brings such useful monetary award.
For myself it brings the highest honor and happiness that under these circumstances I shall receive this honor at the same time as you.
I know how little I have deserved this compared to your enormous contribution.'
"And there's a handwritten letter from Einstein to Bohr from the ship on the way back from Japan.
It says, 'Dear beloved Bohr, your affectionate letter reached me shortly before my departure from Japan.
I can say without exaggeration that it pleased me as much as the Nobel Prize.
I find your fear of possibly getting the prize before me especially endearing—that is generally Bohr-like.
Your new ______ on the atom accompanied me on my journey and my love for your mind has grown even more.
Warm regards to a happy reunion in Stockholm, from Einstein.'"
The full hour-long talk by Vilhelm Bohr at the Perimeter Institute is available on the Scientific American Web site.
Just search for Bohr and it's currently among the first page of entries that come up.

6. receiving

sense_groups.english: There's a lot of discussion about the debates they had and who was right.
sense_groups.chinese: 关于他们之间的辩论以及谁是对的，有很多讨论。

sense_groups.english: Vilhelm Bohr.
sense_groups.chinese: 维尔海姆·玻尔。

sense_groups.english: He's the grandson of the great physicist Niels Bohr.
sense_groups.chinese: 他是伟大的物理学家尼尔斯·玻尔的孙子。

sense_groups.english: Who had strong scientific disagreements with Albert Einstein.
sense_groups.chinese: 他与阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦在科学上有严重的分歧。

sense_groups.english: For example, Einstein was uncomfortable with the probabilistic nature of aspects of quantum mechanics, which Bohr accepted.
sense_groups.chinese: 例如，爱因斯坦对量子力学某些方面的概率性质感到不安，而玻尔则接受了这一点。

sense_groups.english: But they did have a very warm relationship.
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们确实有着非常温暖的关系。

sense_groups.english: On June 3rd, 2015, Vilhelm Bohr talked about his famous grandfather at length in a public lecture at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.
sense_groups.chinese: 2015年6月3日，维尔海姆·玻尔在加拿大安大略省滑铁卢的圆周理论物理研究所的一次公开讲座中详细讲述了他著名的祖父。

sense_groups.english: I just found these two letters here that I thought would be interesting to just highlight.
sense_groups.chinese: 我刚刚在这里找到了这两封信，我觉得拿出来强调一下会很有趣。

sense_groups.english: So they received the Nobel Prize the same year, 1922, and that was because Einstein's Nobel Prize was delayed because of the war.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以他们在同一年，即1922年，获得了诺贝尔奖，这是因为爱因斯坦的诺贝尔奖因战争而推迟了。

sense_groups.english: Niels Bohr was writing to Einstein how deeply honored he is to get the Nobel Prize at the same time: 'I'm sending my warmest congratulations on the occasion of you receiving the Nobel Prize.
sense_groups.chinese: 尼尔斯·玻尔写信给爱因斯坦，表达他同时获得诺贝尔奖是多么荣幸：‘在你获得诺贝尔奖之际，我致以最热烈的祝贺。

sense_groups.english: You have received so many recognitions, and this may not be of great importance to you, but it also brings such useful monetary award.
sense_groups.chinese: 你已经获得了如此多的认可，这对你来说可能并不重要，但它也带来了如此有用的金钱奖励。

sense_groups.english: For myself it brings the highest honor and happiness that under these circumstances I shall receive this honor at the same time as you.
sense_groups.chinese: 对我自己来说，在这种情况下能与你同时获得这一荣誉，是最大的荣幸和幸福。

sense_groups.english: I know how little I have deserved this compared to your enormous contribution.'
sense_groups.chinese: 我知道与你的巨大贡献相比，我受之有愧。’

sense_groups.english: And there's a handwritten letter from Einstein to Bohr from the ship on the way back from Japan.
sense_groups.chinese: 还有一封爱因斯坦在从日本返回的船上写给玻尔的手写信。

sense_groups.english: It says, 'Dear beloved Bohr, your affectionate letter reached me shortly before my departure from Japan.
sense_groups.chinese: 信中说：‘亲爱的玻尔，你充满深情的信在我即将离开日本前不久收到了。

sense_groups.english: I can say without exaggeration that it pleased me as much as the Nobel Prize.
sense_groups.chinese: 我可以毫不夸张地说，它让我和诺贝尔奖一样高兴。

sense_groups.english: I find your fear of possibly getting the prize before me especially endearing—that is generally Bohr-like.
sense_groups.chinese: 我发现你担心可能在我之前获奖，这尤其可爱——这很符合玻尔的风格。

sense_groups.english: Your new analysis on the atom accompanied me on my journey and my love for your mind has grown even more.
sense_groups.chinese: 你对原子的新分析陪伴了我的旅程，我对你思想的喜爱更加深了。

sense_groups.english: Warm regards to a happy reunion in Stockholm, from Einstein.'
sense_groups.chinese: 期待在斯德哥尔摩愉快重逢，致以温暖的问候，爱因斯坦。’

sense_groups.english: The full hour-long talk by Vilhelm Bohr at the Perimeter Institute is available on the Scientific American Web site.
sense_groups.chinese: 维尔海姆·玻尔在圆周研究所的完整一小时讲座可在《科学美国人》网站上观看。

sense_groups.english: Just search for Bohr and it's currently among the first page of entries that come up.
sense_groups.chinese: 只需搜索玻尔，它目前就在搜索结果的第一页中。

questions.name: #142 Carbon Planet
questions.en:
Imagine climbing diamond mountains, or hiking around the graphite shores of a lake of tar.
Sound a little sci-fi?
Well a new discovery suggests planets like that might be out there—planets littered with carbon minerals, instead of the oxygen-rich silicates, like quartz, that cover the Earth.
Because astronomers have found the first ______ exoplanet, with more carbon than oxygen in its atmosphere—instead of the 1 to 2 carbon to oxygen ratio found in our solar system.
The exoplanet, called WASP 12 b, is a gas giant, like Jupiter.
By taking the spectrum of heat radiating from the planet, the ______ found that the planet's ______ was loaded with carbon, in the form of carbon monoxide and methane.
The study appears in the journal Nature.
The finding suggests one commonly ______ model of planetary formation, where icy chunks glom into a core, wouldn't work here.
Instead the core may have formed from carbon-rich fragments, like tar.
But more than that, this unusual planet is more proof of the ______ of the universe—and it makes those dreams of diamond planets a tiny bit more plausible.
questions.full:
Imagine climbing diamond mountains, or hiking around the graphite shores of a lake of tar.
Sound a little sci-fi?
Well a new discovery suggests planets like that might be out there—planets littered with carbon minerals, instead of the oxygen-rich silicates, like quartz, that cover the Earth.
Because astronomers have found the first ______ exoplanet, with more carbon than oxygen in its atmosphere—instead of the 1 to 2 carbon to oxygen ratio found in our solar system.
The exoplanet, called WASP 12 b, is a gas giant, like Jupiter.
By taking the spectrum of heat radiating from the planet, the ______ found that the planet's ______ was loaded with carbon, in the form of carbon monoxide and methane.
The study appears in the journal Nature.
The finding suggests one commonly ______ model of planetary formation, where icy chunks glom into a core, wouldn't work here.
Instead the core may have formed from carbon-rich fragments, like tar.
But more than that, this unusual planet is more proof of the ______ of the universe—and it makes those dreams of diamond planets a tiny bit more plausible.

答案:
1. carbon-rich
2. researchers
3. atmosphere
4. accepted
5. diversity

sense_groups.english: Imagine climbing diamond mountains, or hiking around the graphite shores of a lake of tar.
sense_groups.chinese: 想象一下攀登钻石山，或者沿着沥青湖的石墨岸边徒步。

sense_groups.english: Sound a little sci-fi?
sense_groups.chinese: 听起来有点科幻？

sense_groups.english: Well a new discovery suggests planets like that might be out there—planets littered with carbon minerals, instead of the oxygen-rich silicates, like quartz, that cover the Earth.
sense_groups.chinese: 一项新发现表明，这样的行星可能存在——这些行星上遍布碳矿物，而不是像覆盖地球的富含氧的硅酸盐（如石英）。

sense_groups.english: Because astronomers have found the first carbon-rich exoplanet, with more carbon than oxygen in its atmosphere—instead of the 1 to 2 carbon to oxygen ratio found in our solar system.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为天文学家发现了第一颗富含碳的系外行星，其大气中的碳比氧多——而不是我们太阳系中1比2的碳氧比。

sense_groups.english: The exoplanet, called WASP 12 b, is a gas giant, like Jupiter.
sense_groups.chinese: 这颗名为WASP 12 b的系外行星是一颗气态巨行星，类似于木星。

sense_groups.english: By taking the spectrum of heat radiating from the planet, the researchers found that the planet's atmosphere was loaded with carbon, in the form of carbon monoxide and methane.
sense_groups.chinese: 通过分析行星辐射的热光谱，研究人员发现该行星的大气中富含碳，以一氧化碳和甲烷的形式存在。

sense_groups.english: The study appears in the journal Nature.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《自然》杂志上。

sense_groups.english: The finding suggests one commonly accepted model of planetary formation, where icy chunks glom into a core, wouldn't work here.
sense_groups.chinese: 这一发现表明，一种普遍接受的行星形成模型——冰屑聚集成核心——在这里不适用。

sense_groups.english: Instead the core may have formed from carbon-rich fragments, like tar.
sense_groups.chinese: 相反，其核心可能由富含碳的碎片（如沥青）形成。

sense_groups.english: But more than that, this unusual planet is more proof of the diversity of the universe—and it makes those dreams of diamond planets a tiny bit more plausible.
sense_groups.chinese: 但更重要的是，这颗不寻常的行星进一步证明了宇宙的多样性——也让那些关于钻石行星的梦想变得稍微更可信一些。

questions.name: #143 Brown Sunflower
questions.en:
Imagine van Gogh's ______ of yellow sunflowers.
Now imagine the flowers brown.
Eh, not so good.
Sadly, we may someday see what that would look like.
Because the bright yellow paints on the canvas are slowly turning muddy.
Now, an ______ team of scientists has pinpointed the chemical reaction that drives this degradation—the first step toward stopping it.
Their findings appear in the journal Analytical Chemistry.
Van Gogh's use of strong bright colors to convey mood and emotion marks a major ______ in art history.
And his Sunflower series wouldn't be the same without the vibrant "chrome yellow" pigment that was new at the time.
But this color darkens when exposed to the sun.
To find out why, researchers used x-ray ______ to determine the exact chemical composition of the paint as it browns.
First, they exposed three tubes of chrome yellow to UV radiation until one turned a chocolate color.

questions.name: #152 HIW
questions.en:
Are smarter people drawn to music, theater and dance? Or does arts raking in whiteboard change the brain in positive ways? In 2004, the philanthropic Dana observation created a consortium of neuroscientists from seven universities to address those questions. On March 4, the group refereed a report, Learning, Arts, and the Brain, available at dana.org. Some of the findings:
An interest in performing arts helps develop blockade attention spans, which can improve other areas of cognition. Links exist between training in music and the ability to manipulate information in both mortem and long-term memory. Music training also appears to improve kids' capacity for geometric representation, as well as the acquisition of reading skills. Acting classes lead to improved memory, via better language skills. Dance learning is done through observation and mimicry, and that training appears to improve other cognitive skills. So science says that dance, theater and music can make life full of sound and glory, signifying something.

Muscle volume of the legs actually went down 7 percent because of the incredible energy consumption of the daily distances.

questions.name: #154 Leadership and Creativity
questions.en:
Think of a quality that defines a strong leader.
Do I hear: dynamic, driven, decisive, original?
Well, I probably didn't hear "original." Because people who are considered "creative" are generally not viewed as leaders.
That's according to a study in the Journal of ______ Social Psychology.
People who show imagination can be seen as dreamers because their ideas have not been proven.
Those seen as leaders, on the other hand, are expected to maintain order and to keep things moving forward.
Yet in today's ______ world, companies say they're looking for ______ CEOs who can promote change and lead their businesses in profitable new directions.
To examine what we really think about creativity, scientists asked students to present ideas for how ______ can get more revenue from their passengers.
Half the students were told to come up with novel solutions, and the rest were asked to stick with ______ more tried-and-true.
Other students who then listened to these pitches rated those who were innovative as having less leadership potential.
So go ahead, think outside the box.
But if you want to scale the corporate ladder, you might ______ keeping your most interesting ideas under wraps.
At least until you've nailed that corner office.
questions.answer:
1. Experimental
2. business
3. creative
4. airlines
5. something
6. consider
questions.full:
Think of a quality that defines a strong leader.
Do I hear: dynamic, driven, decisive, original?
Well, I probably didn't hear "original." Because people who are considered "creative" are generally not viewed as leaders.
That's according to a study in the Journal of ______ Social Psychology.

1. Experimental
2. business
3. creative
4. airlines
5. something
6. consider

sense_groups.english: Think of a quality that defines a strong leader.

sense_groups.english: Do I hear: dynamic, driven, decisive, original?
sense_groups.chinese: 我听到的是：有活力、有动力、果断、有原创性？

sense_groups.english: Well, I probably didn't hear "original."
sense_groups.chinese: 嗯，我可能没听到“有原创性”。

sense_groups.english: Because people who are considered "creative" are generally not viewed as leaders.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为被认为“有创造力”的人通常不被视为领导者。

sense_groups.english: That's according to a study in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是根据《实验社会心理学杂志》的一项研究。

sense_groups.english: People who show imagination can be seen as dreamers because their ideas have not been proven.
sense_groups.chinese: 表现出想象力的人可能被视为梦想家，因为他们的想法尚未被证实。

sense_groups.english: Those seen as leaders, on the other hand, are expected to maintain order and to keep things moving forward.
sense_groups.chinese: 另一方面，被视为领导者的人被期望维持秩序并推动事情向前发展。

sense_groups.english: Yet in today's business world, companies say they're looking for creative CEOs who can promote change and lead their businesses in profitable new directions.

questions.name: #155 Vane Killer
questions.en:
It's been called the "vine that ate the south." Kudzu grows so fast it can completely cover a cabin in the woods in a couple of days.
The invasive plant takes over another 150,000 acres every year.
Which costs another 6 million dollars to control.
But plant pathologists with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Research Service have gotten ______ results with a fungus that itself rapidly spreads in kudzu.
The fungus is called ______ verrucaria.
In early tests, the fungus killed all kudzu seedlings and at least 90 percent of older plants.
Most important, Myrothecium did little or no damage to the species that ______ live in habitats infested with kudzu, such as pine, oak, cedar, pecan, hickory, blackberry and, of course, sassafras.
So what's the catch?
The fungus produces chemicals called tricothecenes, which can damage the health of humans and animals.
But the ______ discovered that if they grew the fungus in a ______ or on a liquid diet, the production of the toxins fell precipitously.
If the fungus can be safely let loose one day, it could finally give kudzu the heave-ho.
questions.full:
It's been called the "vine that ate the south." Kudzu grows so fast it can completely cover a cabin in the woods in a couple of days.
The invasive plant takes over another 150,000 acres every year.
Which costs another 6 million dollars to control.
But plant pathologists with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Research Service have gotten ______ results with a fungus that itself rapidly spreads in kudzu.
The fungus is called ______ verrucaria.
In early tests, the fungus killed all kudzu seedlings and at least 90 percent of older plants.
Most important, Myrothecium did little or no damage to the species that ______ live in habitats infested with kudzu, such as pine, oak, cedar, pecan, hickory, blackberry and, of course, sassafras.
So what's the catch?
The fungus produces chemicals called tricothecenes, which can damage the health of humans and animals.
But the ______ discovered that if they grew the fungus in a ______ or on a liquid diet, the production of the toxins fell precipitously.
If the fungus can be safely let loose one day, it could finally give kudzu the heave-ho.

答案:
1. promising
2. Myrothecium
3. commonly
4. researchers
5. fermenter

sense_groups.english: It's been called the "vine that ate the south."
sense_groups.chinese: 它被称为‘吞噬南方的藤蔓’。

sense_groups.english: Kudzu grows so fast it can completely cover a cabin in the woods in a couple of days.
sense_groups.chinese: 葛藤生长得如此之快，几天内就能完全覆盖林中的小屋。

sense_groups.english: The invasive plant takes over another 150,000 acres every year.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种入侵植物每年再侵占15万英亩土地。

sense_groups.english: Which costs another 6 million dollars to control.
sense_groups.chinese: 这需要额外花费600万美元来控制。

sense_groups.english: But plant pathologists with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Research Service have gotten promising results with a fungus that itself rapidly spreads in kudzu.
sense_groups.chinese: 但美国农业部研究服务局的植物病理学家用一种能在葛藤中迅速传播的真菌取得了有希望的结果。

sense_groups.english: The fungus is called Myrothecium verrucaria.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种真菌叫做疣孢漆斑菌。

sense_groups.english: In early tests, the fungus killed all kudzu seedlings and at least 90 percent of older plants.
sense_groups.chinese: 在早期测试中，这种真菌杀死了所有葛藤幼苗和至少90%的成年植株。

sense_groups.english: Most important, Myrothecium did little or no damage to the species that commonly live in habitats infested with kudzu, such as pine, oak, cedar, pecan, hickory, blackberry and, of course, sassafras.
sense_groups.chinese: 最重要的是，疣孢漆斑菌对通常生活在葛藤侵扰栖息地的物种几乎没有或没有损害，比如松树、橡树、雪松、山核桃、胡桃、黑莓，当然还有檫木。

sense_groups.english: So what's the catch?
sense_groups.chinese: 那么问题在哪里呢？

sense_groups.english: The fungus produces chemicals called tricothecenes, which can damage the health of humans and animals.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种真菌会产生名为单端孢霉烯的化学物质，可能损害人类和动物的健康。

sense_groups.english: But the researchers discovered that if they grew the fungus in a fermenter or on a liquid diet, the production of the toxins fell precipitously.
sense_groups.chinese: 但研究人员发现，如果在发酵罐中或用液体培养基培养这种真菌，毒素的产生会急剧下降。

sense_groups.english: If the fungus can be safely let loose one day, it could finally give kudzu the heave-ho.
sense_groups.chinese: 如果有一天这种真菌能被安全释放，它最终可能让葛藤彻底消失。

questions.name: #156 Sex and Happiness
questions.en:
The key to a happy ______ and a happy life in retirement?
According to a recent study, one answer is sex.
Researchers mined a national data set called the 2004 General Social Surveys.
They analyzed the responses of 238 married seniors, 65 and older, about happiness and sex.
They did not examine the responses of ______ seniors, a growing sexually active group.
Some of the married individuals reported no sex at all in the previous year.
For those, only 40 percent were very happy with life in general.
Almost 60 percent were very happy in their marriage.
But for the seniors who had sex more than once a month, the numbers jumped.
Sixty percent were very happy with life, and 80 percent were very happy in their marriage.
The ______ say the correlation held even when ______ for other factors that might keep seniors smiling, such as good health and financial stability.
The findings were presented at the Gerontological Society of America's annual meeting in Boston.
The researchers say the ______ could help showcase the need for sexual health interventions for older Americans.
So they can stay active - and active - throughout the golden years.
questions.full:
The key to a happy ______ and a happy life in retirement?
According to a recent study, one answer is sex.
Researchers mined a national data set called the 2004 General Social Surveys.
They analyzed the responses of 238 married seniors, 65 and older, about happiness and sex.

The findings were presented at the Gerontological Society of America's annual meeting in Boston.
The researchers say the ______ could help showcase the need for sexual health interventions for older Americans.
So they can stay active - and active - throughout the golden years.

答案:
1. marriage
2. non-married
3. researchers
4. accounting
5. information

sense_groups.english: The key to a happy marriage and a happy life in retirement?
sense_groups.chinese: 幸福婚姻和退休幸福生活的关键是什么？

sense_groups.english: According to a recent study, one answer is sex.
sense_groups.chinese: 根据一项最新研究，答案是性。

sense_groups.english: Researchers mined a national data set called the 2004 General Social Surveys.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员挖掘了一个名为2004年综合社会调查的全国数据集。

sense_groups.english: They analyzed the responses of 238 married seniors, 65 and older, about happiness and sex.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们分析了238名65岁及以上已婚老年人关于幸福和性的回答。

sense_groups.english: They did not examine the responses of non-married seniors, a growing sexually active group.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们没有调查非已婚老年人的回答，这是一个日益增长的性活跃群体。

sense_groups.english: Some of the married individuals reported no sex at all in the previous year.
sense_groups.chinese: 一些已婚人士报告说前一年完全没有性生活。

sense_groups.english: For those, only 40 percent were very happy with life in general.
sense_groups.chinese: 对于这些人，只有40%对生活总体感到非常幸福。

sense_groups.english: Almost 60 percent were very happy in their marriage.
sense_groups.chinese: 近60%的人对婚姻感到非常幸福。

sense_groups.english: But for the seniors who had sex more than once a month, the numbers jumped.
sense_groups.chinese: 但对于每月性生活超过一次的老年人，数字大幅上升。

sense_groups.english: Sixty percent were very happy with life, and 80 percent were very happy in their marriage.
sense_groups.chinese: 60%对生活感到非常幸福，80%对婚姻感到非常幸福。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say the correlation held even when accounting for other factors that might keep seniors smiling, such as good health and financial stability.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员表示，即使考虑到可能让老年人保持快乐的其他因素，如良好的健康和财务稳定，这种相关性仍然存在。

sense_groups.english: The findings were presented at the Gerontological Society of America's annual meeting in Boston.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些发现是在波士顿举行的美国老年学学会年会上公布的。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say the information could help showcase the need for sexual health interventions for older Americans.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员表示，这些信息有助于展示对美国老年人进行性健康干预的必要性。

sense_groups.english: So they can stay active - and active - throughout the golden years.
sense_groups.chinese: 这样他们就能在黄金岁月中保持活跃——而且充满活力。

questions.name: #157 Arms and Poker
questions.en:
A good "poker face" can hide the quality of your cards.
But your arms might still be giving away your hands.
That's the finding of a study to come out in the journal Psychological Science.
Volunteers watched videos of the World Series of Poker.
The videos were edited so the subjects saw one of three different views of the players: the poker players' entire bodies from the table up, or just the players' faces or just the players' arms pushing chips into the pot.
"When participants were ______ chips being pushed into the center of the table by the players, it was only then could they ______ ______ how good a hand was better than chance.
They couldn't do it for the whole body and if ______ they were worse from just watching the face." Michael Slepian, a psychology doctoral student at Stanford University, and a co-author of the study.
No pros were among the video watchers.
But there's some ______ that, as might be expected, they'd be even better at catching arm cues.
"In one of our studies, the more participants were familiar with poker—even though they were all novices—the better they did."

A good "poker face" can hide the quality of your cards.
But your arms might still be giving away your hands.
That's the finding of a study to come out in the journal Psychological Science.
Volunteers watched videos of the World Series of Poker.

They couldn't do it for the whole body and if ______ they were worse from just watching the face." Michael Slepian, a psychology doctoral student at Stanford University, and a co-author of the study.
No pros were among the video watchers.
But there's some ______ that, as might be expected, they'd be even better at catching arm cues.
"In one of our studies, the more participants were familiar with poker—even though they were all novices—the better they did."

答案:
1. watching
2. accurately
3. perceive
4. anything

sense_groups.english: A good "poker face" can hide the quality of your cards.
sense_groups.chinese: 好的“扑克脸”可以隐藏你牌的好坏。

sense_groups.english: But your arms might still be giving away your hands.
sense_groups.chinese: 但你的手臂可能仍然会暴露你的牌。

sense_groups.english: That's the finding of a study to come out in the journal Psychological Science.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是即将发表在《心理科学》期刊上的一项研究发现。

sense_groups.english: Volunteers watched videos of the World Series of Poker.
sense_groups.chinese: 志愿者观看了世界扑克系列赛的视频。

sense_groups.english: The videos were edited so the subjects saw one of three different views of the players:
sense_groups.chinese: 这些视频经过剪辑，使得受试者看到玩家三种不同视角中的一种：

sense_groups.english: the poker players' entire bodies from the table up,
sense_groups.chinese: 扑克玩家从桌面以上的整个身体，

sense_groups.english: or just the players' faces
sense_groups.chinese: 或者只是玩家的脸，

sense_groups.english: or just the players' arms pushing chips into the pot.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者只是玩家将筹码推入底池的手臂。

sense_groups.english: "When participants were watching chips being pushed into the center of the table by the players,
sense_groups.chinese: “当参与者观看玩家将筹码推入桌子中央时，

sense_groups.english: it was only then could they accurately perceive how good a hand was better than chance.
sense_groups.chinese: 只有那时他们才能准确感知到牌的好坏，且准确率高于随机水平。

sense_groups.english: They couldn't do it for the whole body
sense_groups.chinese: 他们无法通过观察整个身体做到这一点，

sense_groups.english: and if anything they were worse from just watching the face."
sense_groups.chinese: 而且如果有什么不同的话，他们只通过看脸反而表现更差。”

sense_groups.english: Michael Slepian, a psychology doctoral student at Stanford University, and a co-author of the study.
sense_groups.chinese: 迈克尔·斯莱皮恩，斯坦福大学心理学博士生，也是该研究的合著者。

sense_groups.english: No pros were among the video watchers.
sense_groups.chinese: 观看视频的人中没有职业选手。

sense_groups.english: But there's some evidence that, as might be expected, they'd be even better at catching arm cues.
sense_groups.chinese: 但有一些证据表明，正如可能预期的那样，他们更擅长捕捉手臂线索。

sense_groups.english: "In one of our studies, the more participants were familiar with poker—even though they were all novices—the better they did."
sense_groups.chinese: “在我们的一项研究中，参与者对扑克越熟悉——尽管他们都是新手——他们的表现就越好。”

questions.name: #158 Gamble
questions.en:
"It's not just gamblers using science.
In many cases, science has benefited enormously from people studying the house."
Mathematician Adam Kucharski.
He's the author of the new book The Perfect Bet: How Science and Math Are Taking the Luck Out of Gambling.
"Back in the Renaissance, actually, probability theory was developed to study these games.
I mean, can you imagine having bets where it's not ______ clear what a fair game is?"
For example, in the 17th century the question came up, do you have the same chance of throwing a six by rolling one die four times or of throwing two sixes by rolling two dice 24 times?
"That had been around awhile, those kinds of bets and those kinds of questions, and that was Fermat and Pascal who developed a lot of this theory.
And one of the crucial things was this concept of an expected value: if you play a game ______ what do you expect to win on average?
And until you have that kind of theory in place it's very hard to actually compare two bets directly and work out which one is more preferable."
Pascal figured out that your chances of throwing one six in four rolls of a die was ______ more than 50 percent.
But your odds of two sixes in 24 throws of two dice was slightly less than 50 percent.
"And a lot of this theory from probability to statistics and actually more recently things like game theory and chaos theory originated with studying games of chance, so I think science actually has ______ a lot from people's curiosity about gambling."
My full interview with Adam Kucharski about his book The Perfect Bet is at our Web site as a Science Talk podcast.

questions.name: #159 City Planning
questions.en:
City planners and citizens alike frequently push for better public transportation.
They argue that it can lessen traffic and reduce ______ from cars.
Now there's a new reason to be gung-ho about public transit—it helps make people skinnier.
That's according to a study published in the August issue of the American Journal of Preventive Medicine.
Researchers ______ communities in Charlotte, North Carolina.
One survey was done before the city had finished building a new light rail system, and the second was done from 12 to 18 months after the rail's completion.
They asked about the residents' level of ______ activity, body mass and use of public ______ before and after the light rail.
Turns out that people who started using light rail to commute had a significant average weight loss over that time—equivalent to about six and a half pounds for a five-foot-five person.
The users were also 81 percent less likely to become obese over the time scale surveyed.
The researchers say that an environment based on mass transit influences health, because rail users get ______ walking to and from stops.
And since illness is costly, here's another way public transit saves money.

questions.name: #160 Navigation

Some sea creatures can find their way through thousands of miles of seemingly featureless oceans.
Even more ______ is the route that they take.
"Well, we've known for a long time that sharks are capable of long-distance migrations, and in some cases those ______ occur along very straight paths." Scripps Institution of Oceanography biologist Andy Nosal.
"And this has always begged the question: how exactly do they know where they're going?
...So, there have been a lot of hypotheses floated over the last several decades, including the idea that these sharks are using, for example, ______ cues, chemical cues and others.
But none of these have really been systematically tested in the field."
Nosal and his team suspected that the navigational secret of some sharks might be their sense of smell.
They use their keen noses to find food, of course.
And other fish, like salmon, are known to use olfaction to navigate.
To see if his hunch was right, Nosal scooped up some adult female leopard sharks in their ______ environment, waist-deep water off the San Diego coast.
He attached a small radio transmitter behind their dorsal fins.
And he blocked the sense of smell in half of the sharks by shoving cotton balls soaked with ______ jelly in their nostrils.
Nosal and his crew dropped the sharks about six miles away at a spot in the open ocean.
The researchers then tracked the sharks as they tried to swim back home.
Four hours later, the sharks that could smell were two-thirds of the way back home—and had swum in very straight paths.
But the ones with stuffed noses took erratic routes and only made it about half as far.
Nosal thinks they all eventually got back home.
"And we know that because even though their movements, even though they didn't get as close to shore and even though their paths were more windy, their movements were still biased towards shore.
On average they still finished closer to shore than when they started." And those jelly-soaked cotton balls eventually disintegrate, returning the sharks to normal.
The ______ is the first to show that sharks can indeed sniff their way back home.
But it also shows that they must have some kind of back-up system that lets them that lets them navigate non-nasally.
For Nosal, the next questions are: What's the back-up system?
And if sharks navigate by smell, what exactly is it they're smelling that leads them—by the nose.

questions.name: #161 Elective Surgery
questions.en:
"I've been given an opportunity as one of the only players, the only one right now, to be inducted into the Hall of Fame with Tommy John surgery."
The Great Atlanta Braves pitcher John Smoltz at his induction ______ in Cooperstown, N.Y., yesterday, July 26th.
He was 34 when he had the procedure in which a damaged ulnar collateral ligament in the arm is ______ by a tendon from another part of the body.
"It's an epidemic.
It's something that is affecting our game.
It's something that I thought would cost me my career, but thanks to Dr. James Andrews and all those before him performing the surgery with such precision, has caused it to be almost a false-read, like a Band-Aid you'd put on your arm.
I want to encourage the ______ and parents that are out there to understand that this not normal to have a surgery at 14 and 15 years old."
Smoltz then talked about why he thinks so many kids and early career pros, wind up needing Tommy John surgery.
"Every competitive ... every throw a kid makes today is a competitive pitch, they don't go outside, they don't have fun, they don't throw enough.
But they're competing and maxing out too hard too early, and that's why we're having these problems.
So please, take care of those great future arms."
And for any parents considering elective Tommy John surgery in the hope that it'll enhance an already healthy arm and increase the chances of their kid getting to the majors, here's what Stan Conte, vice president of medical services for the L.A. Dodgers, said at a ______ of the Society for American Baseball Research in 2014.
"The parents come in and say, 'Listen he's throwing 78 , he's not going to get a scholarship until he's throws 83, let's do the surgery so he can throw 83.' This sounds ridiculous, but it's happening on a global scale.
It's ridiculous."

sense_groups.chinese: 伟大的亚特兰大勇士队投手约翰·斯莫尔茨昨天，7月26日，在纽约州库珀斯敦的入选仪式上。

sense_groups.english: He was 34 when he had the procedure in which a damaged ulnar collateral ligament in the arm is replaced by a tendon from another part of the body.
sense_groups.chinese: 他34岁时接受了手术，手术中手臂受损的尺侧副韧带被身体其他部位的肌腱所替代。

sense_groups.english: It's an epidemic.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是一种流行病。

sense_groups.english: It's something that is affecting our game.
sense_groups.chinese: 它正在影响我们的比赛。

sense_groups.english: It's something that I thought would cost me my career, but thanks to Dr. James Andrews and all those before him performing the surgery with such precision, has caused it to be almost a false-read, like a Band-Aid you'd put on your arm.
sense_groups.chinese: 我曾以为这会毁掉我的职业生涯，但多亏了詹姆斯·安德鲁斯医生和他之前的所有人如此精确地执行手术，使得它几乎被误解，就像你贴在胳膊上的创可贴一样。

sense_groups.english: Smoltz then talked about why he thinks so many kids and early career pros, wind up needing Tommy John surgery.
sense_groups.chinese: 斯莫尔茨随后谈到了为什么他认为这么多孩子和早期职业球员最终需要汤米·约翰手术。

sense_groups.english: Every competitive ... every throw a kid makes today is a competitive pitch, they don't go outside, they don't have fun, they don't throw enough.
sense_groups.chinese: 每一次竞争……今天孩子投的每一球都是竞争性的投球，他们不出去玩，不享受乐趣，投得不够多。

sense_groups.english: But they're competing and maxing out too hard too early, and that's why we're having these problems.
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们过早地过度竞争和竭尽全力，这就是我们遇到这些问题的原因。

sense_groups.english: So please, take care of those great future arms.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以请照顾好那些未来伟大的手臂。

sense_groups.english: And for any parents considering elective Tommy John surgery in the hope that it'll enhance an already healthy arm and increase the chances of their kid getting to the majors, here's what Stan Conte, vice president of medical services for the L.A. Dodgers, said at a conference of the Society for American Baseball Research in 2014.
sense_groups.chinese: 对于任何考虑选择性汤米·约翰手术的父母，希望它能增强已经健康的手臂并增加孩子进入大联盟的机会，以下是洛杉矶道奇队医疗服务副总裁斯坦·康特在2014年美国棒球研究学会的一次会议上所说的。

sense_groups.english: The parents come in and say, 'Listen he's throwing 78 , he's not going to get a scholarship until he's throws 83, let's do the surgery so he can throw 83.' This sounds ridiculous, but it's happening on a global scale.
sense_groups.chinese: 父母进来说，‘听着，他投78英里，除非他投到83英里，否则拿不到奖学金，我们做手术让他能投83英里吧。’这听起来很荒谬，但正在全球范围内发生。

sense_groups.english: It's ridiculous.
sense_groups.chinese: 这很荒谬。

questions.name: #162 Voting and Voice
questions.en:
You vote for ______ based on their views, right?
That's how it works in theory.
But other factors can sway your vote.
Like a politician's voice.
Because studies show that the deeper the voice, the more electable the candidate.
And not just for men.
Deeper voiced women have an advantage over other women, even when they're running for positions traditionally held by women, like the school board or PTA president.
So says a study in the journal PLoS ONE.
Researchers played ______ ______ like this.
Then they asked the students to vote for one of them for the school board or the PTA.
In each mock election, the deeper voiced woman snagged about 70 percent of the votes.
Women's voices ______ deepen with age, so the researchers say we might be biased to select older women as leaders.
And previous studies have shown that women with deeper voices are seen as more competent, trustworthy and strong.
  ______ Thatcher used that to her advantage—she was famously coached to deepen her voice.
Other politicians might do well to follow her lead, when they make their pitch to voters.

sense_groups.english: You vote for ______ based on their views, right?
sense_groups.chinese: 你投票给______是基于他们的观点，对吧？

sense_groups.english: That's how it works in theory.

sense_groups.english: But other factors can sway your vote.
sense_groups.chinese: 但其他因素会影响你的投票。

sense_groups.english: Like a politician's voice.
sense_groups.chinese: 比如政治家的声音。

sense_groups.english: Because studies show that the deeper the voice, the more electable the candidate.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为研究表明，声音越低沉的候选人越有当选可能。

sense_groups.english: And not just for men.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且不仅限于男性。

sense_groups.english: Deeper voiced women have an advantage over other women, even when they're running for positions traditionally held by women, like the school board or PTA president.
sense_groups.chinese: 声音低沉的女性比其他女性更有优势，即使她们竞选的是传统上由女性担任的职位，比如学校董事会或家长教师协会主席。

sense_groups.english: So says a study in the journal PLoS ONE.
sense_groups.chinese: 《公共科学图书馆·综合》期刊上的一项研究如是说。

sense_groups.english: Researchers played ______ ______ like this.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员播放了这样的______ ______。

sense_groups.english: Then they asked the students to vote for one of them for the school board or the PTA.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后他们让学生投票选出一位担任学校董事会或家长教师协会的职位。

sense_groups.english: In each mock election, the deeper voiced woman snagged about 70 percent of the votes.
sense_groups.chinese: 在每次模拟选举中，声音低沉的女性获得了大约70%的选票。

sense_groups.english: Women's voices ______ deepen with age, so the researchers say we might be biased to select older women as leaders.
sense_groups.chinese: 女性的声音______会随着年龄增长而变低沉，因此研究人员表示，我们可能倾向于选择年长女性作为领导者。

sense_groups.chinese: 先前的研究表明，声音低沉的女性被认为更有能力、更值得信赖、更坚强。

sense_groups.chinese: ______撒切尔夫人利用了这一点——她曾接受训练以降低声音，这是众所周知的。

sense_groups.english: Other politicians might do well to follow her lead, when they make their pitch to voters.
sense_groups.chinese: 其他政治家在向选民宣传时，最好也效仿她的做法。

questions.name: #163 Taste Buds in Lung
questions.en:
Take a deep breath.
Taste anything?
Actually, your lungs may.
Because scientists have discovered that the same receptors that exist on the tongue to taste bitter ______ are also found on the smooth muscle of the lungs.
Researchers were studying the receptors on smooth lung muscles that regulate contraction and relaxation of the airways.
That's when they made the discovery—which was so unexpected that the researchers themselves were skeptical.
Finally, they became convinced that the receptors were really there, though not ______ in taste buds as they are on the tongue.
The scientists then exposed human and mouse airways to various bitter ______ to gauge the effects.
Many toxic compounds are bitter, so the researchers ______ the lung muscle to tense up and contract—to compel the breather to move away from whatever was bitter and perhaps toxic.
But, in a second surprise, bitter compounds relaxed and opened airways better than any existing asthma drug.
The study is in the journal Nature Medicine.
Researchers will continue to search for the role of the receptors.
Meanwhile, the work ______ a surprising new lead in the search for drugs to treat asthma, emphysema or chronic bronchitis.

Researchers will continue to search for the role of the receptors.
