sense_groups.english: What's the best way for students to really learn basic science?
sense_groups.chinese: 对于学生来说，真正学习基础科学的最佳方法是什么？

sense_groups.english: New research just presented at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science suggests an answer: freedom.
sense_groups.chinese: 刚刚在美国科学促进会年会上展示的新研究给出了一个答案：自由。

sense_groups.english: After years of watching nonscience majors struggle with biology courses, Steve Rissing of Ohio State University decided to see how the boring old cookbook method of teaching stacked up against something new.
sense_groups.chinese: 在多年观察非科学专业学生挣扎于生物课程后，俄亥俄州立大学的史蒂夫·里辛决定看看那种枯燥的旧式照本宣科的教学方法与新方法相比如何。

sense_groups.english: The old way was to give students a big textbook to follow and dumb down experiments.
sense_groups.chinese: 旧方法是给学生一本大教科书让他们跟着做，并简化实验。

sense_groups.english: Many students still scored poorly when asked about the basics.
sense_groups.chinese: 许多学生在被问及基础知识时仍然得分很低。

sense_groups.english: The new method gave students freedom.
sense_groups.chinese: 新方法给了学生自由。

sense_groups.english: They prepared their own enzyme solutions and were encouraged to come up with their own methods.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们自己准备酶溶液，并被鼓励提出自己的方法。

sense_groups.english: The result?
sense_groups.chinese: 结果呢？

sense_groups.english: Eighty-three percent of the free students gave the right answer to the simple question, "Where do enzymes occur in nature?"
sense_groups.chinese: 83%的自由组学生正确回答了简单问题：“酶在自然界中存在于何处？”

sense_groups.english: Just 23 percent of the cookbook group answered correctly.
sense_groups.chinese: 而照本宣科组只有23%回答正确。

sense_groups.english: The new methods could help train students to better see and understand the beauty of science.
sense_groups.chinese: 新方法有助于培养学生更好地观察和理解科学之美。

questions.name: #191 Dark Matter
questions.en:
Most of the universe's stuff is apparently dark matter, invisible material pervading the ______ and supplying the bulk of the ______ ______ holding galaxy ______ together.
The matter contained in the visible stars in the cluster just isn't enough to keep the clusters from flying apart.
Now comes one of the ______ pieces of evidence for dark matter.
The Hubble space ______ has found what looks like a ghostly ring, the remnant of a massive collision between two galaxy clusters sometime in the last two billion years.
The ring is about 2.6 million light years across and lies about five billion light years from earth.
A Johns Hopkins research team noticed the ring.
They can't directly see it, of course.
But they infer its existence because its gravity bends the light of more distant galaxies in the background.
One ______ was initially annoyed with the ring because he assumed the ring was some kind of problem or error.
A literature search turned up evidence of a collision between galactic clusters near the ring.
And computer simulations showed that a dark matter ring would indeed result, like the ripples on a pond.
questions.answer:
1. universe
2. gravitational
3. attraction
4. clusters
5. strongest
6. telescope
7. researcher
questions.full:
Most of the universe's stuff is apparently dark matter, invisible material pervading the ______ and supplying the bulk of the ______ ______ holding galaxy ______ together.
The matter contained in the visible stars in the cluster just isn't enough to keep the clusters from flying apart.
Now comes one of the ______ pieces of evidence for dark matter.

A Johns Hopkins research team noticed the ring.
They can't directly see it, of course.

One ______ was initially annoyed with the ring because he assumed the ring was some kind of problem or error.
A literature search turned up evidence of a collision between galactic clusters near the ring.
And computer simulations showed that a dark matter ring would indeed result, like the ripples on a pond.

答案:
1. universe
2. gravitational
3. attraction
4. clusters
5. strongest
6. telescope

sense_groups.english: Most of the universe's stuff is apparently dark matter,
sense_groups.chinese: 宇宙中的大部分物质显然是暗物质，

sense_groups.english: invisible material pervading the universe
sense_groups.chinese: 一种看不见的物质，遍布宇宙

sense_groups.english: and supplying the bulk of the gravitational attraction
sense_groups.chinese: 并提供了大部分的引力

sense_groups.english: holding galaxy clusters together.
sense_groups.chinese: 将星系团维系在一起。

sense_groups.english: The matter contained in the visible stars in the cluster just isn't enough to keep the clusters from flying apart.
sense_groups.chinese: 星系团中可见恒星所含的物质不足以阻止星系团飞散。

sense_groups.english: Now comes one of the strongest pieces of evidence for dark matter.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在出现了暗物质最有力的证据之一。

sense_groups.english: The Hubble space telescope has found what looks like a ghostly ring,
sense_groups.chinese: 哈勃太空望远镜发现了一个幽灵般的环，

sense_groups.english: the remnant of a massive collision between two galaxy clusters sometime in the last two billion years.
sense_groups.chinese: 这是过去二十亿年间两个星系团大规模碰撞的遗迹。

sense_groups.english: The ring is about 2.6 million light years across
sense_groups.chinese: 这个环直径约260万光年，

sense_groups.english: and lies about five billion light years from earth.
sense_groups.chinese: 距离地球约50亿光年。

sense_groups.english: A Johns Hopkins research team noticed the ring.
sense_groups.chinese: 约翰霍普金斯大学的一个研究团队注意到了这个环。

sense_groups.english: They can't directly see it, of course.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，他们无法直接看到它。

sense_groups.english: But they infer its existence because its gravity bends the light of more distant galaxies in the background.
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们推断其存在，因为它的引力弯曲了背景中更遥远星系的光线。

sense_groups.english: One researcher was initially annoyed with the ring
sense_groups.chinese: 一位研究人员最初对这个环感到恼火，

sense_groups.english: because he assumed the ring was some kind of problem or error.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为他以为这个环是某种问题或错误。

sense_groups.english: A literature search turned up evidence of a collision between galactic clusters near the ring.
sense_groups.chinese: 文献检索发现了环附近星系团碰撞的证据。

sense_groups.english: And computer simulations showed that a dark matter ring would indeed result,
sense_groups.chinese: 计算机模拟显示，确实会产生一个暗物质环，

sense_groups.english: like the ripples on a pond.
sense_groups.chinese: 就像池塘里的涟漪。

questions.name: #192 Recession and Health
questions.en:
It sounds paradoxical, but in wealthy countries, there's nothing like a recession to boost the population's health.
According to a report in the ______ 1st Canadian Medical ______ Journal, when our paychecks get lighter, we do more than tighten our purse strings—we also cinch our belts, kick bad habits and manage to lower our mortality rates.
Economic growth is usually ______ with increased life spans, but the report says that's only true for very poor countries.
  ______ looked at data from dozens of 20th century ______ health studies and found that, once per-capita income passed $5,000, recessions ______ helped health.
During lean times, people in ______ wealthy countries drink and smoke less and stop overeating.
They also go out less, which means fewer trips in the car.
It all adds up to fewer deaths from things like lung cancer, liver disease, heart attacks and car crashes.
The researchers say that fewer hours in the office can also mean more time with family and friends.
These close social interactions lead to less stress and better health.
Of course, some people may find more family time to be like a lot of good medicine—hard to swallow.
questions.answer:
1. September
2. Association
3. associated
4. Researchers
5. international
6. actually
7. relatively
questions.full:
It sounds paradoxical, but in wealthy countries, there's nothing like a recession to boost the population's health.

During lean times, people in ______ wealthy countries drink and smoke less and stop overeating.
They also go out less, which means fewer trips in the car.
It all adds up to fewer deaths from things like lung cancer, liver disease, heart attacks and car crashes.
The researchers say that fewer hours in the office can also mean more time with family and friends.
These close social interactions lead to less stress and better health.
Of course, some people may find more family time to be like a lot of good medicine—hard to swallow.

答案:
1. September
2. Association
3. associated
4. Researchers
5. international
6. actually
7. relatively

sense_groups.english: It sounds paradoxical, but in wealthy countries, there's nothing like a recession to boost the population's health.
sense_groups.chinese: 这听起来矛盾，但在富裕国家，没有什么比经济衰退更能促进人口健康了。

sense_groups.english: According to a report in the September 1st Canadian Medical Association Journal,
sense_groups.chinese: 根据《加拿大医学会杂志》9月1日的一篇报道，

sense_groups.english: when our paychecks get lighter, we do more than tighten our purse strings—we also cinch our belts, kick bad habits and manage to lower our mortality rates.
sense_groups.chinese: 当我们的薪水变少时，我们不仅勒紧钱包，还收紧腰带、改掉坏习惯，并设法降低死亡率。

sense_groups.english: Economic growth is usually associated with increased life spans, but the report says that's only true for very poor countries.
sense_groups.chinese: 经济增长通常与寿命延长相关，但报道称这仅对非常贫穷的国家成立。

sense_groups.english: Researchers looked at data from dozens of 20th century international health studies
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员查看了20世纪数十项国际健康研究的数据，

sense_groups.english: and found that, once per-capita income passed $5,000, recessions actually helped health.
sense_groups.chinese: 并发现一旦人均收入超过5000美元，经济衰退实际上有助于健康。

sense_groups.english: During lean times, people in relatively wealthy countries drink and smoke less and stop overeating.
sense_groups.chinese: 在经济不景气时期，相对富裕国家的人们饮酒和吸烟减少，并停止暴饮暴食。

sense_groups.english: They also go out less, which means fewer trips in the car.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们外出也减少，这意味着开车出行更少。

sense_groups.english: It all adds up to fewer deaths from things like lung cancer, liver disease, heart attacks and car crashes.
sense_groups.chinese: 这一切加起来，导致肺癌、肝病、心脏病发作和车祸等导致的死亡减少。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say that fewer hours in the office can also mean more time with family and friends.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员表示，办公室工作时间减少也意味着与家人和朋友相处的时间增多。

sense_groups.english: These close social interactions lead to less stress and better health.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些亲密的社交互动带来更少的压力和更好的健康。

sense_groups.english: Of course, some people may find more family time to be like a lot of good medicine—hard to swallow.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，有些人可能会觉得更多的家庭时间就像良药——难以下咽。

questions.name: #193 Talking to Teens

Watching CSI, where the victim is often dead and treated as another piece of evidence, was ______ with lowered intentions to seek consent and a greater acceptance of rape myths.

Previous research found that the Law & Order shows directly challenge myths and stereotypes related to sexual assaults.
While CSI has been criticized for plotlines that reinforce rape myths.
So it turns out ______ those shows—at least for college-aged kids—may have some effect on sexual consent intentions and behavior.
And when it comes to Law & Order, that effect could be positive.

3. activity
4. associated
5. decreased
6. watching

sense_groups.chinese: “在刑事司法系统中，基于性的犯罪被认为特别令人发指……”

sense_groups.english: Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.
sense_groups.chinese: 《法律与秩序：特殊受害者》。

sense_groups.english: Really.
sense_groups.chinese: 真的。

sense_groups.english: Compared with other TV shows, anyway.
sense_groups.chinese: 至少和其他电视节目相比。

sense_groups.english: Because a study finds that college students who watched episodes of the various Law & Orders had a better understanding of sexual consent issues than those who watched two other crime procedural franchises, NCIS and CSI.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为一项研究发现，观看各种《法律与秩序》剧集的大学生比观看另外两部犯罪程序剧《海军罪案调查处》和《犯罪现场调查》的大学生更了解性同意问题。

sense_groups.english: The research is in the Journal of Health Communication.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《健康传播杂志》上。

sense_groups.english: For the study, researchers asked more than 300 college freshmen if they agreed or disagreed that if a woman is raped she is at least somewhat responsible, a concept called rape myth acceptance.
sense_groups.chinese: 在这项研究中，研究人员询问了300多名大学新生是否同意“如果女性被强奸，她至少负有一定责任”这一观点，这个概念被称为强奸迷思接受度。

sense_groups.english: The students were also asked about their intentions to seek consent for sexual activity and their intentions to refuse sexual activity.
sense_groups.chinese: 学生们还被问及他们寻求性活动同意的意图以及拒绝性活动的意图。

sense_groups.english: The results: the college students who watched ripped-from-the-headline Law & Order versus the other shows had stronger views about consent and were less likely to accept rape mythology.
sense_groups.chinese: 结果显示：观看取材自头条新闻的《法律与秩序》而非其他节目的学生对同意有更强烈的看法，并且不太可能接受强奸迷思。

sense_groups.english: Watching CSI, where the victim is often dead and treated as another piece of evidence, was associated with lowered intentions to seek consent and a greater acceptance of rape myths.
sense_groups.chinese: 观看《犯罪现场调查》——其中受害者通常死亡并被当作另一件证据——与寻求同意的意图降低和强奸迷思接受度增加有关。

sense_groups.english: Exposure to the NCIS franchise was associated with decreased intentions to refuse unwanted sexual activity.
sense_groups.chinese: 接触《海军罪案调查处》系列与拒绝不想要的性活动的意图下降有关。

sense_groups.english: Previous research found that the Law & Order shows directly challenge myths and stereotypes related to sexual assaults.
sense_groups.chinese: 先前的研究发现，《法律与秩序》节目直接挑战了与性侵犯相关的迷思和刻板印象。

sense_groups.english: While CSI has been criticized for plotlines that reinforce rape myths.
sense_groups.chinese: 而《犯罪现场调查》则因强化强奸迷思的情节而受到批评。

sense_groups.english: So it turns out watching those shows—at least for college-aged kids—may have some effect on sexual consent intentions and behavior.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以，观看这些节目——至少对大学生年龄的孩子来说——可能对性同意意图和行为有一定影响。

sense_groups.english: And when it comes to Law & Order, that effect could be positive.
sense_groups.chinese: 而对于《法律与秩序》，这种影响可能是积极的。

questions.name: #194 Death of Bee
questions.en:
You've probably heard that the world's honeybees have ______ stinging losses lately.
That's a big story for us, too—up to twelve billion dollars in crops rely on the fuzzy flyers for pollination.
Of the 2.4 million honeybee ______ in the U.S., about one million died off this past winter.
Big declines have also been seen in Europe and Asia.
The die-off has been dubbed colony collapse ______ and the vanishing bee syndrome.
A couple of species of mites that attack bees were ______ for similar dieoffs in the winters of '95-'96 and 2000-2001.
And the mites may be partly to blame for the most recent honeybee losses.
But a quarter of the current carnage seems unrelated to mites or any other pests.
Other ______ causes of the bee decline include genetically modified foods, parasites, pesticides, and cell phone radiation.
But bee expert Nicholas Calderone of Cornell University said last week that a definitive cause remains elusive.
He will spend this summer investigating honeybee colonies throughout the northeast trying to solve the case of the dead bees.
Here's hoping he buzzes in with an answer.
questions.full:
You've probably heard that the world's honeybees have ______ stinging losses lately.
That's a big story for us, too—up to twelve billion dollars in crops rely on the fuzzy flyers for pollination.
Of the 2.4 million honeybee ______ in the U.S., about one million died off this past winter.
Big declines have also been seen in Europe and Asia.
The die-off has been dubbed colony collapse ______ and the vanishing bee syndrome.
A couple of species of mites that attack bees were ______ for similar dieoffs in the winters of '95-'96 and 2000-2001.
And the mites may be partly to blame for the most recent honeybee losses.
But a quarter of the current carnage seems unrelated to mites or any other pests.
Other ______ causes of the bee decline include genetically modified foods, parasites, pesticides, and cell phone radiation.
But bee expert Nicholas Calderone of Cornell University said last week that a definitive cause remains elusive.
He will spend this summer investigating honeybee colonies throughout the northeast trying to solve the case of the dead bees.
Here's hoping he buzzes in with an answer.

答案:
1. suffered
2. colonies
3. disorder
4. responsible
5. suggested

sense_groups.english: You've probably heard that the world's honeybees have suffered stinging losses lately.
sense_groups.chinese: 你可能听说过，世界上的蜜蜂最近遭受了惨重的损失。

sense_groups.english: That's a big story for us, too—up to twelve billion dollars in crops rely on the fuzzy flyers for pollination.
sense_groups.chinese: 这对我们来说也是个大新闻——高达120亿美元的农作物依赖这些毛茸茸的飞行者进行授粉。

sense_groups.english: Of the 2.4 million honeybee colonies in the U.S., about one million died off this past winter.
sense_groups.chinese: 在美国的240万个蜜蜂蜂群中，大约有100万个在去年冬天死亡。

sense_groups.english: Big declines have also been seen in Europe and Asia.
sense_groups.chinese: 欧洲和亚洲也出现了大幅下降。

sense_groups.english: The die-off has been dubbed colony collapse disorder and the vanishing bee syndrome.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种死亡现象被称为蜂群崩溃失调症和蜜蜂消失综合征。

sense_groups.english: A couple of species of mites that attack bees were responsible for similar dieoffs in the winters of '95-'96 and 2000-2001.
sense_groups.chinese: 几种攻击蜜蜂的螨虫是1995-1996年和2000-2001年冬季类似死亡事件的元凶。

sense_groups.english: And the mites may be partly to blame for the most recent honeybee losses.
sense_groups.chinese: 而螨虫可能对最近的蜜蜂损失负有部分责任。

sense_groups.english: But a quarter of the current carnage seems unrelated to mites or any other pests.
sense_groups.chinese: 但目前四分之一的大规模死亡似乎与螨虫或其他害虫无关。

sense_groups.english: Other suggested causes of the bee decline include genetically modified foods, parasites, pesticides, and cell phone radiation.
sense_groups.chinese: 其他被提出的蜜蜂减少原因包括转基因食品、寄生虫、杀虫剂和手机辐射。

sense_groups.english: But bee expert Nicholas Calderone of Cornell University said last week that a definitive cause remains elusive.
sense_groups.chinese: 但康奈尔大学的蜜蜂专家尼古拉斯·卡尔德隆上周表示，确切原因仍然难以捉摸。

sense_groups.english: He will spend this summer investigating honeybee colonies throughout the northeast trying to solve the case of the dead bees.
sense_groups.chinese: 他将在今年夏天调查整个东北部的蜜蜂蜂群，试图解开蜜蜂死亡之谜。

sense_groups.english: Here's hoping he buzzes in with an answer.
sense_groups.chinese: 希望他能嗡嗡地带来答案。

questions.name: #195 Formation of Cluster
questions.en:
Astronomers have discovered a trove of ______ that are ______ invisible—because they're made almost entirely of dark matter.
The Subaru telescope in Hawaii spotted 854 of these oddballs, which are referred to as "ultradiffuse galaxies," by detecting what little light they do produce.
They were all found in what's called the Coma Cluster of galaxies.
The report is in The ______ Journal Letters.
Of course, scientists still do not know just what dark matter is.
But they can detect its ______ through its gravitational effects on the normal matter that we can see.
That's how we know that dark matter seems to be ubiquitous in the universe—especially in these newly found, barely visible galaxies.
Many of these galaxies are about the size of our Milky Way, but contain just a thousandth as many stars.
  ______ estimate that dark matter accounts for 99 percent of these galaxies' mass.
How such objects could form is a mystery.
They probably started out with a healthy complement of ______ gas, just like normal galaxies, but somehow lost it.
The gas might have blown away as the galaxies moved through the Coma Cluster, or maybe other galaxies' gravity dragged it off.
Further study of these ______ galaxies should clarify the situation, and may even shine some light on the fundamental nature of dark matter.
questions.answer:
1. galaxies
2. virtually
3. Astrophysical
4. presence
5. Researchers
6. star-forming
7. ultradiffuse
questions.full:
Astronomers have discovered a trove of ______ that are ______ invisible—because they're made almost entirely of dark matter.
The Subaru telescope in Hawaii spotted 854 of these oddballs, which are referred to as "ultradiffuse galaxies," by detecting what little light they do produce.
They were all found in what's called the Coma Cluster of galaxies.
The report is in The ______ Journal Letters.
Of course, scientists still do not know just what dark matter is.
But they can detect its ______ through its gravitational effects on the normal matter that we can see.
That's how we know that dark matter seems to be ubiquitous in the universe—especially in these newly found, barely visible galaxies.
Many of these galaxies are about the size of our Milky Way, but contain just a thousandth as many stars.
  ______ estimate that dark matter accounts for 99 percent of these galaxies' mass.
How such objects could form is a mystery.
They probably started out with a healthy complement of ______ gas, just like normal galaxies, but somehow lost it.
The gas might have blown away as the galaxies moved through the Coma Cluster, or maybe other galaxies' gravity dragged it off.
Further study of these ______ galaxies should clarify the situation, and may even shine some light on the fundamental nature of dark matter.

答案:
1. galaxies
2. virtually
3. Astrophysical
4. presence
5. Researchers
6. star-forming
7. ultradiffuse

sense_groups.english: Astronomers have discovered a trove of galaxies
sense_groups.chinese: 天文学家发现了一大批星系

sense_groups.english: that are virtually invisible
sense_groups.chinese: 它们几乎看不见

sense_groups.english: because they're made almost entirely of dark matter.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为它们几乎完全由暗物质构成。

sense_groups.english: The Subaru telescope in Hawaii spotted 854 of these oddballs,
sense_groups.chinese: 夏威夷的斯巴鲁望远镜发现了854个这样的怪家伙，

sense_groups.english: which are referred to as "ultradiffuse galaxies,"
sense_groups.chinese: 它们被称为“超弥散星系”，

sense_groups.english: by detecting what little light they do produce.
sense_groups.chinese: 通过探测它们发出的微弱光线。

sense_groups.english: They were all found in what's called the Coma Cluster of galaxies.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们都位于一个叫做后发座星系团的地方。

sense_groups.english: The report is in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
sense_groups.chinese: 该报告发表在《天体物理杂志快报》上。

sense_groups.english: Of course, scientists still do not know just what dark matter is.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，科学家们仍然不知道暗物质到底是什么。

sense_groups.english: But they can detect its presence
sense_groups.chinese: 但他们能探测到它的存在

sense_groups.english: through its gravitational effects on the normal matter that we can see.
sense_groups.chinese: 通过它对我们可以看到的普通物质的引力效应。

sense_groups.english: That's how we know that dark matter seems to be ubiquitous in the universe
sense_groups.chinese: 这样我们就知道暗物质似乎在宇宙中无处不在

sense_groups.english: —especially in these newly found, barely visible galaxies.
sense_groups.chinese: ——尤其是在这些新发现的、几乎看不见的星系中。

sense_groups.english: Many of these galaxies are about the size of our Milky Way,
sense_groups.chinese: 这些星系中许多大小与我们的银河系相当，

sense_groups.english: but contain just a thousandth as many stars.
sense_groups.chinese: 但所含恒星数量只有银河系的千分之一。

sense_groups.english: Researchers estimate that dark matter accounts for 99 percent of these galaxies' mass.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员估计，暗物质占这些星系质量的99%。

sense_groups.english: How such objects could form is a mystery.
sense_groups.chinese: 这样的天体如何形成是一个谜。

sense_groups.english: They probably started out with a healthy complement of star-forming gas,
sense_groups.chinese: 它们可能一开始拥有充足的恒星形成气体，

sense_groups.english: just like normal galaxies, but somehow lost it.
sense_groups.chinese: 就像普通星系一样，但不知何故失去了它。

sense_groups.english: The gas might have blown away as the galaxies moved through the Coma Cluster,
sense_groups.chinese: 当这些星系穿过后发座星系团时，气体可能被吹走，

sense_groups.english: or maybe other galaxies' gravity dragged it off.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者可能是其他星系的引力将其拖走。

sense_groups.english: Further study of these ultradiffuse galaxies should clarify the situation,
sense_groups.chinese: 对这些超弥散星系的进一步研究应该能澄清情况，

sense_groups.english: and may even shine some light on the fundamental nature of dark matter.
sense_groups.chinese: 甚至可能揭示暗物质的基本性质。

questions.name: #196 Solar Cells
questions.en:
Imagine a world where sunlight can be captured to produce electricity anywhere, on any surface.
The makers of thin-film ______ solar cells imagine that world too.
But a big problem has been the amount of silicon needed to harvest a little sunshine.
Now, researchers at Caltech say they've designed a device that gets comparable solar ______ while using just one percent of the silicon per unit area that current solar cells need.
The work was published in the journal Nature Materials.
The research team tried silicon wire arrays instead of traditional silicon panels.
These wires have been charged to do a good job ______ sunlight to usable energy on the nanoscale.
But the ______ had to create wires a thousand times longer.
Light bounces around within the wires and is eventually ______ when it hits at the correct angle.
But there was a problem: too much light was leaking out.
Adding nanoparticles of alumina kept much more of the light ______ until it got absorbed.
The result is a system that virtually matches silicon wafer light absorption and may be more ______ at converting light to electricity, while using a tiny fraction of the material.
Adding nanoparticles of alumina kept much more of the light **scattering until it got absorbed.
The result is a system that virtually matches silicon wafer light absorption and may be more **efficient at converting light to electricity, while using a tiny fraction of the material.
questions.answer:
1. flexible
2. absorption
3. converting
4. scientists
5. absorbed
6. scattering
7. efficient

sense_groups.english: Imagine a world where sunlight can be captured to produce electricity anywhere, on any surface.
sense_groups.chinese: 想象一个世界，阳光可以在任何地方、任何表面被捕获来发电。

sense_groups.english: The makers of thin-film ______ solar cells imagine that world too.
sense_groups.chinese: 薄膜______太阳能电池的制造商也想象着那个世界。

sense_groups.english: But a big problem has been the amount of silicon needed to harvest a little sunshine.
sense_groups.chinese: 但一个大问题是，收获一点阳光需要大量的硅。

sense_groups.english: Now, researchers at Caltech say they've designed a device that gets comparable solar ______ while using just one percent of the silicon per unit area that current solar cells need.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，加州理工学院的研究人员表示，他们设计了一种设备，其太阳能______与现有太阳能电池相当，但每单位面积使用的硅仅为现有太阳能电池的百分之一。

sense_groups.english: The work was published in the journal Nature Materials.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《自然·材料》杂志上。

sense_groups.english: The research team tried silicon wire arrays instead of traditional silicon panels.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究团队尝试了硅线阵列，而不是传统的硅板。

sense_groups.english: These wires have been charged to do a good job ______ sunlight to usable energy on the nanoscale.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些线被充电，在纳米尺度上很好地______阳光为可用能量。

sense_groups.english: But the ______ had to create wires a thousand times longer.
sense_groups.chinese: 但______必须制造出长一千倍的线。

sense_groups.english: Light bounces around within the wires and is eventually ______ when it hits at the correct angle.
sense_groups.chinese: 光线在线内反弹，最终在正确角度撞击时被______。

sense_groups.english: But there was a problem: too much light was leaking out.
sense_groups.chinese: 但有一个问题：太多光线泄漏出去了。

sense_groups.english: Adding nanoparticles of alumina kept much more of the light ______ until it got absorbed.
sense_groups.chinese: 添加氧化铝纳米颗粒使更多光线______直到被吸收。

sense_groups.english: The result is a system that virtually matches silicon wafer light absorption and may be more ______ at converting light to electricity, while using a tiny fraction of the material.
sense_groups.chinese: 结果是一个系统，几乎与硅片光吸收相当，并且在将光转化为电能方面可能更______，同时只使用了一小部分材料。

questions.name: #197 Singapore
questions.en:
I am here in Durban, South Africa to report on the just ______ climate change negotiations.
While an agreement was reached, negotiations were in doubt throughout the three final nights.
The sticking point was Singapore.
Not ______ specifically so much, but what Singapore represents.
In 1992, Singapore was a rich ______ but not yet a developed one.
Nearly 20 years later, Singapore is a financial titan and a global city.
So what should its obligations be to cut ______ gas emissions?
Under old treaties, such as the Kyoto Protocol, Singapore has none.
The essence of the package agreed to here in Durban is that, by 2020, Singapore will have some.
Of course, Singapore in total represents less than one percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
But Singapore is joined by ______ like South Korea—and even the world's largest greenhouse gas polluter, China—in this category of no obligations.
If the Durban deal brings climate change negotiations into the 21st century and if countries like Singapore begin reducing CO2 ______ after 2020, the world may not be quite as unpleasantly warm by the 22nd century.
questions.answer:
1. finished
2. Singapore
3. city-state
4. greenhouse
5. countries
6. emissions
questions.full:
I am here in Durban, South Africa to report on the just ______ climate change negotiations.
While an agreement was reached, negotiations were in doubt throughout the three final nights.

If the Durban deal brings climate change negotiations into the 21st century and if countries like Singapore begin reducing CO2 ______ after 2020, the world may not be quite as unpleasantly warm by the 22nd century.

答案:
1. finished
2. Singapore
3. city-state
4. greenhouse
5. countries
6. emissions

sense_groups.english: I am here in Durban, South Africa
sense_groups.chinese: 我现在在南非德班

sense_groups.english: to report on the just finished climate change negotiations.
sense_groups.chinese: 报道刚刚结束的气候变化谈判。

sense_groups.english: While an agreement was reached,
sense_groups.chinese: 虽然达成了协议，

sense_groups.english: negotiations were in doubt throughout the three final nights.
sense_groups.chinese: 但最后三晚的谈判一直悬而未决。

sense_groups.english: The sticking point was Singapore.
sense_groups.chinese: 症结在于新加坡。

sense_groups.english: Not Singapore specifically so much,
sense_groups.chinese: 并非特指新加坡本身，

sense_groups.english: but what Singapore represents.
sense_groups.chinese: 而是新加坡所代表的意义。

sense_groups.english: In 1992, Singapore was a rich city-state
sense_groups.chinese: 1992年，新加坡是一个富裕的城市国家，

sense_groups.english: but not yet a developed one.
sense_groups.chinese: 但还不是发达国家。

sense_groups.english: Nearly 20 years later,
sense_groups.chinese: 近20年后，

sense_groups.english: Singapore is a financial titan and a global city.
sense_groups.chinese: 新加坡已成为金融巨头和全球城市。

sense_groups.english: So what should its obligations be
sense_groups.chinese: 那么它的义务应该是什么？

sense_groups.english: to cut greenhouse gas emissions?
sense_groups.chinese: 减少温室气体排放？

sense_groups.english: Under old treaties, such as the Kyoto Protocol,
sense_groups.chinese: 根据《京都议定书》等旧条约，

sense_groups.english: Singapore has none.
sense_groups.chinese: 新加坡没有任何义务。

sense_groups.english: The essence of the package agreed to here in Durban
sense_groups.chinese: 在德班达成的这一揽子协议的核心是，

sense_groups.english: is that, by 2020, Singapore will have some.
sense_groups.chinese: 到2020年，新加坡将承担一些义务。

sense_groups.english: Of course, Singapore in total
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，新加坡总共

sense_groups.english: represents less than one percent
sense_groups.chinese: 只占不到百分之一

sense_groups.english: of global greenhouse gas emissions.
sense_groups.chinese: 的全球温室气体排放量。

sense_groups.english: But Singapore is joined by countries like South Korea
sense_groups.chinese: 但新加坡与韩国等国家一样，

sense_groups.english: —and even the world's largest greenhouse gas polluter, China—
sense_groups.chinese: 甚至包括全球最大的温室气体排放国中国，

sense_groups.english: in this category of no obligations.
sense_groups.chinese: 都属于无义务类别。

sense_groups.english: If the Durban deal brings climate change negotiations
sense_groups.chinese: 如果德班协议将气候变化谈判

sense_groups.english: into the 21st century
sense_groups.chinese: 带入21世纪

sense_groups.english: and if countries like Singapore begin reducing CO2 emissions after 2020,
sense_groups.chinese: 并且像新加坡这样的国家在2020年后开始减少二氧化碳排放，

sense_groups.english: the world may not be quite as unpleasantly warm
sense_groups.chinese: 那么到22世纪，世界可能不会那么令人不适地温暖

sense_groups.english: by the 22nd century.
sense_groups.chinese: 了。

questions.name: #198 Aspirin
questions.en:
Aspirin is a popular painkiller, and chances are you have some in your medicine chest right now.
You might even have some in your flesh-and-blood, ______ chest.
Because a new study suggests that humans can make their own salicylic acid, which forms the bulk of aspirin's active ingredient.
Scientists at Scotland's National Health Service previously ______ that people can have salicylic acid in their blood even if they haven't recently swallowed an aspirin.
Vegetarians have really high concentrations, which makes sense, given that plants make salicylic acid, so fruits and veggies are full of it.
But their recent study suggests that not all of the chemical comes through the diet, because humans can take a precursor molecule and turn it into salicylic acid—results ______ in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry.
The ______ say that people might make salicylic acid to fight inflammation or disease…which would also make sense…because plants make the stuff to fight off infections.
In fact, a recent study published online in the journal Nature shows how calcium released at the site of an infection tells plants to ramp up ______ of the protective compound.
Just Mother Nature's way of saying, "Make two aspirin and call me when you flower."

questions.name: #199 Urban Life
questions.en:
City living has obviously ______ human culture—as have often been noted, how you gonna keep 'em down on the farm after they've seen Paree'?
But urban life may have also influenced human genes, making the descendants of ancient city dwellers more resistant to disease.
That's according to a study in the journal Evolution.
The researchers started from the premise that densely populated cities would be good places for infectious diseases, which could spread easily from person to person.
That situation should have set up selection pressure for the ability to survive such infections.
The ______ sampled the DNA of 17 populations from Africa, Asia and Europe, ______ longtime urbanites—like Italians, Turks and Iranians—and traditionally rural or nomadic groups, like Malawians or the Saami people of northern Scandinavia.
Then the researchers zeroed in on a gene variant that offers protection against diseases like tuberculosis or leprosy.
After controlling for any shared ______ between the groups, they indeed found that the protective gene was significantly more common in cultures with a long history of urban settlement.
Which may be some comfort next time someone's sneezing near you on the subway.
questions.full:

sense_groups.english: City living has obviously influenced human culture—

questions.name: #200 Hearing
questions.en:
Our ears are highly attuned to sounds in the world around us.
It's not just the frequency of the sound itself.
There are also subtle differences and shifts in loudness and pitch.
That's what tells us, for instance, whether that baby crying belongs to us and just where it's located.
But ______ to a recent study, what you and I hear may not sound the same.
  ______ at the ______ of Oxford are trying to understand how the ears and the brain work together.
They fit ferrets with auditory implants, trained them to respond to sound, and then looked at the way their neurons reacted.
It turns out that each ferret's neurons in the auditory cortex ______ to changes in gradual differences in sound ­ but each ferret responded differently.
The researchers say this is ______ to humans.
They say this means that our brains are wired to process sounds depending on how our ears deliver that sound.
So if you ______ heard the world through my ears, it might sound quite different.
The scientists say this research could help in the quest to design better hearing aids and speech recognition systems.
questions.answer:
1. according
2. Scientists
3. University
4. responded
5. applicable
6. suddenly
questions.full:
Our ears are highly attuned to sounds in the world around us.
It's not just the frequency of the sound itself.
There are also subtle differences and shifts in loudness and pitch.
That's what tells us, for instance, whether that baby crying belongs to us and just where it's located.
But ______ to a recent study, what you and I hear may not sound the same.
  ______ at the ______ of Oxford are trying to understand how the ears and the brain work together.
They fit ferrets with auditory implants, trained them to respond to sound, and then looked at the way their neurons reacted.
It turns out that each ferret's neurons in the auditory cortex ______ to changes in gradual differences in sound ­ but each ferret responded differently.
The researchers say this is ______ to humans.
They say this means that our brains are wired to process sounds depending on how our ears deliver that sound.
So if you ______ heard the world through my ears, it might sound quite different.
The scientists say this research could help in the quest to design better hearing aids and speech recognition systems.

答案:
1. according
2. Scientists
3. University
4. responded
5. applicable
6. suddenly

sense_groups.english: Our ears are highly attuned to sounds in the world around us.
sense_groups.chinese: 我们的耳朵对周围世界的声音非常敏感。

sense_groups.english: It's not just the frequency of the sound itself.
sense_groups.chinese: 这不仅仅是声音本身的频率。

sense_groups.english: There are also subtle differences and shifts in loudness and pitch.
sense_groups.chinese: 还有响度和音调的细微差异和变化。

sense_groups.english: That's what tells us, for instance, whether that baby crying belongs to us and just where it's located.
sense_groups.chinese: 比如，这告诉我们那个哭闹的婴儿是不是我们的，以及它在哪里。

sense_groups.english: But according to a recent study, what you and I hear may not sound the same.
sense_groups.chinese: 但根据最近的一项研究，你我所听到的可能并不相同。

sense_groups.english: Scientists at the University of Oxford are trying to understand how the ears and the brain work together.
sense_groups.chinese: 牛津大学的科学家们正试图理解耳朵和大脑是如何协同工作的。

sense_groups.english: They fit ferrets with auditory implants, trained them to respond to sound, and then looked at the way their neurons reacted.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们给雪貂安装听觉植入物，训练它们对声音做出反应，然后观察它们神经元反应的方式。

sense_groups.english: It turns out that each ferret's neurons in the auditory cortex responded to changes in gradual differences in sound — but each ferret responded differently.
sense_groups.chinese: 结果发现，每只雪貂听觉皮层中的神经元对声音的逐渐差异变化都有反应——但每只雪貂的反应不同。

sense_groups.english: The researchers say this is applicable to humans.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究人员说这同样适用于人类。

sense_groups.english: They say this means that our brains are wired to process sounds depending on how our ears deliver that sound.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们说这意味着我们的大脑会根据耳朵传递声音的方式来处理声音。

sense_groups.english: So if you suddenly heard the world through my ears, it might sound quite different.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以如果你突然通过我的耳朵听到世界，听起来可能会很不一样。

sense_groups.english: The scientists say this research could help in the quest to design better hearing aids and speech recognition systems.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家们表示，这项研究有助于设计更好的助听器和语音识别系统。

questions.name: #201 Dog's Walking
questions.en:
If you have a dog, you know you gotta walk it.
But do you know how it walks?
Well, if you have no idea which foot Fido puts forward when, you're in good company.
Because according to a study ______ in the journal Current Biology, even places like natural history museums get it wrong half the time.
Studies published back in the late 1800s showed that all ______ animals walk the same way.
They start by moving forward their left hind leg, ______ by the left front leg.
Then they repeat the sequence on the right-hand side.
Different animals differ in the timing of their steps.
The reason they walk that way is for stability.
Lifting one leg at a time leaves three feet on the ground, forming a nice stable tripod to stand on.
But not ______ seems to know that, even folks who should.
Scientists looked at 300 depictions of animals walking—in museums, anatomy textbooks, and even children's toys.
And they found that nearly half the time these images get it wrong.
For a toy, that kind of inattention to detail might mean that Rex has a tendency to roll over.
But for museums to mess up like that?
They just don't have a leg to stand on.

For a toy, that kind of inattention to detail might mean that Rex has a tendency to roll over.

They just don't have a leg to stand on.

答案:
1. published
2. four-legged
3. followed
4. everyone

sense_groups.english: If you have a dog, you know you gotta walk it.
sense_groups.chinese: 如果你有狗，你知道得遛它。

sense_groups.english: But do you know how it walks?
sense_groups.chinese: 但你知道它是怎么走的吗？

sense_groups.english: Well, if you have no idea which foot Fido puts forward when, you're in good company.
sense_groups.chinese: 好吧，如果你不知道菲多什么时候迈哪只脚，你并不孤单。

sense_groups.english: Because according to a study published in the journal Current Biology, even places like natural history museums get it wrong half the time.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为根据发表在《当代生物学》期刊上的一项研究，就连自然历史博物馆这样的地方也有一半时间是错的。

sense_groups.english: Studies published back in the late 1800s showed that all four-legged animals walk the same way.
sense_groups.chinese: 早在19世纪末发表的研究就表明，所有四条腿的动物走路方式都一样。

sense_groups.english: They start by moving forward their left hind leg, followed by the left front leg.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们先向前移动左后腿，然后是左前腿。

sense_groups.english: Then they repeat the sequence on the right-hand side.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后在右侧重复这个顺序。

sense_groups.english: Different animals differ in the timing of their steps.
sense_groups.chinese: 不同动物在步伐的节奏上有所不同。

sense_groups.english: The reason they walk that way is for stability.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们那样走路是为了稳定。

sense_groups.english: Lifting one leg at a time leaves three feet on the ground, forming a nice stable tripod to stand on.
sense_groups.chinese: 一次抬起一条腿，地上还有三只脚，形成一个稳定的三脚架支撑。

sense_groups.english: But not everyone seems to know that, even folks who should.
sense_groups.chinese: 但似乎不是每个人都知道这一点，即使是那些应该知道的人。

sense_groups.english: Scientists looked at 300 depictions of animals walking—in museums, anatomy textbooks, and even children's toys.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家们查看了300个动物行走的描绘——在博物馆、解剖学教科书，甚至儿童玩具中。

sense_groups.english: And they found that nearly half the time these images get it wrong.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现这些图像近一半时间是错的。

sense_groups.english: For a toy, that kind of inattention to detail might mean that Rex has a tendency to roll over.
sense_groups.chinese: 对于玩具来说，这种对细节的疏忽可能意味着雷克斯容易翻倒。

sense_groups.english: But for museums to mess up like that?
sense_groups.chinese: 但博物馆也这样搞错？

sense_groups.english: They just don't have a leg to stand on.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们简直站不住脚。

questions.name: #202 Obesity in America
questions.en:
America's problem with obesity is well known.
And more and more cats and dogs are also suffering from obesity.
Now veterinarians have found that another favorite animal is in danger of serious health problems due to being just too fat: horses.
Horses in Virginia were found being experiencing a big ______ in cases of laminitis, a ______ where the ______ tissue between the hoof and bone falls apart.
It's what got the racehorse Barbaro.
  ______ at the Virginia-Maryland Regional College of Veterinary Medicine theorized that the ______ increase might be related to an epidemic of obesity, which could bring about chronic inflammation and other deleterious conditions.
So they examined 300 horses randomly chosen from over a hundred farms during the summer of 2006.
And they found that just over half, 51percent, were either overweight or obese.
And for the same reasons as people—too many calories and too little exercise.
The horses may not be overeating, though.
Modern pasture plant materials were themselves bred to help foraging animals, like cattle, pack the weight on faster.
Looks like horses may have been cowed into becoming fat.

questions.name: #204 Genome Sequence
questions.en:
Since the first human genome sequence was published, ______ of people have submitted their DNA for scientific analysis.
They made these donations anonymously—or so they thought.
Now, using publicly available information, researchers found they could figure out the identities of 50 individuals who had loaned their genes to science.

  ______ looked at a ______ set of markers in genomes whose ______ were in a public database.

questions.name: #205 Happy Hour
questions.en:

In the May 29th issue of Cell, ______ report ______ a gene that controls fruit flies' ______ to ethanol.

Some flies, like some people, just can't hold their drink.
One sip and they're tripping over their own wings.

And they turned up a gene they call happyhour.
Flies with a normal version of this gene are liquor light-weights, while ______ mutants can drink their fly friends under the table.
In the normal flies, happyhour blocks a hormone called EGF.
And the scientists found that two anticancer drugs, which also inhibit EGF, make boozing flies more woozy—a feeling that's as unpleasant for flies as it is for people.
Rats, too, will take a nip and say enough when they're on these drugs.
Robbing booze of its buzz is one way to attack alcoholism.

questions.name: #206 HIW
questions.en:
The floor of ______ Valley is littered with piles of rocks that crumbled off the park's iconic cliffs.
These rockfalls happen all the time, because Yosemite's granite walls are riddled with cracks produced by geologic stress.
Scientists know the rockfalls can be triggered by things like earthquakes, rainfall, and freezing and thawing ice.
But many falls occur without an obvious cause.
Now ______ think that heat may be the culprit.
"We noticed that there had been a bunch of rockfalls that were happening in the summertime, on particularly hot days." Brian Collins, a research civil engineer with the U.S. Geological Survey.
"And we noticed when we looked at the timing that they were happening in the afternoon, when we thought the temperatures were at their hottest."
Collins and Greg Stock, Yosemite's park geologist, wanted to know if small rock movements, induced by changing temperatures, might weaken cracks and contribute to rockfalls.
So the researchers—who are both climbers—found a suitable ______ near the base of a 500-meter-tall cliff and installed instruments called crackmeters, which monitored the width of the crack over time.
The devices ______ that the crack grew almost a centimeter wider during the warmest part of the day.
It shrank again when temperatures cooled off, for instance, at night and during the winter.
But overall, the scientists found that the average width of the fracture grew over the course of a summer and over the entire three and a half-year study period, bringing the crack closer to breaking.
"We think that what happened was that every cycle — as the rock goes back and forth and back and forth — you're getting to a part that we call subcritical crack growth.
And that means that the crack where the rock is attached to the cliff is actually fracturing at a microscopic level.
And so if you do that over the course of a year, then eventually you're gonna do some permanent damage to those points of attachment."
The study is in the journal Nature Geoscience.
The slab of rock the scientists studied hasn't fallen yet, and Collins doesn't know how many cycles it will take before this or any other fracture finally breaks.
When it does, the trigger might be a particularly sweltering day, when the partially ______ slab is farthest away from the cliff.
Or it could be another process, helped along by the fact that temperature changes already weakened the crack.
Either way, the results will help researchers assess the rockfall hazard in steep, rugged terrain.
Because now they know when the mercury goes up, rocks are more likely to come down.

sense_groups.chinese: 但总体而言，科学家发现裂缝的平均宽度在一个夏季以及整个三年半的研究期间都在增加，使裂缝更接近断裂。

sense_groups.english: "We think that what happened was that every cycle — as the rock goes back and forth and back and forth — you're getting to a part that we call subcritical crack growth.
sense_groups.chinese: “我们认为，每个循环——岩石来回移动——都会达到我们称之为亚临界裂纹扩展的阶段。

sense_groups.english: And that means that the crack where the rock is attached to the cliff is actually fracturing at a microscopic level.
sense_groups.chinese: 这意味着岩石附着在悬崖上的裂缝实际上在微观层面上正在断裂。

sense_groups.english: And so if you do that over the course of a year, then eventually you're gonna do some permanent damage to those points of attachment."
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，如果这种情况持续一年，最终会对这些附着点造成永久性损伤。”

sense_groups.english: The study is in the journal Nature Geoscience.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项研究发表在《自然·地球科学》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: The slab of rock the scientists studied hasn't fallen yet, and Collins doesn't know how many cycles it will take before this or any other fracture finally breaks.
sense_groups.chinese: 科学家研究的这块岩石尚未掉落，柯林斯不知道需要多少个循环这块或其他裂缝才会最终断裂。

sense_groups.english: When it does, the trigger might be a particularly sweltering day, when the partially ______ slab is farthest away from the cliff.
sense_groups.chinese: 当它发生时，触发因素可能是一个特别闷热的日子，那时部分______的岩板离悬崖最远。

sense_groups.english: Or it could be another process, helped along by the fact that temperature changes already weakened the crack.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者可能是另一个过程，而温度变化已经削弱了裂缝这一事实助长了它。

sense_groups.english: Either way, the results will help researchers assess the rockfall hazard in steep, rugged terrain.
sense_groups.chinese: 无论如何，这些结果将帮助研究人员评估陡峭崎岖地形中的落石危险。

sense_groups.english: Because now they know when the mercury goes up, rocks are more likely to come down.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为现在他们知道，当温度计上升时，岩石更有可能掉落。

questions.name: #207 HIW
questions.en:
The element mercury has been shown to damage the human nervous system.
Yet, since 1856, mercury amalgam is "the" filling dentists have used to repair our teeth.
Now a study in the journal Chemical Research in Toxicology ______ that mercury fillings actually lose their toxic potential over time.
  ______ ______ used x-ray spectroscopy to compare new mercury amalgams to those about 20 years old.
After two decades, 95 percent of the elemental mercury on the surface of a filling had gone through a chemical reaction.
It became ______ sulfide, a black-colored solid.
Which ______ why fillings dull with age.
And the compound isn't absorbed by the body, which means it can't affect the body the way elemental mercury can.
Of course, this study does not settle the ______ of how ______ harmful a new mercury filling is.
But sulfide-rich foods, such as coffee, garlic and onions, may accelerate the change from metallic mercury into the safer sulfide.
So if you have a new mercury filling, an odiferous chili dog with a cup of coffee may be just what the doctor ordered.
questions.answer:
1. indicates
2. Canadian
3. scientists
4. beta-mercury
5. explains
6. question
7. potentially
questions.full:
The element mercury has been shown to damage the human nervous system.
Yet, since 1856, mercury amalgam is "the" filling dentists have used to repair our teeth.
Now a study in the journal Chemical Research in Toxicology ______ that mercury fillings actually lose their toxic potential over time.
  ______ ______ used x-ray spectroscopy to compare new mercury amalgams to those about 20 years old.
After two decades, 95 percent of the elemental mercury on the surface of a filling had gone through a chemical reaction.
It became ______ sulfide, a black-colored solid.
Which ______ why fillings dull with age.
And the compound isn't absorbed by the body, which means it can't affect the body the way elemental mercury can.
Of course, this study does not settle the ______ of how ______ harmful a new mercury filling is.
But sulfide-rich foods, such as coffee, garlic and onions, may accelerate the change from metallic mercury into the safer sulfide.
So if you have a new mercury filling, an odiferous chili dog with a cup of coffee may be just what the doctor ordered.

答案:
1. indicates
2. Canadian
3. scientists
4. beta-mercury
5. explains
6. question
7. potentially

sense_groups.english: The element mercury has been shown to damage the human nervous system.
sense_groups.chinese: 元素汞已被证明会损害人类神经系统。

sense_groups.english: Yet, since 1856, mercury amalgam is "the" filling dentists have used to repair our teeth.
sense_groups.chinese: 然而，自1856年以来，汞合金一直是牙医用来修复牙齿的填充物。

sense_groups.english: Now a study in the journal Chemical Research in Toxicology indicates that mercury fillings actually lose their toxic potential over time.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，《毒理学化学研究》杂志上的一项研究表明，汞填充物实际上会随着时间的推移失去其毒性潜力。

sense_groups.english: Canadian scientists used x-ray spectroscopy to compare new mercury amalgams to those about 20 years old.
sense_groups.chinese: 加拿大科学家使用X射线光谱学将新的汞合金与大约20年旧的汞合金进行了比较。

sense_groups.english: After two decades, 95 percent of the elemental mercury on the surface of a filling had gone through a chemical reaction.
sense_groups.chinese: 二十年后，填充物表面95%的元素汞已经经历了一次化学反应。

sense_groups.english: It became beta-mercury sulfide, a black-colored solid.
sense_groups.chinese: 它变成了β-硫化汞，一种黑色固体。

sense_groups.english: Which explains why fillings dull with age.
sense_groups.chinese: 这解释了为什么填充物会随着时间变暗。

sense_groups.english: And the compound isn't absorbed by the body, which means it can't affect the body the way elemental mercury can.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且这种化合物不被人体吸收，这意味着它不会像元素汞那样影响身体。

sense_groups.english: Of course, this study does not settle the question of how potentially harmful a new mercury filling is.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，这项研究并没有解决新的汞填充物潜在危害有多大的问题。

sense_groups.english: But sulfide-rich foods, such as coffee, garlic and onions, may accelerate the change from metallic mercury into the safer sulfide.
sense_groups.chinese: 但富含硫化物的食物，如咖啡、大蒜和洋葱，可能会加速金属汞向更安全的硫化物的转变。

sense_groups.english: So if you have a new mercury filling, an odiferous chili dog with a cup of coffee may be just what the doctor ordered.
sense_groups.chinese: 所以，如果你有新的汞填充物，一个气味浓郁的辣椒热狗配上一杯咖啡可能正是医生所要求的。

questions.name: #208 Antibiotic Resistance
questions.en:
For years, ______ and physicians have been up in arms about the rise in antibiotic resistance.
Seems that many bacteria, devious buggers that they are, are able to share genetic information—including, say, the instructions for ______ penicillin.
Well, if that's not bad enough, scientists from the N.Y.U. School of Medicine have found that some bacteria can use viruses to help them pass along the recipe for their favorite toxin, results published in the journal Science.
Like humans, bacteria are also prone to infection by viruses.
And most of these viruses—called bacteriophage, or phage for short—make their bacterial victims sick.
Or even dead.
But in the laboratory, the scientists discovered that Staphylococcus aureus, the bug that causes toxic shock ______ among other things, can ______ co-opt phage, using them to shuttle the gene for toxic-shock toxin to another bacteria, in this case Listeria.
That's doubly nasty, because Listeria on its own causes food poisoning, so if it added toxic shock to its repertoire, well, that would be one seriously bad bug.
Whether Staph aureus can pull off this stunt outside the lab's not clear.
But in this particular battle, ya gotta hope the viruses come out on top.
questions.full:
For years, ______ and physicians have been up in arms about the rise in antibiotic resistance.
Seems that many bacteria, devious buggers that they are, are able to share genetic information—including, say, the instructions for ______ penicillin.
Well, if that's not bad enough, scientists from the N.Y.U. School of Medicine have found that some bacteria can use viruses to help them pass along the recipe for their favorite toxin, results published in the journal Science.
Like humans, bacteria are also prone to infection by viruses.
And most of these viruses—called bacteriophage, or phage for short—make their bacterial victims sick.
Or even dead.
But in the laboratory, the scientists discovered that Staphylococcus aureus, the bug that causes toxic shock ______ among other things, can ______ co-opt phage, using them to shuttle the gene for toxic-shock toxin to another bacteria, in this case Listeria.
That's doubly nasty, because Listeria on its own causes food poisoning, so if it added toxic shock to its repertoire, well, that would be one seriously bad bug.
Whether Staph aureus can pull off this stunt outside the lab's not clear.
But in this particular battle, ya gotta hope the viruses come out on top.

答案:
1. scientists
2. destroying
3. syndrome
4. actually

sense_groups.english: For years, scientists and physicians have been up in arms about the rise in antibiotic resistance.
sense_groups.chinese: 多年来，科学家和医生一直对抗生素耐药性的增加感到愤怒。

sense_groups.english: Seems that many bacteria, devious buggers that they are, are able to share genetic information—including, say, the instructions for destroying penicillin.
sense_groups.chinese: 似乎许多细菌，这些狡猾的家伙，能够共享遗传信息——比如，破坏青霉素的指令。

sense_groups.english: Well, if that's not bad enough, scientists from the N.Y.U. School of Medicine have found that some bacteria can use viruses to help them pass along the recipe for their favorite toxin, results published in the journal Science.
sense_groups.chinese: 好吧，如果这还不够糟糕，纽约大学医学院的科学家发现，一些细菌可以利用病毒来帮助它们传递它们最喜欢的毒素的配方，研究结果发表在《科学》杂志上。

sense_groups.english: Like humans, bacteria are also prone to infection by viruses.
sense_groups.chinese: 像人类一样，细菌也容易受到病毒感染。

sense_groups.english: And most of these viruses—called bacteriophage, or phage for short—make their bacterial victims sick.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些病毒中的大多数——称为噬菌体，或简称噬菌体——使它们的细菌宿主生病。

sense_groups.english: Or even dead.
sense_groups.chinese: 甚至死亡。

sense_groups.english: But in the laboratory, the scientists discovered that Staphylococcus aureus, the bug that causes toxic shock syndrome among other things, can actually co-opt phage, using them to shuttle the gene for toxic-shock toxin to another bacteria, in this case Listeria.
sense_groups.chinese: 但在实验室里，科学家发现金黄色葡萄球菌——这种引起中毒性休克综合征的细菌——实际上可以劫持噬菌体，利用它们将中毒性休克毒素的基因运送到另一种细菌，这里指的是李斯特菌。

sense_groups.english: That's doubly nasty, because Listeria on its own causes food poisoning, so if it added toxic shock to its repertoire, well, that would be one seriously bad bug.
sense_groups.chinese: 这加倍恶心，因为李斯特菌本身会引起食物中毒，所以如果它再增加中毒性休克，那将是一种非常糟糕的细菌。

sense_groups.english: Whether Staph aureus can pull off this stunt outside the lab's not clear.
sense_groups.chinese: 金黄色葡萄球菌是否能在实验室外完成这一特技还不清楚。

sense_groups.english: But in this particular battle, ya gotta hope the viruses come out on top.
sense_groups.chinese: 但在这场特殊的战斗中，你只能希望病毒能占上风。

questions.name: #209 HIW
questions.en:
As kids, many of us pondered what stars are made of.
Some ______ astronomers, on the other hand, wonder about where stars came from.
Now, a study serves up a surprise.
Because it seems that the smallest galaxies in the ______ gave rise to an ______ large proportion of stars.
The findings are in the Astrophysical Journal.
Most of the stars we see in the sky were formed when the universe was young, just a few billion years after the Big Bang.
So to study stellar origins, scientists use telescopes that allow them to see galaxies that are so far away, they're ______ looking back in time.
Previous observations had focused on the star-forming powers of larger galaxies.
But in this latest study, researchers used data collected by a ______ camera aboard the Hubble Space Telescope.
With this instrument, they could eyeball smaller, dwarf galaxies.
And they found that these diminutive dynamos churned out stars at a furious rate, fast enough to double their mass in only 150 million years.
That ______ feat would take most ______ "normal" galaxies one to three billion years.
Seems the universe has long known what Danny Devito, Michael J. Fox and Dustin Hoffmann later proved: You don't have to be big to have real star power.
questions.answer:
1. grown-up
2. universe
3. unexpectedly
4. essentially
5. powerful
6. reproductive
7. so-called
questions.full:
As kids, many of us pondered what stars are made of.
Some ______ astronomers, on the other hand, wonder about where stars came from.
Now, a study serves up a surprise.
Because it seems that the smallest galaxies in the ______ gave rise to an ______ large proportion of stars.
The findings are in the Astrophysical Journal.
Most of the stars we see in the sky were formed when the universe was young, just a few billion years after the Big Bang.
So to study stellar origins, scientists use telescopes that allow them to see galaxies that are so far away, they're ______ looking back in time.
Previous observations had focused on the star-forming powers of larger galaxies.
But in this latest study, researchers used data collected by a ______ camera aboard the Hubble Space Telescope.
With this instrument, they could eyeball smaller, dwarf galaxies.
And they found that these diminutive dynamos churned out stars at a furious rate, fast enough to double their mass in only 150 million years.
That ______ feat would take most ______ "normal" galaxies one to three billion years.
Seems the universe has long known what Danny Devito, Michael J. Fox and Dustin Hoffmann later proved: You don't have to be big to have real star power.

答案:
1. grown-up
2. universe
3. unexpectedly
4. essentially
5. powerful
6. reproductive
7. so-called

sense_groups.english: As kids, many of us pondered what stars are made of.
sense_groups.chinese: 小时候，我们很多人都思考过星星是由什么构成的。

sense_groups.english: Some grown-up astronomers, on the other hand, wonder about where stars came from.
sense_groups.chinese: 而一些成年天文学家则好奇星星来自哪里。

sense_groups.english: Now, a study serves up a surprise.
sense_groups.chinese: 现在，一项研究带来了一个惊喜。

sense_groups.english: Because it seems that the smallest galaxies in the universe gave rise to an unexpectedly large proportion of stars.
sense_groups.chinese: 因为宇宙中最小的星系似乎产生了出乎意料的大量恒星。

sense_groups.english: The findings are in the Astrophysical Journal.
sense_groups.chinese: 这项发现发表在《天体物理学杂志》上。

sense_groups.english: Most of the stars we see in the sky were formed when the universe was young, just a few billion years after the Big Bang.
sense_groups.chinese: 我们在天空中看到的大多数恒星都是在宇宙年轻时期形成的，也就是大爆炸后仅几十亿年。

sense_groups.english: So to study stellar origins, scientists use telescopes that allow them to see galaxies that are so far away, they're essentially looking back in time.
sense_groups.chinese: 因此，为了研究恒星起源，科学家使用望远镜观测非常遥远的星系，这基本上是在回望过去。

sense_groups.english: Previous observations had focused on the star-forming powers of larger galaxies.
sense_groups.chinese: 之前的观测主要关注较大星系的恒星形成能力。

sense_groups.english: But in this latest study, researchers used data collected by a powerful camera aboard the Hubble Space Telescope.
sense_groups.chinese: 但在这项最新研究中，研究人员使用了哈勃太空望远镜上搭载的强大相机收集的数据。

sense_groups.english: With this instrument, they could eyeball smaller, dwarf galaxies.
sense_groups.chinese: 借助这一仪器，他们可以观测到更小的矮星系。

sense_groups.english: And they found that these diminutive dynamos churned out stars at a furious rate, fast enough to double their mass in only 150 million years.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，这些小型发电机以惊人的速度制造恒星，速度快到仅需1.5亿年就能使其质量翻倍。

sense_groups.english: That reproductive feat would take most so-called "normal" galaxies one to three billion years.
sense_groups.chinese: 这种繁殖壮举对于大多数所谓的“正常”星系来说需要10到30亿年。

sense_groups.english: Seems the universe has long known what Danny Devito, Michael J. Fox and Dustin Hoffmann later proved: You don't have to be big to have real star power.
sense_groups.chinese: 看来宇宙早就知道丹尼·德维托、迈克尔·J·福克斯和达斯汀·霍夫曼后来证明的道理：你不必身材高大也能拥有真正的明星魅力。

questions.name: #210 Bookworm
questions.en:
What does a bookworm have in common with a ______ marmoset?
They both like a little quiet.
Or so say ______ in the Royal Society journal Biology Letters.
As urban areas continue to expand, their human inhabitants spread all sorts of pollution: air pollution, light pollution, even noise pollution.
Each of these environmental ______ affects the survival and behavior of local wildlife.
And monkeys are no exception.
  ______ in Brazil were ______ how marmosets in a city park cope with ambient noise.
And they found that the monkeys tend to settle down in ______ part of the park is most quiet.
On weekdays, the marmosets steered clear of the roar of traffic, and on Sundays they shunned the clamor of visiting crowds.
They dodged all the din, even when moving meant that they had to leave behind the places that offered them the most food.
It could be that the monkeys are just skittish when it comes to unwelcome sounds.
Or they can't hear what their friends are saying when it gets too loud.
Either way, next time you see a cute little marmoset, forget "oooh" or "awwww" or "ee-ee-ee." Try shhhh.
questions.answer:
1. black-tufted
2. scientists
3. encroachments
4. Scientists
5. studying
6. whatever

sense_groups.english: What does a bookworm have in common with a ______ marmoset?
sense_groups.chinese: 书虫和______狨猴有什么共同点？

sense_groups.english: They both like a little quiet.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们都喜欢安静一点。

sense_groups.english: Or so say ______ in the Royal Society journal Biology Letters.
sense_groups.chinese: 或者至少______在《皇家学会期刊·生物学快报》上是这么说的。

sense_groups.english: As urban areas continue to expand, their human inhabitants spread all sorts of pollution: air pollution, light pollution, even noise pollution.
sense_groups.chinese: 随着城市地区不断扩张，人类居民传播了各种污染：空气污染、光污染，甚至噪音污染。

sense_groups.english: Each of these environmental ______ affects the survival and behavior of local wildlife.
sense_groups.chinese: 这些环境______中的每一种都会影响当地野生动物的生存和行为。

sense_groups.english: And monkeys are no exception.
sense_groups.chinese: 猴子也不例外。

sense_groups.english: ______ in Brazil were ______ how marmosets in a city park cope with ambient noise.
sense_groups.chinese: 巴西的______正在______城市公园里的狨猴如何应对环境噪音。

sense_groups.english: And they found that the monkeys tend to settle down in ______ part of the park is most quiet.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现这些猴子倾向于在公园里最安静的______部分安顿下来。

sense_groups.english: On weekdays, the marmosets steered clear of the roar of traffic, and on Sundays they shunned the clamor of visiting crowds.
sense_groups.chinese: 在工作日，狨猴避开交通的轰鸣声；在周日，它们躲避参观人群的喧闹声。

sense_groups.english: They dodged all the din, even when moving meant that they had to leave behind the places that offered them the most food.
sense_groups.chinese: 它们躲避所有噪音，即使移动意味着它们必须离开那些提供最多食物的地方。

sense_groups.chinese: 不管怎样，下次你看到一只可爱的小狨猴时，忘掉“哦”、“啊”或“咿咿咿”，试试“嘘”。

questions.name: #211 Astronaut
questions.en:

When he was old enough to take flying lessons, Ford paid for them with money he earned bagging groceries.
Mission Specialist Jose ______ was born in California, into a family of migrant farm workers.

questions.name: #212 Bird Buffet
questions.en:
If you've ever been to an all-you-can-eat buffet, you know how ______ it is to carefully weigh your options.
You don't want to fill up on salad when so many calorie-laden ______ await.
It seems some birds also weigh their mealtime choices—literally.
A study finds that Mexican Jays pick up and shake peanuts to assess their relative heft before choosing one.
That report is served up in the Journal of Ornithology.
Foods that hide their edible bits on the inside present a challenge to hungry diners.
How can you tell which fruits are ripe or which shells harbor the biggest nuts?
We humans knock on melons or squeeze avocados.
But how do other species select the highest quality snacks?
To find out how the jays do it, ______ fiddled with their feed.
First they ______ peanuts so that some ______ three nuts while others had none.
When they offered these pods to some jays, the birds turned their beaks up at the empty shells and instead chose those that were full.
And when the jays were allowed to choose between normal peanuts and those that weighed just one gram more, because the researchers had stuffed them with clay, the birds again went for the heavier meal.
Videos ______ that the jays shake the nuts before selecting one, which apparently lets them gauge the nut's mass and perhaps also listen for the rattle of a well-packed shell.
Pretty clever for a bird brain.

2. delights
3. researchers
4. doctored
5. contained
6. revealed

questions.name: #213 Eating Background
questions.en:
In lab tests, music and lighting can affect how much people eat.
Now a study has found that changing the ambiance of a fast food restaurant to more of a fine-dining atmosphere lessened the amount of food people crammed into their pie holes.
To quote the paper, "softening the lighting and music led people to eat less, to rate the food as more enjoyable, and to spend just as much."
That last finding means that fast food joints, which are accused of ______ to the obesity epidemic, might ______ try it.
The study was led by well-known eating behaviorist Brian Wansink from Cornell University and appears in the journal Psychological Reports.
The researchers ______ part of a Hardee's so that it had soft lighting and slow jazz instrumentals.
The patrons were expected to possibly eat more in the relaxed section, because they'd linger, maybe get dessert.
But they actually averaged 18 percent fewer ______ per meal than the folks in the rowdy section—down from an average of 949 calories to 775.
The overall experience appears to have been a more satisfying meal.
Even if there was less of it.

questions.name: #214 Volcano and Electricity
questions.en:
Some ______ ______ ______ in the clouds of ash drifting around Europe as a result of that Icelandic volcano.
Models predicted that electrical charge should be limited to the top and bottom of any ash plume, which is often the site of spectacular lightning.
But info obtained by a weather balloon found significant electrical charge within the plume.
And that such charge was being generated within the plume—it wasn't a remnant of the energy of the volcanic eruption or a result of any local weather events.

The practical reason for understanding the electrical nature of ash plumes is that they can interfere with aircraft radio communication.
And if any charged ash infiltrates a plane, it could be an electrostatic hazard, to the plane's systems and to the plane's passengers.

questions.name: #215 Chameleons
questions.en:
Chameleons have it easy.
If they need to hide from a predator they just change their appearance, and disappear against whatever they happen to be standing on.
  ______ by leaves?
Turn green.
Tree trunk?
Brown it is.
But Aegean wall lizards have a different strategy.
They live on the Greek Islands.
And instead of changing their appearance, they find a safer spot.
That is, they're really good at picking out just the right ______ to ______ the chances that they'll be spotted by a hungry crow or raptor.
That's according to a new study in the journal Scientific Reports.
Birds can perceive both visible and ______ light, so researchers snapped regular and UV photos of lizards basking on rocks to figure out how the lizards look to birds.
The scientists discovered that the lizards' ______ is precisely tuned to avian eyeballs, helping them seem to disappear.
Lizards with darker backs hang out on darker rocks.
Lighter ones choose lighter rocks.
It's the first time that wild animals have been recorded explicitly choosing the best background to enhance their own camouflage.
Another observation: when lizards aren't under the constant threat of death, they're less picky.
"On the island with the lower risk this kind of background choice, to improve their level of camouflage, is much less evident than on the island with high predation risk."
University of Cambridge zoologist Kate Marshall, lead researcher of the study.
To pick out the right rocks, Aegean wall lizards must have an awareness of what color they are.
But how do they know?
"It's a big puzzle, and I'm fascinated by the answer.
Unfortunately, I don't know the answer yet, and hopefully this study will inspire future research into it."

questions.name: #218 Choir Practice
questions.en:
This isn't your typical choir practice.
And it's not held in a traditional practice space either.
These singers are all dealing with cancer, theirs or a loved one's. "There are people in our choirs who are undergoing ______ right now.
There are some people who are waiting for treatment." Rosie Dow leads the choir groups at Tenovus Cancer Care, in the U.K. "We do have some ______ ill patients as well in our choirs, so people in palliative care.
And then we also have people who've lost people to cancer.
So carers and supporters."
Anecdotally, chorus members have said that belting out tunes makes them feel good.
But Dow and her colleagues wanted to see if that psychological effect might ______ to a ______ effect.
So they selected five choir groups in Wales—with a total of 193 singers—and took saliva samples both before and after an hour of singing.
They found that singers had significantly lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol after the session than they'd had prior to choir.
Along with an increase in proteins called cytokines—which the ______ say might suggest a boost in immune activity.
The results are in the journal eCancer Medical Science.
Of course it's still not clear whether those biochemical changes translate to any better outcome for patients.
And choir practice is in addition to—not instead of—conventional treatments.
"Of course we wouldn't recommend it as an alternative to chemotherapy or radiotherapy or surgery or any of the other conventional cancer treatments, but in terms of people's mental health, this might be a good complement to the treatment that they're having."
Next up, the researchers will conduct a follow-up study at the U.K.'s biggest cancer center to see if these biological changes hold up over the long term.
After all, singing is certainly a cheap treatment.
And it does no harm, either…as long as you don't wail too hard.

sense_groups.english: This isn't your typical choir practice.
sense_groups.chinese: 这不是你典型的合唱团练习。

sense_groups.english: And it's not held in a traditional practice space either.

sense_groups.english: "There are people in our choirs who are undergoing treatment right now.
sense_groups.chinese: “我们的合唱团里有人正在接受治疗。

sense_groups.english: There are some people who are waiting for treatment."
sense_groups.chinese: 有些人正在等待治疗。”

sense_groups.english: Rosie Dow leads the choir groups at Tenovus Cancer Care, in the U.K.
sense_groups.chinese: 罗西·道在英国Tenovus癌症护理中心领导合唱团。

sense_groups.english: "We do have some terminally ill patients as well in our choirs, so people in palliative care.
sense_groups.chinese: “我们的合唱团里确实也有一些绝症患者，也就是接受姑息治疗的人。

sense_groups.english: And then we also have people who've lost people to cancer.
sense_groups.chinese: 然后还有因癌症失去亲人的人。

sense_groups.english: So carers and supporters."
sense_groups.chinese: 所以还有护理者和支持者。”

sense_groups.chinese: 据传闻，合唱团成员说大声唱歌让他们感觉良好。

sense_groups.english: But Dow and her colleagues wanted to see if that psychological effect might translate to a biological effect.
sense_groups.chinese: 但道和她的同事想看看这种心理效应是否可能转化为生理效应。

sense_groups.english: So they selected five choir groups in Wales—with a total of 193 singers—and took saliva samples both before and after an hour of singing.
sense_groups.chinese: 于是他们选择了威尔士的五个合唱团——共有193名歌手——并在唱歌一小时前后采集了唾液样本。

sense_groups.english: They found that singers had significantly lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol after the session than they'd had prior to choir.
sense_groups.chinese: 他们发现，歌手在唱歌后的压力激素皮质醇水平显著低于唱歌前。

sense_groups.english: Along with an increase in proteins called cytokines—which the researchers say might suggest a boost in immune activity.
sense_groups.chinese: 同时一种叫做细胞因子的蛋白质增加——研究人员说这可能表明免疫活动增强。

sense_groups.english: The results are in the journal eCancer Medical Science.
sense_groups.chinese: 研究结果发表在《eCancer医学科学》期刊上。

sense_groups.english: Of course it's still not clear whether those biochemical changes translate to any better outcome for patients.
sense_groups.chinese: 当然，目前还不清楚这些生化变化是否会给患者带来更好的结果。

sense_groups.english: And choir practice is in addition to—not instead of—conventional treatments.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且合唱练习是常规治疗的补充，而不是替代。

sense_groups.english: "Of course we wouldn't recommend it as an alternative to chemotherapy or radiotherapy or surgery or any of the other conventional cancer treatments, but in terms of people's mental health, this might be a good complement to the treatment that they're having."
sense_groups.chinese: “当然，我们不建议用它替代化疗、放疗、手术或其他任何常规癌症治疗，但就人们的心理健康而言，这可能是他们正在接受的治疗的一个很好的补充。”

sense_groups.english: Next up, the researchers will conduct a follow-up study at the U.K.'s biggest cancer center to see if these biological changes hold up over the long term.
sense_groups.chinese: 接下来，研究人员将在英国最大的癌症中心进行一项后续研究，看看这些生理变化是否长期持续。

sense_groups.english: After all, singing is certainly a cheap treatment.
sense_groups.chinese: 毕竟，唱歌当然是一种廉价的治疗方式。

sense_groups.english: And it does no harm, either…as long as you don't wail too hard.
sense_groups.chinese: 而且它也没有害处……只要你别唱得太用力。

questions.name: #219 Genetic Variation
questions.en:
As we look back at 2007, it's time to judge the best books, the best movies—and the best scientific discoveries. The prestigious journal Science came out with its "Breakthrough of the Year" in the trickster 20th edition. The conglomerate was the discovery that skin cells could be unsophisticated to behave like embryonic stem cells. The number one pick? Human genetic variation.
Scientists have been learning increasing amounts about how genes influence traits and diseases. At the same time, we hear about how little difference there is between us and our not-so-distant cousins, chimps and gorillas. But this year, researchers sequenced the genomes of thousands of individual people. They looked at dedications in short stretches of DNA called single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs. We each have millions of SNPs in our DNA. Scientists extracted how much we vary from one another on this basic level—crucial info for coughing everything from who gets diabetes to who's at risk for breast cancer to maybe even why I can't stand cilantro.
For more information on the breakthroughs of the year, go to sciencemag.org.

questions.name: #220 Camera
questions.en:
Cameras that catch drivers who blow through red lights are there to improve safety, by discouraging light running.
But such cameras actually increase the likelihood of car crashes.
Because more drivers jam on the breaks in an attempt to make a late stop at ______ camera intersections.
That's the finding of a study done by ______ at the University of South Florida College of Public Health.
They decided to look into the issue because Florida ______ are considering installing many more such cameras around the state.
The researchers contend that other studies ______ cameras with fewer crashes and ______ are flawed—those studies were linked with the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, an industry group.
But insurers may profit from red light cameras, because revenues go up with increased citations and accidents.
The new report notes that North Carolina, Virginia and Ontario all had increased crash rates and injuries associated with red light cameras.
In Florida, injuries related to red light running are down anyway.
So drivers needing to make a quick decision at a yellow light may be better off not seeing red.
